CaPITeN: Design and validation of an innovative methodology for thermal and visual comfort assessment in tropical climates
abstract: CaPITeN is a low-cost, field-ready platform designed to investigate thermo-visual comfort in tropical buildings under real operating conditions. It combines individualised physiological and subjective monitoring with time-synchronised environmental measurements, including thermal, visual, and hygro-aeraulic parameters, recorded on a common timeline. The platform follows a structured measurement protocol integrating pre-experimental sociodemographic and personality data, continuous physico-physiological monitoring, and repeated thermo-visual comfort assessments. A dual-storage strategy, combining cloud-based transmission and local backups, ensures robust data acquisition. CaPITeN was deployed in a naturally lit and ventilated university classroom, achieving over 99 % data completeness despite transient communication losses. Reliability tests showed mean absolute errors below 1 C for temperature, 0.25 m/s for air velocity, and 6 lx for illuminance. Used in this study for the time-resolved, in-situ analysis of coupled thermo-visual perceptions, CaPITeN relies on a modular, reproducible architecture that could readily be extended to investigate other sensory modalities. It therefore provides a robust methodological framework for multivariate comfort studies and the development of large-scale comfort databases adapted to tropical climates.

title: A helium-based surrogate method for thermal airflow in an idealized street canyon via CFD simulations
abstract: Understanding urban heat distribution and airflow is crucial for climate-resilient planning, yet laboratory studies of non-isothermal conditions remain scarce compared to isothermal investigations. Conventional heated-model wind tunnel experiments face limitations in simulating realistic urban thermal environments at reduced scales, as achieving proper thermal similarity requires impractically high temperatures that are difficult to maintain and may pose fire risks. To overcome these constraints, helium, a lifting gas with lower density than air, is proposed as a safer and cost-effective buoyancy surrogate for urban thermal airflow studies. In this study, a quantitative relationship between helium-based and heated-air models is established through preliminary theoretical scaling analysis. A practical correlation is proposed to predict equivalent air temperature based on helium fraction, offering a valuable tool for experimental design and interpretation. A series of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations was conducted for a street canyon model across wide-ranging flow and thermal conditions (0.7 ≤ Fr ≤ 17.3) to verify the validity of the helium-based method. Detailed comparisons of flow velocity and air temperature distributions between sub-scale models and full-scale protocols demonstrate the method effectiveness in capturing key urban airflow features, including flow patterns and heat distribution. The method shows promising performance for most cases at higher Froude numbers, while some limitations may arise at lower Froude numbers. These findings inform a practical experimental protocol for safer laboratory investigations of urban thermal flows and theoretical insights for further exploration of non-isothermal urban environment studies.

title: Beyond land surface temperature: Thermal spatial patterns of urban heat islands under transit-oriented development
Shading inequality and mean radiant temperature exposure in high-density tropical and subtropical urban areas: A Delhi–Singapore comparison
Comparative analysis of auditory and olfactory complaints: spatiotemporal patterns and multi-scale built environment drivers in urban fringes
abstract: Urban fringes in rapidly urbanizing regions face multisensory environmental challenges, where auditory and olfactory nuisances interact and impair resident well-being. This study developed a data-driven framework based on approximately 560,000 civic complaint records from Bao’an district, Shenzhen in 2024, integrating multi-level built environment factors to analyse auditory complaint rates (ACR) and olfactory complaint rates (OCR). Using the Qwen large language model for multi-label classification with population-standardised complaint rates per 10,000 residents as dependent variables. Spatial and temporal patterns were examined through Getis-Ord Gi* for hotspot/coldspot identification, dynamic time warping (DTW) for temporal similarity quantification, and spatial similarity assessment. Driving factors were modelled with geographically weighted random forest (GWRF), with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values and partial dependence plots (PDP) revealing nonlinear effects and spatial heterogeneity. Finally, government responses were contrasted with model-derived driver priorities to form a closed-loop validation. Results showed high similarity between auditory and olfactory complaints across diurnal and annual scales, with hotspots concentrated in southern mixed-function areas, though ACR hotspots were broader and more intense. Public function facilities contributed most strongly to both complaint types, while residential function, crowd attraction, and traffic flow exhibited positive nonlinear influences, with multiple variables displaying threshold and saturation effects. Government responses prioritise human activity optimisation yet deviated from model-identified functional facility optimisation priorities, while community management optimisation received greater policy attention than its actual driving strength warrants. This study established a multisensory comparative framework centred on urban fringes, achieving closed-loop validation of spatial and temporal dynamics, driving mechanisms, and policy responses. These insights provided targeted, threshold-based recommendations for multisensory urban governance and contributed to more human-centred urban planning.

title: A novel causal-Bayesian network modelling approach for urban heat vulnerability-mitigation assessment and forecasting
abstract: Heat vulnerability refers to the propensity of individuals and communities to be adversely affected by urban heat, shaped by exposure, built environment, and socio-economic conditions. As heatwaves intensify under climate change, understanding not only who is vulnerable but how vulnerability may change under different mitigation strategies has become critical for safeguarding public health, energy performance, and economic productivity. However, most existing studies rely on static, index-based assessments and lack the capacity to robustly forecast how vulnerability changes under interventions while representing the complex interactions across urban systems. To address this gap, this study proposes a causal-Bayesian network modelling approach to assess urban heat vulnerability and forecast its changes under alternative mitigation strategies. The framework integrates structured causal knowledge with probabilistic modelling through three core processes: causality-informed structure construction, hybrid parameter learning, and vulnerability assessment and forecasting through probability propagation. A neighbourhood-scale case study demonstrates the systematic workflow and confirms its practical feasibility using profile-based datasets. By linking real-world data, probabilistic inference, and expert-informed causal reasoning, the proposed modelling approach enables robust forecasting of vulnerability reduction by interventions and uncovers interconnected, cross-sector dynamics. This integrated modelling approach offers a practical and scalable analytical tool for forward-looking, policy-relevant urban planning in the context of urban overheating.

title: Layered and policy-driven thermal retrofit strategies for historic districts under extreme high temperature
Melanopic light exposure in urban built environments predicts sleep quality: Real-world evidence from wearable spectral monitoring
Climate-adaptive performance and energy-saving potential of thermochromic façade materials across China climatic zones
Comparative laboratory analysis of window sound insulation across glazing types in the 50–5000 Hz range: Evaluation of different low-frequency methods
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the sound insulation performance of windows by presenting laboratory measurements from 50 to 5000 Hz on two window types, with and without an integrated shutter box, each tested across five glazing configurations. While all measurements were conducted under controlled laboratory conditions, particular attention was given to the low-frequency range (50–100 Hz), where every measurement method available in the standard was applied. These included procedures based on the laboratory standard (ISO 10140), the in situ standard (ISO 16283), and a hybrid approach, all implemented within the laboratory setting. The results reveal that below 100 Hz, sound insulation values and differences between window types vary significantly depending on the measurement method. The in situ procedure, when applied only to the receiving room—as is common in façade assessments—yields the lowest insulation values and minimizes differentiation between window types, likely due to room modal effects. In contrast, applying the same procedure to both the source and receiving rooms produces results that more closely align with those obtained using laboratory standards. Furthermore, while the window without a shutter box generally provided higher insulation above 100 Hz, it exhibited a more pronounced reduction in insulation below 100 Hz under laboratory conditions, highlighting a potential source of low-frequency discomfort not reflected in standard manufacturer ratings. These findings underscore that low-frequency sound insulation ratings are highly dependent on the measurement approach, emphasizing the need to refine standardized protocols and enhance the reliability and perceptual relevance of acoustic descriptors in this frequency range.

Stock-scale scenario analysis of retrofit impacts on operational energy demand and carbon emissions in hotels across England and Wales
abstract: Hotels run almost nonstop, carry overlapping thermal and service loads, and therefore are important targets for operational energy and carbon reduction. This study builds a physics-based, building-by-building stock model for all hotels in England and Wales to compare predefined retrofit scenarios for operational energy and carbon. Each asset is represented using its geometry, construction era, future weather conditions, and percentage-based internal zoning, and dynamic simulations are then run from business as usual to combined retrofit packages. The baseline aligns with official totals within about 4 percent, providing a credible foundation. Heating drives the main gains. Fabric upgrades cut heating loads, and pairing fabric with high-efficiency electric systems produces the largest operational carbon reductions. Envelope-only strategies could potentially raise cooling demand, so effective scenarios combine envelope and systems. Under the projected 2050 electricity carbon factor and stock-scale building system performance assumptions, packages that electrify heat and improve cooling cut operational emissions by about 98 percent relative to the current stock. Residual emissions remain, so further reductions would depend on secure low-carbon electricity and flexible operation alongside retrofit. The results provide stock-scale comparative evidence that helps avoid cooling backfire and prioritise fabric plus electrification for reliable, scalable impact.

title: Indoor air pollution and direct second-hand exposure from single E-cigarette puff
A multi-criteria computational workflow for solar-driven urban district design
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper presents a solar-informed, multi-criteria computational workflow for shaping climate-responsive urban districts. Building on and extending the Solar Envelope principle towards a practical “Solar Envelope 2.0,” the method integrates simplified radiation-based and geometry-driven predictors within a multi-objective optimisation (MOO) framework to support district-scale evaluation of solar access, photovoltaic potential, energy demand, daylight availability, and outdoor thermal comfort. Tested on a redevelopment site in Holon, Israel, the workflow compares solid and voxelated morphologies, using solar-exposure metrics as the primary optimisation drivers. Results show that voxelated forms provide finer control of solar access and achieve higher PV potential and improved summer shading, while solid forms offer more stable seasonal behaviour and stronger contextual daylight performance. Detailed multi-domain simulation benchmarking indicates that the solar-based predictors support comparative evaluation of energy, daylight, and outdoor-comfort outcomes. Under future climatic conditions (2070, RCP 8.5), energy demand rises while solar availability remains broadly stable, demonstrating the robustness of the solar-based optimisation logic under climatic warming. The study establishes a scalable evaluation workflow for next-generation solar urban design, where solar radiation becomes the organising parameter for district morphology and a basis for balancing cross-domain environmental objectives. This contributes a computational pathway for solar-adaptive, climate-resilient urban form generation and early-stage decision support.

title: From field to wall: On-site ground corn-cob infill for low-cost passive thermal-comfort retrofits in rural cold-climate China
abstract: Ground corn-cob infill is evaluated as a low-cost wall retrofit strategy to improve thermal performance and assess building-level impact in rural dwellings in cold-climate China. Field measurements of indoor temperature and relative humidity were conducted in ten occupied households representing five household typologies during summer and winter. Median indoor temperatures were 29.8°C in summer and 5.5°C in winter, with only 1.3% of winter hours meeting the GB/T 18883-2022 comfort standard, indicating severe under-heating. The thermal transmittance of four wall configurations was determined using in-situ heat-flux measurements in accordance with ISO 9869-1. Ground corn-cob infill achieved the lowest U-value (0.981 W/(m²·K) under ΔT ≥ 10°C), representing a 46.6% reduction relative to an unfilled hollow-brick wall. Measured U-values were implemented in calibrated building performance simulation models to assess envelope-only retrofit scenarios. Under free-running conditions, none of the configurations met the national winter comfort standard. However, when evaluated against a locally derived comfort range (9.9–17.5°C), the addition of a corn-cob-infilled outer layer increased winter comfort duration by up to 197 hours in multi-generational households. No improvement in summer comfort was observed under sealed conditions due to reduced nocturnal heat dissipation. The results demonstrate that finely processed corn-cob infill can substantially reduce wall heat loss and improve winter thermal conditions in low-income rural housing. However, its effectiveness is seasonally dependent and requires integration with ventilation strategies to address summer performance. The proposed retrofit offers a scalable, low-cost solution for energy-poor rural contexts using locally available agricultural residues.

title: Person-to-person airborne transmission and exposure characterized with surrogates in high-speed train environments
Effects of inflow turbulence conditions on velocity and temperature fields around building arrays under unstable conditions
A full-scale hybrid acoustic meta-enclosure enabling natural ventilation
Airborne infection risk between patients and healthcare staff under different air distribution strategies: A test chamber study
abstract: ABSTRACT Healthcare-associated infections have increased across European hospitals in recent years, raising attention to indoor air quality in healthcare environments. This chamber study investigates strategies to reduce airborne infection risk between patients and healthcare staff in a simulated double-bed patient room by examining the effects of heat gain, airflow rate, air distribution, infector location, and curtain position. Three air distribution methods were evaluated: mixing ventilation (MV), occupant-targeted ventilation (OTV), and wall attachment ventilation (ATT). Virus-laden aerosols were simulated using sulfur hexafluoride (SF 6 ) released from a thermal breathing manikin. When the infector was a patient, ATT maintained lower mean concentrations than MV at 40 L/s, whereas the performance of OTV was limited on the near-field side due to spatial constraints. The average contaminant removal effectiveness (CRE) with ATT on the infected side was 42.7% higher than that with MV at 17 W/m² and 80 L/s. However, ATT was sensitive to diffuser location, with the lowest CRE observed on the exposed side. When the infector was a staff member, notable concentration fluctuations were observed with ATT on the near-field side, whereas OTV significantly improved dilution effectiveness at 80 L/s. Increasing airflow from 40 L/s to 80 L/s reduced infection probability in the exposed area, with 8 of 12 tests achieving ≥50.0% reduction across the different ventilation configurations. Overall, the findings support the optimized selection of local air distribution systems for practical application and provide insights into improving microenvironmental safety in complex healthcare scenarios.

title: Multimodal evaluation of rural landscape ergonomics based on light and shadow temporal experience—a case study of Huizhou Area, China
Microplastics emissions from residential space floorings under thermal and friction aging: Evaluating indoor air quality improvement performance of biomaterial flooring
A dynamic thermal comfort model for energy flexibility in buildings with open-source implementation

From short-term thermal–humidity interventions to enthalpy–humidity path optimization in elderly women with osteoarthritis
A practical engineering method to map microclimate-driven degradation risks on building façades
abstract: Assessing moisture-induced degradation risks across façades typically relies on Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to resolve wind-driven rain (WDR) distribution and spatially varying microclimate conditions. This paper presents an alternative engineering-based methodology combining semi-empirical WDR models with detailed solar irradiation analysis to derive spatially varying boundary conditions for hygrothermal simulations. Freeze-thaw performance indicators are then used to estimate degradation risks, enabling spatial mapping of façade vulnerability. The methodology is demonstrated on a brick façade in Gothenburg, Sweden, where degradation had been previously documented across 104 façade sections. Two WDR models—ISO 15927-3:2009 and Straube-Burnett (SB)—were applied over a 31-year simulation period. The ISO model at a 75% relative humidity (RH) threshold—used as the criterion for counting freeze-thaw cycles—showed the strongest agreement with observed degradation patterns (PCC = 0.6). The SB model required a higher RH threshold (90%) to achieve moderate agreement (PCC = 0.32). These differences highlight how RH thresholds act as compensating parameters for differences in modeled moisture load rather than direct indicators of critical saturation. Similar correlation levels were obtained with a second brick type, using 85% RH thresholds for both models, indicating that façade microclimate, rather than material properties, dominates the spatial distribution of degradation. The results show that the proposed methodology can reproduce key spatial patterns of degradation risk without CFD, although the absolute risk quantification remains limited. The methodology offers designers, consultants, and building owners a cost‑efficient basis for prioritizing inspections, maintenance planning, and retrofit strategies by identifying the most microclimate-vulnerable façade sections.

title: Temporal evolution of nocturnal thermal comfort for healthcare workers based on field evidence
Rain garden reimagined: A computational approach to urban water retention and infiltration
abstract: Rain gardens, as Nature-based Solutions are becoming increasingly implemented in cities. Although the use of rain gardens is increasing, there needs to be more knowledge about their retention and infiltration abilities. In recent years various researchers have attempted to test hydrological performance using available tools and scale. Many physically-based models have been constructed to simulate the rain garden performance. However, some of these models have used limited data to establish the relationship between environmental indicators and predict the performance of rain gardens. The purpose of this study was to develop machine learning models to predict whether a ground-based rain garden will retain runoff (binary classification: Yes/No) under varying rainfall and environmental conditions, in a field experiment, in Wrocław (Poland). Information on rainfall quantity and duration, substrate moisture in the rain garden, water retention time and its level, and air thermal and humidity conditions were used as input data for the model. To address the limitations of current models, advanced machine learning techniques are proposed to enhance the prediction and analysis of rain garden performance. The study focuses on employing Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN). Rain garden retention was found to be closely related to total rainfall, rainfall intensity and duration. Saturation deficit at 1 p.m. and 7 a.m. showed moderate predictive value. Within the analysed models, the ANN and Logistic Regression models achieved the highest accuracy (99.0%), closely followed by Decision Trees (98.5%), with SVM demonstrating slightly lower performance (94.1%).

title: The inpatient exposome in neurorehabilitation wards: a systematic review of indoor environmental exposures and patient-centered outcomes
abstract: Background Inpatient neurorehabilitation is delivered in wards where indoor environmental exposures may influence sleep, arousal, mobility, wayfinding and engagement outside therapy sessions. Objective To synthesize evidence on modifiable ward- or facility-level indoor exposures (the inpatient exposome) and patient-centered outcomes in neurological inpatients, with domain-specific validity appraisal. Methods We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Embase, EBSCOhost and Scopus from inception to 28 Oct 2025. Eligible studies quantified measurable, modifiable indoor exposures independent of therapy content and reported patient-level outcomes. Two reviewers screened studies and extracted data. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, ROBINS-I and ROBINS-E; certainty per exposure-outcome pairing was assessed using a GRADE-informed approach. Results Thirty studies addressed light/circadian lighting, sound/noise, spatial layout and legibility, enrichment/communal communication spaces, nocturnal ward ecology, and thermal/indoor air quality as an a priori gap domain. Circadian-supportive lighting and structured nocturnal noise/care approaches showed the clearest signals for sleep quality, fatigue or perceived energy. Architectural configuration, spatial legibility and functional walking space were associated with out-of-bed behaviour, lower prolonged sedentary time and higher light-intensity physical activity; no consistent association emerged with moderate-to-vigorous activity. Enriched and communicative environments increased meaningful physical, cognitive and social engagement. Downstream functional recovery, discharge readiness and long-term outcomes remained heterogeneous and uncertain. Overall certainty was moderate for a small number of proximal comparisons and low or very low for most pairings because of confounding, exposure misclassification and outcome heterogeneity. Conclusions Ward ecology is a modifiable co-determinant of sleep, activity and participation in inpatient neurorehabilitation, but current evidence should not be interpreted as strong causal proof for downstream functional benefit. Pragmatic multicenter studies with objective exposure measurement, fidelity metrics and standardized outcomes are needed to inform scalable ward interventions and design standards.

title: Complex urban surface mitigates the impact of intra-urban heat effect on vegetation phenology
A novel low-resistance cylindrical annular vent plenum chamber with uniform outflow designed via three-dimensional flow topology optimization
Explainable machine learning-based study on the applicability of thermal indicators for university classrooms in summer
A review of research on multi-stakeholder approaches to sustainable built environments
abstract: To effectively deal with the role of the built environment regarding global challenges such as energy transition, climate change, and communal resilience, multiple stakeholders must collaborate in a complex spatio-temporal context. These include buildings’ users, planners and engineers, policy makers, as well as experts from fields such as psychology, sociology, and economics. Given the complexity of the challenges and the multiplicity of the agents involved, mono-dimensional (e.g., technology-centric) approaches are unlikely to yield optimal solutions. The relevance of this assertion is further supported by the observation that, whilst challenges such as climate change and energy transition have a global nature, the decision scope of local agents are limited. In this context, the present contribution entails a systematic review, following the PRISMA framework, of recent scientific literature regarding multi-stakeholder approaches to sustainability-oriented interventions in the built environments. After a multi-step identification and screening process, 84 peer-reviewed publications were selected for an in-depth review. The results of the review include key characteristics of stakeholders’ roles and involvement, as well as methods and tools of collaboration. A central finding pertains to the underrepresentation of those stakeholders who are not directly responsible for technical project execution (including occupants, financial consultants, public interest groups) but are rather viewed as consultants. As such, the decision authority lies predominantly with professional actors. Furthermore, the review shows weak formalization of decision-making logic. Moreover, the review highlights lessons learnt from past initiatives in this area and potential implications for future multi-stakeholder strategies for designing and operating sustainable built environments.

title: A numerical framework to evaluate the impact of HEPA filtration on classroom air quality
abstract: This paper presents a CFD-based framework to assess classroom air quality with portable HEPA filtration, explicitly resolving the interaction between filter-induced airflow and realistic human exhalation of CO 2 and aerosols. Unlike existing approaches, the framework captures spatially resolved contaminant transport and removal under occupied conditions and is complemented by a statistical method to quantify contaminant dispersion dynamics and local airflow mixing intensity. The model is validated against in situ measurements of CO 2 and aerosol concentrations (0.7–1 μ m ) in a classroom under matched scenarios with one and three HEPA units, alongside a stale-air baseline, showing good agreement. Results demonstrate that HEPA filtration significantly alters airflow by enhancing mixing and suppressing occupant thermal plumes, leading to a more spatially uniform CO 2 distribution despite largely unchanged mean concentrations. In situ measurements indicate aerosol reductions of approximately 21% for a single HEPA unit and up to 90% for a three-HEPA configuration. While, the CFD results and statistical analysis reveal that, although increasing the number of units improves aerosol removal through higher CADR, the removal performance remains strongly dependent on filter placement relative to the emission source. This is evident as single-HEPA configurations are highly sensitive to placement and may promote contaminant dispersion through discharge airflow, whereas multi-unit configurations provide more robust control when the filter intake is aligned with the emission source. These findings highlight the critical role of filter number and placement and demonstrate the limitations of CO 2 as a proxy for aerosol exposure in HEPA-filtered classrooms.

title: A network theory tool for evaluating synergies and conflicts among resilience strategies for buildings in early decision making
abstract: Buildings function within interconnected urban systems where resilience strategies can synergize or conflict. Understanding these interactions is essential for early-stage decision-making but remains underexplored. This study develops a network-based decision-support tool to evaluate and optimize building-level resilience strategies in cold climates (Köppen Dfb) based on their synergies and conflicts, informing prefeasibility studies. Strategies and their interactions are identified through relevant literature and represented as weighted, undirected adjacency matrices. Synergy and conflict networks are analyzed using centrality metrics—weighted degree ( WD ), betweenness ( B ), harmonic closeness ( HC ), and eigenvector ( E )—interpreted as reach, bridging, catalysis, and influence to support intuitive use. Composite synergies (Syn) and conflicts (Con) are calculated. Results show that renewable energy systems of photovoltaics, Trombe walls, envelope insulation, high window-to-wall ratios, and heat pumps exhibit strong synergistic potential. In contrast, compact buildings, vertical greening systems, and highly airtight envelopes demonstrate higher conflict tendencies despite their benefits. Heat pumps and smart building operation systems achieve the highest net synergies. Findings also highlight key trade-offs, where the same strategies both synergize and conflict, emphasizing the importance of coordinated strategy selection. Application to a case study in West 5 neighborhood, Ontario, demonstrates that adding strategies to the existing resilience system can increase overall synergies while maintaining manageable conflict levels. Multi-objective optimization and Pareto analysis support prioritization and sequencing. Sensitivity analysis reveals optimal strategy selection converge around similar strategies with some dependence on objectives (synergy-focused or conflict-focused). The tool enables systematic evaluation, scenario testing, and evidence-based prioritization for early-stage resilience planning.

title: A prognostic HVAC model for multi-physics urban simulations
How can building retrofits adapt to climate change? A framework integrating future climate scenario, interpretable machine learning, and multi-objective optimization
Pulsating impinging jet ventilation combined with a constructal radiation floor cooling system to improve comfort and indoor air quality
Objective measurements and subjective assessments of home and office work environment after the COVID-19 pandemic: A TELEWORK study in Japan
abstract: (max 250 words) The rapid expansion of working-from-home (WFH) practices during the COVID-19 pandemic led to the application of office environmental standards (18–28°C for indoor temperature, 40–70% for relative humidity, and ≥300 lx for desk illuminance) to home workspaces in Japan. However, actual environmental conditions at home remain largely unverified. This study aimed to clarify indoor environmental quality (IEQ) of home workspaces and their relationship with subjective perceptions. We evaluated IEQ across temperature, relative humidity, and desk illuminance using objective measurements and subjective evaluations, involving 171 teleworkers from six companies. Measurements were conducted from April to August 2024 both at home and in the office. While nearly all office environments met standards, 19.3% of participants experienced temperature, 2.9% humidity, and 80.1% illuminance levels outside the recommended ranges at home. Nonetheless, many participants still reported satisfaction with their home lighting environment despite having a median illuminance of only 125 lx, revealing a substantial mismatch between subjective and objective assessments. Moreover, satisfaction with lighting was not correlated with overall environmental satisfaction, suggesting that lighting quality is a low priority for teleworkers. This underscores the importance of objective assessments in domains like lighting, where subjective evaluations may not accurately capture inadequate conditions. Notably, participants who made efforts to ensure comfortable desk illuminance had significantly higher illuminance than those who did not. This finding demonstrates that even simple self-reported efforts may be associated with observable improvements. Therefore, objectively understanding WFH environment is a crucial first step toward creating healthier and more productive spaces.

title: Utilizing advanced energy sharing approaches to enhance the coastal zero-emission building resilience with the mitigation of ocean impact
The climate impact of office-to-residential adaptive reuse: A Swedish case study
abstract: Sweden faces persistent affordable housing shortages while simultaneously experiencing elevated office vacancy rates. Given that the building sector accounts for roughly one third of global energy demand and two fifths of energy-related greenhouse gas emissions, adaptive reuse presents a promising strategy for mitigating emissions while addressing housing needs. This study investigated the greenhouse gas emissions associated with adapting a Swedish office building to residential use. It examined how the global warming potential of the energy mix and the anticipated extension of service life influences the level of renovation and reconstruction required to minimize these emissions, in comparison with continued office use and replacement with a new residential building. Emissions were calculated using the Swedish life cycle assessment framework, modified to account for avoided emissions through retention, and operational emissions estimated from energy simulations using the IDA ICE (EQUA®) software. The results showed that adaptive reuse could be a climate‑effective strategy for extending a building’s functional lifespan, causing as little as 26% of the embodied emissions of new construction. When operational emissions over the service life were included, the adapted building caused between 47% and 74% of the emissions of a new residential building, depending on its assumed service life. However, the study also demonstrated that each adaptive‑reuse scenario must be evaluated individually, as required interventions and performance improvements vary significantly. Ensuring environmental benefit over the building’s extended service life should remain the central objective.

title: Low-carbon and resilient innovation in traditional biomass fire-pit heating: coupling residual heat with natural ventilation to enhance nighttime thermal comfort
Reassessing evidence and policy claims in Coulburn et al. (2026) on Mould, Insurance and regulation
Urban vitality under extreme heat and energy infrastructure expansion: Evidence from Austin and Phoenix, USA
Microclimate design: cool pocket networks as a sustainable local outdoor comfort strategy
Cognitive workload evaluation using skin temperature variations in thermoneutral indoor environments
Summer thermal heterogeneity and overheating risk among older adults in elderly care facilities in the severe cold region of China
Wind-driven natural ventilation of cube-shaped buildings: The effects of roof design and wind direction
abstract: The effect of roof design on wind-driven natural ventilation of cube-shaped buildings was studied experimentally in a boundary-layer wind tunnel. The focus was on gable and single-pitched roofs and the flow incidence angle ( β ) in single-sided and cross ventilation of a model subjected to a modeled rural atmospheric boundary layer. Natural ventilation was quantified by the air change rate (ACH) based on tracer gas measurements. For the single-sided ventilation cases, the maximum occurred for the single-pitched roof with the roof pitch at β = 270°. For the cross-ventilation cases, the maximum was achieved for the single-pitched roof with the roof pitch at β = 90°. The ACH was up to 20 times higher for cross‐ventilation cases than for single‐sided ventilation. In general, β and the ventilation type have a more pronounced effect on the ACH than the roof design. The maximum difference in the ACH due to various roof types was 41%, which was observed in cross ventilation at β = 75°. In single-sided ventilation, pitched-roof buildings outperformed the flat-roof building model at most β , except at β = 0°, 15°, 75°, and 90°. In cross ventilation, pitched-roof building models are characterized by higher ACH than flat-roofed building models for 0° < β < 30°. For β close to 90°, the ACH was higher for the flat-roof than for the pitched-roof building model. Design curves for the ACH relative to β are proposed for all roof types to be used as a reference for estimating ventilation trends under the investigated conditions.

title: A hierarchical machine learning framework for real-time reconstruction of urban wind fields from sparse sensor networks
abstract: Real-time urban wind-field awareness is increasingly needed for structural health monitoring and digital-twin applications, yet high-fidelity CFD/LES and wind-tunnel testing remain too computationally intensive or scenario-specific for operational use, while field measurements provide only sparse information. This paper presents a sensor-driven hierarchical reconstruction framework for estimating time-resolved, high-resolution wind fields from constrained sensor networks. Unlike conventional single-stage approaches, which become ineffective when the resolution gap between sparse measurements and the target flow field is large, the proposed hierarchical formulation addresses the ill-conditioned nature of sparse-to-full-field reconstruction by replacing a single difficult inversion with successive coarse-to-fine mappings. This strategy promotes stable learning of multi-scale urban flow structures, improves reconstruction fidelity, and enables accurate real-time wind-field reconstruction under practical sensor constraints. The approach combines (i) progressive coarse-to-fine enrichment through intermediate resolution levels to avoid a single ill-conditioned sparse-to-high-resolution mapping, (ii) reduced-order learning in a Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) coefficient space at each hierarchical level, thereby reducing dimensionality and improving learning tractability, (iii) LSTM-based temporal modeling to capture unsteady dynamics, and (iv) a constrained-aware sensor-placement strategy that integrates practical deployment considerations with QR pivoting on retained POD modes. The framework is evaluated on a three-dimensional half-cylinder benchmark spanning multiple Reynolds numbers and vertical planes, and on a large-eddy-simulation dataset of a real urban district (Niigata, Japan) under multiple heights and inflow wind directions. The results demonstrate accurate recovery of dominant spatial structures and temporal dynamics, with robust generalization to unseen conditions including an unseen Reynolds number, held-out height levels, and unseen temporal segments under different inflow directions. The framework consistently achieves high reconstruction accuracy across all evaluated protocols, supporting near-real-time operations under practical sensor constraints.

title: Comparative study on energy-saving performance of outdoor-air and indoor-air circulation ventilation modes in industrial buildings
How to evaluate indoor radon using consumer-grade devices?
abstract: This short paper discusses the challenges posed by the Internet of Things (IoT) in indoor radon measurements. Until 2010, most radon measurements were carried out using passive dosimeters exposed over long-term periods (more than one month). However, this paradigm began to change in the 2010s, with the increasing availability of electronic radon devices enabling real-time monitoring for a wider population. Although this development has made radon more visible and better known to the public, it is important to note that significant performance differences exist among radon real-time measurement devices. These differences are notably related to the device brand, detection technique, and cost. This paper provides an overview of several intercomparison studies of radon measurement devices, which highlights the influence of environmental conditions, radon concentration levels, technologies used in the devices, as well as their long-term performance, on real-time radon devices’ performances.

title: 3D high resolution urban microclimate reconstruction and sensor placement optimization based on diffusion-based deep learning
abstract: 3D high resolution urban microclimate is essential for optimizing sustainable city design and operation, pedestrian thermal and wind comfort, and district-scale energy resilience. However, real-world microclimate sensing is limited by sparse measurements, and high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations are computationally expensive. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a hierarchical generative-refinement (HGR) framework for urban microclimate modeling with limited computing resources. In Step 1, an initial diffusion-based generative model is trained to predict low-resolution flow and temperature fields, which is enhanced through maximum a posterior gradient ascent (MAP-GA) to incorporate sparse measurements as conditional constraints. To enable a more efficient and explainable selection of locations for measurements (virtual measurements) in MAP-GA, a spatiotemporal variability analysis combined with SHAP-based sensitivity evaluation is conducted. In Step 2, a CNN-based model refines the low-resolution predictions in Step 1 into high-resolution microclimate fields by integrating urban morphology information, allowing the model to reconstruct fine-scale circulation patterns around complex urban geometries. On a 4 m × 4 m resolution dataset, the proposed framework achieves reconstruction errors on unseen test dataset (RMSEs) of 0.32 m/s, 0.28 m/s, 0.34 m/s, and 0.41°C for U, V, W, and T, respectively, while requiring approximately 90-120 seconds of computation. The results demonstrate that, for the tested Montréal heat-wave case, the HGR framework can efficiently reproduce high-resolution microclimate fields from limited measurements, supporting its potential for fast urban microclimate reconstruction.

title: Dynamic simulation and control strategy for particulate matter in subway stations by moving overset grid method
Beyond air change rates: Optimizing near-source extraction to eliminate recirculation zones in negative-pressure ambulances
Review of cross-modal and combined effects in real-world multi-domain outdoor environment on human responses
An investigation into winter thermal comfort of adolescents under chronic psychological stress
abstract: ABSTRACT Chinese adolescents often experience chronic psychological stress from academic pressure. Stress affects thermal comfort, but its effect on adolescents is unclear. This paper investigates this relationship and proposes changes to PMV (Predicted Mean Vote) models to improve predictions of the thermal comfort of adolescents. Surveys and environmental measurements were conducted in winter classrooms in China's Hot Summer and Cold Winter (HSCW) zone. Over 1,300 students aged 10–18 years participated. Main findings: (1) Based on TSV (Thermal Sensation Vote), thermal neutral temperature was 16.7 °C (thermal comfort range was 13.8–19.6 °C); mean clothing insulation was 1.5 clo, higher than ASHRAE's 1.0 clo. (2) PMV overestimated neutral temperature by 1.8 °C, even after correcting for adolescent metabolic rate. (3) Psychological stress raised neutral temperature: 15.9 °C (low stress), 16.7 °C (medium stress), 17.6 °C (high stress). Thermal comfort range narrowed with increasing stress. (4) A new PMV-based model including stress and adolescent metabolic rate better predicted thermal comfort. (5) Neutral temperature increased with age: 16.1 °C (primary), 16.8 °C (junior high), 18.2 °C (senior high). Based on lower comfort limits, heating design temperatures for primary, junior high, and senior high classrooms are 13.4 °C, 15.2 °C, and 15.0 °C. (6) Middle adolescents (13–15 years) were most temperature-sensitive; females felt colder, with a neutral temperature 0.7 °C higher than males. This study provides evidence for the selection of suitable heating temperatures for the design and operation of classrooms for adolescents during cold seasons.

title: Assessing thermal comfort and heat strain in multilayer chemical protective clothing under varied environmental conditions
Extreme heat reshapes urban green space vitality: Dynamic response typologies, nonlinear built-environment associations, and configuration patterns in Nanjing
abstract: Urban green spaces (UGS) are critical for climate adaptation, yet it remains unclear how different UGS change their vitality under extreme heat relative to optimal-temperature conditions and how such changes are associated with nonlinear built-environment relationships. Using Nanjing as a case study, this study combined PCA–GMM clustering and XGBoost–SHAP explainable machine learning to identify dynamic response typologies from EH–OT 48-hour vitality-difference curves and compare the importance, nonlinear thresholds, marginal effects, and configuration patterns of built-environment features across scenario–day-type subsets and dynamic response typologies. Compared with the OT scenario, overall UGS vitality under the EH scenario was 20.38% lower, but the relative changes varied substantially across UGS. Two dynamic response typologies were identified: Heat-Enhanced Dominant and Heat-Inhibited Dominant UGS. Area showed the highest importance in most scenarios, with its importance ranging from 11.4% to 47.1%. Feature-importance reconfiguration was more pronounced in Heat-Enhanced Dominant UGS under the EH scenario, whereas Heat-Inhibited Dominant UGS showed a more stable importance structure. Single-feature nonlinear trends were generally consistent, whereas typological differences were clearer in multi-feature configurations. For example, Heat-Enhanced Dominant UGS were more often associated with high NDVI (0.47–0.70) and high population density (3.53–26.12), whereas Heat-Inhibited Dominant UGS were more often linked to low population density (0–2.12) and high SVF (0.61–0.68). These findings suggest that changes in UGS vitality under extreme heat should be understood through EH–OT dynamic response typologies, nonlinear threshold shifts, and built-environment configuration patterns. This study provides empirical evidence for type-specific and climate-adaptive UGS planning under increasingly frequent extreme heat.

title: Towards a unified framework for a simulation-based integrative lighting evaluation: A scoping review of procedures applied in educational environments
abstract: Today, lighting design in educational environments is required to address both visual and non-visual needs of users, adhering to the concept of the integrative light. In doing so, it is also fundamental to complement daylight and electric light. However, designers face significant practical difficulties due to fragmented international standards (which consider diverse aspects in isolation) and the variety of simulation software at their disposal, which often yield non-comparable results. These difficulties underscore the lack of a unified framework for lighting condition evaluation. This paper serves as a propaedeutic step for its definition, presenting a scoping review to identify current shared simulation-based procedures to evaluate visual and circadian responses due to both daylight and electric light in educational environments. A literature search was performed in the Scopus and Web of Science databases, selecting 19 contributions. Their analysis demonstrates methodological trends and gaps as well. While work plane illuminance is commonly used to quantify light levels for visual comfort, melanopic Equivalent Daylight Illuminance emerges as the main metric for circadian entrainment evaluation. Reference planes’ height is almost consistent between reviewed studies (70 cm–80 cm for visual tasks and 120 cm for non-visual effects), yet the number and placement of calculation points over the reference plane and view directions vary depending on the study. Glare is an under-researched aspect, and, when considered, different approaches are used. As regards daylight, some of the reviewed papers chose a dynamic approach, while others use a static one, without consensus on the simulation schedule to consider.

title: Rethinking pilotis in multi-family housing: Winter thermal comfort implications—A case study of Minamisuna Danchi, Tokyo
abstract: Against the intensification of global warming and the urban heat island effect, adaptive strategies for urban Multi-Family Housing have attracted growing attention. Among them, the pilotis configuration has been widely adopted in high-density residential environments because of its potential to promote ventilation, provide shading, and enhance spatial openness in summer. However, its winter performance in terms of microclimate and thermal comfort remains insufficiently understood, especially in cold regions where background wind conditions play a significant role. Taking Minamisuna Danchi in Koto Ward, Tokyo, as a representative case, this study employed ENVI-met simulations to evaluate the winter effects of the pilotis configuration under two winter background wind conditions, namely no-wind and windy conditions, from both pedestrian-level and vertical perspectives. Results show that the pilotis configuration produced clear winter microclimatic drawbacks and thermal comfort deterioration. At the pedestrian level, air temperature changed only slightly, increasing under no-wind conditions and decreasing under windy conditions, whereas wind speed increased under both conditions. This combination of limited warming and enhanced wind did not improve thermal comfort; instead, it expanded colder thermal sensations and concentrated them during frequently used daytime periods. Vertical analysis further showed that temperature effects were mainly confined to lower heights, whereas wind-speed effects extended throughout the full height range and were amplified under windy conditions. Overall, the pilotis configuration in winter entails clear microclimatic and thermal comfort costs. This warns against assuming its applicability a priori, and indicates that its use should be carefully weighed against specific climatic conditions.

title: From black to radiative cooling: How fabric radiative properties shape outdoor thermal comfort and heat strain under extreme conditions
Revealing the gaps in multi-domain comfort control: A relationship-graph approach based on a systematic review
abstract: Multi-domain indoor environmental quality (IEQ) control has emerged as a promising approach for balancing occupant comfort and building energy use (BEU). However, the absence of a clear conceptual structure for defining and evaluating such systems has led to inconsistent formulations and limited comparability across studies. This study examines existing approaches and assesses their alignment with a newly developed conceptual structure for multi-domain control. A systematic review was conducted using the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) methodology guided by the CIMO (Context–Intervention–Mechanism–Outcome) logic. An initial identification of 972 studies addressing control strategies across multiple IEQ domains and BEU was identified, from which 125 studies were retained following screening and eligibility assessment. The analysis shows that only 15 studies explicitly integrate more than one IEQ domain with BEU within a control system formulation. All retained studies incorporate energy use and thermal comfort, while indoor air quality (IAQ) appears in one study, visual comfort in two, and acoustic comfort in none. Across these studies, comfort is frequently reduced to single environmental variables and governed through fixed setpoints, with indoor environmental conditions treated as direct proxies for occupant comfort. A relationship graph is introduced to interpret these patterns and reveals structural limitations, including the omission of cross-domain interactions, the absence of an intermediate IEQ layer linking environmental conditions to perceived comfort, and the selective treatment of contextual drivers due to computational and uncertainty-related constraints. These findings indicate that most existing approaches function as autonomous rather than occupant-centric control systems.

title: Optimizing spatially non-uniform skylights for museum galleries: Balancing visual quality, artifact conservation, and geometric complexity
Beyond archetypes: Creating behavior-aware synthetic building populations through probabilistic multi-source data integration for multi-domain urban analysis
abstract: Joint modeling of demographic diversity, physical building characteristics, time-resolved occupancy and activity, and weather conditions is critical for accurate analysis of integrated urban systems. However, this information is scattered across surveys and data products with incompatible sampling frames, spatial units, temporal resolutions, and semantics. The critical problem is that there are often no common identifiers to link these data sources. Consequently, analysts are forced to either oversimplify behavioral heterogeneity or resort to ad hoc imputations and rigid deterministic linkage. This paper presents a population-scale synthesis framework that probabilistically links household/person microdata, physical building attributes, observed time-use diaries, and meteorological drivers to produce an uncertainty-aware synthetic building population. The core methodological innovation extends discrete Fellegi–Sunter probabilistic record linkage with continuous-similarity comparison densities, employing Beta models for ordinal, numeric, and hierarchical features to capture partial agreements. Parameters of the probabilistic linkage model are estimated using a regularized Expectation–Maximization scheme that applies an adaptive log-growing penalty to stabilize early sparse updates. Computational efficiency is achieved through a hierarchical blocking lattice that prunes candidate sets across multiple dimensions. The resulting microdata preserve empirical structural and activity distributions, retain nearly all ex-post best matches, and carry calibrated uncertainty estimates. The framework produces a synthetic building population, i.e., simulation-ready inputs for downstream building energy simulation, rather than physically simulated or validated temporal load profiles. This methodology enables transparent, bottom-up modeling of interconnected urban sectors, spanning energy, infrastructure, and equity at the population scale, while maintaining statistical rigor and interpretability.

title: Adaptive thermal comfort in urban parks across temperate and subtropical climates
abstract: Rapid urbanization has significantly reduced urban green spaces, intensified the urban heat island effect, and increased concerns regarding outdoor thermal comfort and public health. Urban parks play a crucial role in supporting recreation and human well-being. This study addresses the lack of field based evidence linking microclimatic conditions and human thermal responses in urban parks within rapidly urbanizing cities, using Kathmandu and the Rupandehi district of Nepal which are located in temperate and sub-tropical climate respectively. A total of 1,119 visitors were interviewed in shaded areas of urban parks in two districts to obtain thermal comfort votes, accompanied by simultaneous microclimatic measurements conducted over 35 days during the daytime of summer season. The results showed that 50.6% of respondents in both temperate climate (N = 868) and the subtropical climate (N= 251), perceived the environment as “Slightly hot”. The 80% upper limit of thermal acceptability for Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET) and Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) of sub-tropical climate were29.6 °C and 32.0 °C which are 2.6°C and 2.7°C higher than temperate climate. The comfort PET and UTCI values of sub-tropical climate were 29.8 °C and 32.2 °C which are 4.7°C and 4.6°C higher than temperate climate respectively. An outdoor adaptive model for shaded spaces in urban park was developed for both climates. This study provides benchmarks for climate-responsive shaded urban park design and offers actionable insights for urban planners to mitigate thermal stress in rapidly urbanizing cities.

title: Towards bridging the gap between vibration serviceability and acoustics of lightweight floors: A critical review of mitigation strategies
abstract: As modern structures tend to become more lightweight, acoustics and vibration serviceability increasingly govern the design of the floors. A large percentage of the mass of such a structure is normally attributed to solving vibroacoustic problems. Even though the fields of floor acoustics and vibration serviceability are tightly connected, they have been developing independently. This leads to a load-bearing structure being designed without considering acoustics, and then adding a layer to meet the acoustical requirements without considering the vibration serviceability. Integrating the two performance criteria in floor design unlocks potential for further weight savings. This critical review paper provides an initial step towards bridging the gap between vibration serviceability and acoustics of floors by highlighting opportunities for their future integration. First, it synthesises their differences, similarities, and overlapping mechanisms, particularly in the low-frequency range. Then, it reviews the literature to identify existing mitigation strategies and critically evaluates their influence on floor performance from both vibration and acoustic perspectives. Finally, the paper outlines key research gaps, identifies strategies with potential for synergistic interaction, and proposes a starting point for a more holistic, integrated approach to lightweight floor design. The paper identifies the following 10 strategies for improving the vibroacoustic floor performance: reducing excitation, adding stiffness and mass, granular infill, floating floor, suspended ceiling, cavity absorbers, viscoelastic damping layer, tuned mass damper, and active mass damper. Strategies that emerge as especially promising for holistic consideration are those that target the low-frequency range, where lightweight floors are acoustically most problematic and where vibration serviceability and acoustics overlap. Those include adding a viscoelastic layer between the base floor and topping, adding tuned or active mass dampers, and tuning the suspended ceiling to dampen the first floor mode. A key hypothesis is proposed that integrating vibration serviceability and acoustics through mitigation strategies that leverage the damping of low-frequency global modes enables better material utilisation in lightweight floors. To confirm or reject the hypothesis, future studies should jointly investigate low-frequency vibroacoustic floor behaviour within an integrated experimental and modelling framework.

title: Chip control performance of a vortex-enhanced ventilation system in rail grinding machinery
Efficiency loss risk in rotating disk separating droplets: the role of rebound and splashing dynamics
A review of methods for assessing IEQ impacts on learning and teaching performance in classrooms across thermal, air, acoustic and visual domains
abstract: IEQ significantly affects occupant performance, particularly in classrooms, where differing needs and age-related sensitivities are present. While the link between IEQ and performance is well-established, a standardized methodology to assess its impact in educational buildings is still lacking. To support future comparability across studies and standardization, this review, conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, aims to (i) examine methods used to assess learning and teaching performance, and (ii) identify age- and role-related differences in IEQ effects and assessment approaches, and (iii) provide guidance for age- and role-sensitive evaluation to support research on learning-conducive educational environments. Following the screening of 2138 records, 45 studies met the inclusion criteria. Most studies used questionnaires (40%) and cognitive tests (38%), with fewer relying on academic metrics (13%) or other methods (9%). Questionnaires are recommended for teachers and older students to capture self-reported effects on performance, although their reliability depends on individuals’ self-evaluation skills and may differ from objective performance measures. Cognitive tests and academic performance metrics provide valuable quantitative data; cognitive tests are suitable for all ages and can be integrated into regular classroom activities, while academic metrics require cautious interpretation due to limited comparability and the influence of external factors. Interviews and focus groups have also been used, offering qualitative insights useful for preliminary assessments, while physiological methods (e.g., eye tracking) provide additional quantitative data but can be invasive. Moreover, when selecting a performance assessment method, it is essential to consider the age and role of the subjects, as IEQ affects teachers and students differently (both in terms of perception and the types of tasks they perform) and because the suitability of each method varies with the skills being assessed. Based on this, a framework is proposed to assess IEQ’s impact on performance, tailored to specific learning or teaching skills, as a first step toward methodological harmonization.

title: Carbon, energy and cost inefficiencies and future potentials of climate zone-based building envelope codes
Building performance of thermotropic glazed skylights under mixed-mode ventilation: A case study
Perceived classroom visual environment and students’ experience beyond academic performance
abstract: This study explored how classroom visual atmospheres affect students’ affective responses and motivation to learn, providing evidence that considers the user-centred visual environment beyond energy performance and academic outcomes. The study combined observations of 21 classrooms with data from 452 students. Students evaluated the classroom visual environment and lighting attributes using a questionnaire with eight items derived from established research in the field. Motivation to learn was measured with four items covering tasks with varying cognitive demands. Emotional responses were assessed using a simplified circumplex model comprising four dimensions (positive, activation, engagement, and calmness) that capture four positive and four negative affective states. All measures used an 11-point Likert scale, appropriate for assessing nuanced responses among adolescents aged 12 and above. Positive perceptions of the classroom, lighting, and colour significantly influenced motivation. Among visual factors, classroom liking showed the strongest relationship with students’ positive emotions. Perceived warmth of lighting was particularly influential, correlating with higher levels of enthusiasm and interest. Motivation to learn was associated with students’ ratings of lighting and the classroom's overall appearance, with lighting emerging as the strongest predictor. Despite being rated lowest, classroom colour remained significantly related to motivation. Our findings contribute to addressing experiential aspects of learning environments, reinforcing the significant impact of the built environment on emotional states, motivation, and engagement.

title: Stepping outside the office: A stated choice experiment on employees’ preferences for walking meeting routes
abstract: Growing concerns about sedentary office work have increased interest in integrating physical activity into daily work routines. Walking meetings, during which employees hold meetings while walking, are a promising strategy to reduce sitting time, yet little empirical evidence exists on how environmental features influence their appeal. This study examines which built environment and route characteristics shape employees’ preferences for walking meeting routes. A stated choice experiment was administered to 213 office employees, who evaluated hypothetical routes that varied in distance to entrance/ exit, crowdedness, land use, route signage, green space, seating along the route, and bodies of water. Multinomial logit models were used to analyse preferences for walking meetings in small and larger groups. Results showed that natural features, particularly water bodies, along with seating and clear route signage, were the most influential attributes, while office-related and street-related characteristics were less important. Preferences were consistent across group sizes, with seating along the route being slightly more valued in larger groups. These findings offer actionable insights for workplace planners and urban designers aiming to promote walking meetings and enhance employee well-being.

title: Assessing SUEWS-simulated near-surface air temperature and humidity using a paired forcing-validation framework in Xiong’an New Area
abstract: Quantifying the skill of the Urban Canopy Model (UCM) in reproducing near-surface urban meteorological parameters remains challenging due to the rarity of long-term datasets pairing flux-tower forcing with synchronized, dense intra-urban observations. This study evaluates near-surface air temperature, humidity, and wind speed simulations using the Surface Urban Energy and Water Balance Scheme (SUEWS). We utilized a unique long-term (2023–2024) paired forcing–validation dataset in the Xiong’an New Area (temperate climate), consisting of a flux-tower and 39 automatic weather stations. The evaluation spans varying seasons, diurnal cycles, and weather conditions, emphasizing the value of including anthropogenic heat (AH) emissions. The AH flux (QF) peaked in summer at 41 W m⁻² (approximately 80% from buildings). SUEWS effectively captured diurnal variations of near-surface air temperature (R² > 0.99, RMSE < 0.9°C, MAE < 0.7°C), as well as humidity and wind. Incorporating AH consistently enhanced temperature simulations, reducing the 2023 MBE from -0.549 °C to -0.009 °C. The model fit was highest in spring and autumn (R² > 0.98). Winter simulations were most sensitive to AH, with RMSE decreasing from 1.396 °C to 0.926 °C, and nighttime cold biases were significantly mitigated. Across weather conditions, accuracy was highest under rainy conditions, and grids with higher impervious surface fractions exhibited lower errors. This study demonstrates the value of a paired forcing–validation framework for the spatiotemporal assessment of near-surface conditions simulated by neighbourhood-scale UCM and for quantifying localized AH benefits.

title: Development of environmental chamber NUAGE and its digital twin for holistic indoor air quality studies in French dwellings
abstract: Bad indoor air quality (IAQ) plays an important role in people's lives as it has adverse health effects particularly in urban environment, making ventilation essential to the built environment. Studying ventilation strategies as a function of building permeability and its outdoor conditions is challenging, as in situ experiments offer limited control over environmental factors. This demands the development of experimental and numerical setups capable of reproducing well-controlled yet representative real-world conditions. The objective is therefore to create an environmental chamber that enables testing of these strategies under various controlled scenarios, along with the development of a digital twin using CONTAM. This allows studying the impact of ventilation strategies on IAQ parameters (i.e., pollutant concentrations). The comparison with experimental findings for CO2 and PM levels showed that the model was capable of predicting the transport dynamics with an error for CO2 below 10% under carefully monitored conditions. The error rose to about 16% when operating parameter deviations took place. The dynamic buildup and decay patterns for PM were realistically modeled; however, calibration was necessary to bring experimental data closer to numerical results. The discretization of the particle size distribution within the model was identified as the cause of the disparity in PM levels. The combined experimental–numerical framework offers a strong foundation for researching the dynamics of pollutants in ventilated spaces and facilitates the creation and assessment of sophisticated ventilation control techniques, especially demand-controlled ventilation, which are intended to enhance IAQ in residential buildings while reducing their energy footprint.

title: Photovoltaic shading design for outdoor sports spaces: An optimization framework integrating thermal comfort, energy performance, and economic efficiency
Coupled wind–buoyancy driven natural ventilation in urban underground corridors: Mechanisms and geometric optimization
Effects of nozzle height and pressure on misting performance, thermal sensation, and physiological responses in a hot-humid urban open space

Embodied carbon of progressive timber integration in a 47-storey tropical high-rise: A Singapore public housing case study
Towards more reliable non-destructive characterization of Hygric properties: Analysis and enhancement of Karsten tube measurement accuracy

Identification and optimization of factors influencing the vitality of waterfront open spaces: Leisure behavior simulation based on abstract morphological typologies
Quantifying the mitigation potential of sea-breeze cooling on urban overheating and health risks during heatwaves in a typical coastal city
Quantifying whole-house indoor PM2.5 source strengths from time-series data using dynamic and integral approaches
Optimizing indoor air quality in HVAC systems using deep reinforcement learning with multi-objective dynamic weight reward function
abstract: With a growing emphasis on building occupants’ health and well-being, ensuring better Indoor Air Quality (IAQ) while simultaneously managing thermal comfort and energy conservation has become a fundamental challenge for intelligent Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) control. Existing Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) approaches predominantly rely on fixed-weight reward functions that cannot adapt to dynamically changing occupancy conditions, and few studies treat IAQ as a primary optimization objective. This study proposes a novel DRL framework whose core innovation is a CO 2 -driven reward shaping mechanism that couples IAQ sensing with multi-objective control. The relative priorities of thermal comfort, IAQ, and energy cost objectives are controlled in response to real-time indoor CO 2 levels, which is used as an occupancy proxy. A dedicated anti-reward-gaming design is incorporated to prevent agents from exploiting weight transitions rather than genuinely improving building performance. The framework is evaluated by training and comparing two representative algorithms, Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), on the standardized BOPTEST simulation platform, without relying on any predefined occupancy schedules. Both agents achieved 100% CO 2 compliance (zero exceedances above 800 ppm). SAC consistently stabilized indoor CO 2 within 600–700 ppm during occupied periods and demonstrated superior thermal comfort stability, while PPO adopted a more conservative, energy-focused strategy. These IAQ and comfort improvements were achieved with simultaneous energy savings of 6.88% (SAC) and 7.32% (PPO) relative to the RBC baseline. This work demonstrates that occupancy-responsive dynamic reward weighting is an effective and practically viable paradigm for real-time multi-objective HVAC optimization.

title: Mechanisms and effects of wall-attachment ventilation–thermal plume interaction on airflow and aerosol control in dental clinics
Infrared thermography technology in the quantitative evaluation of building envelope thermal performance: Progress and prospects
Subject-specific baseline correction for multimodal physiological sensing: Revealing distinct physiological associations of thermal sensation, comfort, and preference
A novel bio–based concrete building envelopes reinforced with microencapsulated phase change materials for enhanced thermal comfort, energy efficiency, and reduced carbon emissions
The dynamic emergence of thermal discomfort disparities among the elderly: An agent-based modeling of heat-reduction behaviors
A lifecycle mapping of circular economy principles and implementation strategies in construction
abstract: The Circular Economy (CE) has gained momentum as a key concept for operationalising sustainable development, engaging policymakers, scholars and practitioners in an unprecedented discourse. The construction sector is among the most resource-intensive and wasteful sectors, and several countries, including the UK, have prioritised its adoption of CE. However, there remains no consensus on a standardised set of CE principles and implementation strategies tailored for the construction sector. A holistic lifecycle understanding of CE principles, incorporating emerging CE standards (e.g. ISO 59004:2024) and implementation strategies to promote CE adoption, is lacking. Therefore, in an integrative literature review, this paper critically examined existing CE principles and implementation strategies across 248 research and grey literature. A two-stage content analysis (inductive and deductive) and coding process (latent and manifest) was used to analyse the search results. Consequently, a construction-specific CE Principles Wheel (CE-PW) was synthesised, comprising 25 key principles systematically correlated with 37 implementation strategies across product lifecycle stages, circularity loops, and business model value propositions. The mapping of CE principles and implementation strategies exposed three systemic patterns: an emphasis on the design stage, limited adoption of systemic principles, and fragmented focus across CE themes, with notable “blind spots” indicating underexplored areas. The new insights from the CE-PW and the correlated implementation strategies guide CE adoption in both top-down (policy-oriented) and bottom-up (industry-oriented). These findings support industry, future research, policy and standardisation efforts, particularly in expanding on the ongoing BSI B/558/1 standard on “Circular Economy in the Construction Sector - Framework, Principles and Definitions.”

Pathogen survival and antibiotic resistance gene persistence on hospital environmental surfaces: Short-lived disinfection efficacy may enables persistent contamination threat
A physics-guided dual-branch domain-adversarial neural network with orthogonality constraint for cross-domain fault diagnosis of solar-assisted air source heat pump systems
Integrating a low-temperature atmospheric plasma module with an air-conditioner for inactivating airborne microbes
Towards healthy and liveable cities: Realistic modelling of urban pedestrian thermal stress on waterfront greenways
Resource-aware Comfort-Credit control for workstation-differentiated thermal comfort in HVAC–PV–battery office systems
