A GAN-enhanced transfer learning framework for cross-condition chiller fault diagnosis under severe data scarcity
Corrigendum to “The effects of bed cooling on sleep quality and sleep thermal comfort in overheated bedrooms” [Building and Environment, Volume 291, (2026), 114213]
Corrigendum to “Rethinking Pilotis in Multi-Family Housing: Winter Thermal Comfort Implications—A Case Study of Minamisuna Danchi, Tokyo” [Building and Environment Volume 302, 15 August 2026, 114886]
Synergistic cooling effects of UV protective shading and PV-ESS powered ventilation on pedestrian-level microclimate and modelled physiological heat stress
Bedroom thermal conditions and their impacts on sleeping thermal comfort, sleep quality, and next‑day wakefulness
abstract: The thermal environment during sleep influences sleep quality, yet the relationships among in-bedroom conditions, subjective thermal comfort, and sleep outcomes in real-world settings remain insufficiently characterized. To examine how bedroom thermal conditions influence thermal adaptation and subjective comfort, and how these factors relate to self-reported and objective sleep quality and next-day wakefulness, a one-week field study was conducted among 33 healthy university students in Hong Kong during early-to-mid summer (May–August). Results showed that higher bedroom temperatures were associated with warmer TSVs, greater dissatisfaction, and poorer self-reported sleep quality. Minimum dissatisfaction occurred at TSV ≈ −0.57 and approximately 24–24.6°C. Participants adapted primarily via bedding insulation and coverage; females selected higher insulation and showed lower dissatisfaction at cooler sensations. Cooler sensations were linked to better self-reported outcomes, whereas objective metrics showed limited associations with temperature. Mixed-effects models identified air temperature as the dominant predictor of TSV and satisfaction. A negative temperature × insulation interaction indicated that the warming influence of insulation was strongest at lower temperatures and diminished as temperature rose. For satisfaction, a positive interaction suggested attenuation of the adverse main effects at higher temperatures. Improved thermal satisfaction from one night to the next was associated with modestly lower next-day sleepiness at select times. It is concluded that in real-world summer bedroom conditions, maintaining slightly cool bedrooms (~23–25°C) and enabling adaptive bedding can minimize dissatisfaction and support better perceived sleep. Predictive models incorporating temperature and insulation—and their interaction—capture key aspects of sleeping thermal comfort.

title: A Performance-based model for retrofit of existing residential districts using multi-dimensional collaborative optimization: A case study of Shenzhen
Spectrum-dependent performance of spectrally selective glazing across climates and receiving orientations
Exposure-informed ventilation control for nanoparticle pollutants in an enclosed industrial built environment: A laser metal deposition case study
abstract: Advanced metal additive manufacturing systems, such as robotic laser metal deposition (LMD), are emerging as localized nanoparticle sources in enclosed industrial built environments. However, the coupled effects of emission dynamics, airflow non-uniformity, and ventilation effectiveness on nanoparticle persistence remain insufficiently understood. This study investigated indoor nanoparticle dynamics and post-process decay in an enclosed robotic LMD chamber by integrating multi-metric aerosol measurements, size-resolved metal analysis, respiratory deposition modeling, and ventilation decay analysis. The 5-min LMD process produced trimodal particle number and mass distributions dominated by nanoparticles, with peak number concentrations reaching 3.46 × 10 6 #/cm 3 , nearly three orders of magnitude above background levels. Although the chamber was designed for 100 air changes per hour (ACH), measured post-process decay showed that nominal ACH substantially overestimated the effective nanoparticle decay rate under the tested chamber conditions. Air velocity mapping revealed low-velocity and recirculation regions near the robotic arm and worktable, causing delayed nanoparticle decay. A revised mass-balance model incorporating a chamber-specific mixing efficiency factor estimated that approximately 27% of the nominal ventilation capacity effectively contributed to nanoparticle decay under the tested conditions. Based on nanoparticle number concentration as the most conservative clearance endpoint, a case-specific minimum post-process ventilation time of 13 min was required for concentrations to return to background before worker re-entry, more than four times the current 3-min practice. Respiratory deposition and toxic metal risk analysis further confirmed the need for exposure-informed ventilation control. Overall, this work provides a scalable, building-science-based framework for evaluating ventilation effectiveness and optimizing control strategies for engineered nanoparticle sources in enclosed industrial environments.

title: Examining diurnal and seasonal variation in the relative importance of urban form features for the canopy-layer urban heat island
Automated generation of residential site plan layouts via deep reinforcement learning and boundary-adaptive masking
Physics-informed multi-objective placement of indoor multi-modal sensor nodes using a two-dimensional LBM-based simulation framework
abstract: This study presents a physics-informed multi-objective optimization (PI-MOO) method for placing integrated indoor sensor nodes. A two-dimensional lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) model was built on the breathing-zone plane (z = 1.2 m) of an educational building floor and used to generate reference fields for temperature and pollutant concentration variance under summer forced-convection and transitional-season natural-ventilation conditions. NSGA-II optimized three objectives: temperature-field reconstruction error (RMSE), line-of-sight (LoS) coverage, and variance-weighted gas-risk coverage. The Kneedle algorithm selected N = 31 as the cost-effective sensor budget. At this budget, PI-MOO reduced RMSE by 30.3% relative to uniform placement and by 23.6% relative to the virtual-force algorithm; gas-risk coverage increased by 24.6% and 7.7%, respectively. In a Monte Carlo node-failure test, PI-MOO kept the best absolute performance after five failed nodes. The 2D LBM fields are used here as reference fields for comparing layouts. Validation against three-dimensional simulations or field measurements remains future work.

title: A novel artificial component air ventilation system for thermal environment and air quality control in underground refuge chamber
Exploring the spatial sensitivity of environmental parameters: emission source location, building layout, and emission intensity in urban microscale CFD modeling
A comprehensive LMUPO research framework: Integrating outdoor urban microclimates into building performance analysis and optimization
Indoor relative humidity and air mycobiome in eastern Taiwan residences: associations with Aspergillus and Wallemia
Micro-scale spatial forms in urban green spaces and children’s perceived nature restoration: Associations, explanatory pathways, and design translation
Generating moisture reference years for 34 representative Chinese cities for hygrothermal simulations
UAV-based low-altitude remote sensing in built-environment thermal studies: A review across different spatial scales
Beyond land surface temperature: Seasonal variability in urban heat island effects shaped by 2D/3D urban morphological feature
Accurately delineating non-urban reference for urbanization-environmental assessments
Assessing nature-based solutions for heat stress resilience in an urban micro-climate under changing climate scenarios
A physics-informed Gaussian Markov random field framework for indoor airflow field estimation
abstract: An accurate characterization of indoor airflow is essential for assessing air quality, understanding airborne contaminant transport, and evaluating ventilation performance in buildings. In practice, however, obtaining spatially resolved airflow information remains challenging: high-fidelity CFD simulations are computationally intensive, while interpolation of sparse sensor data fails to enforce the underlying physical behavior of the flow.This paper presents a physics-informed mapping approach based on Gaussian Markov Random Fields (GMRF) to reconstruct two-dimensional airflow fields from sparse internal observations. The method embeds simplified physical constraints derived from the Navier–Stokes equations—including mass conservation, advection, and viscous diffusion—into the estimation process, ensuring physically consistent flow reconstruction at a fraction of the computational cost of CFD.Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach accurately recovers airflow structures in a range of indoor environments and remains robust under sparse and irregular sampling conditions. Furthermore, it enables the identification of poorly ventilated (stagnant) regions and the characterization of airflow pathways, providing a practical tool for ventilation assessment and real-time indoor air quality analysis.

title: HVAC subsystem-aligned explainable graph neural network mixture of experts (GNN-MoE) for multi-horizon work order prediction
abstract: Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) maintenance requires forward prediction of component maintenance needs, yet remains dominated by detection and diagnosis. Where prediction exists, components are often modelled as independent sensor-monitored entities, obscuring inter-subsystem degradation propagation and interpretability. Physics-based forecasting depends on thermodynamic parameters requiring instrumentation seldom available. Computerised Maintenance Management System (CMMS) work orders, a knowledge repository of longitudinal maintenance, however, remain underused for prediction. Thus, this study proposes a graph-based unplanned work order prediction at the component-level using time-series CMMS data as the dominant source of information. A large language model-based knowledge extraction pipeline was first developed to transform work order text into structured entities. A time-expanded heterogeneous graph with component and work order nodes connected through twelve edges encoding hydronic, air, control, correlation, spatial, and maintenance relationships was then constructed to model plausible degradation propagation. Next, a sparse gated Graph Neural Network Mixture of Experts (GNN-MoE) analysis model is proposed. HVAC subsystem-aligned expert models, such as heating and cooling, are implemented using Graph Transformer, Graph Attention Network v2, or GraphSAGE matched to sub-graph topology. Threshold-constrained evaluation supports predictions at 14, 30, 90, and 365-day horizons, to support maintenance cycles, validated on a multisite dataset of 19,411 work orders. 14-day horizon achieves 70% precision with 27 times lift at 2.6% prevalence for immediate maintenance dispatch. A 365-day horizon achieves 89.5% recall for long-term maintenance planning. Ablations highlight graph and text feature influence, and interpretable expert routing patterns reflect maintenance dynamics aligned with HVAC sub-systems.

title: Mixed-effects and clustering approaches to thermal comfort in Indian university buildings
abstract: Assessing thermal comfort in naturally ventilated (NV) buildings is complicated by hierarchical data structures and limitations of temperature-centric models in warm, free-running contexts. This study reports a cross-sectional field survey in five NV university buildings in Hyderabad, India (hot semi-arid, BSh climate), across two monsoon seasons (N = 1,139). Operative temperatures (T op ) ranged from 26.1 to 33.8°C (mean 29.6°C). Linear mixed-effects models identified T op (β = 0.360), metabolic rate (β = 0.388), and season (β = 0.431) as significant predictors of thermal sensation; session-level variance exceeded building-level variance in a joint random-intercept model (ICC 0.163 vs. 0.020). Regression yielded a neutral temperature of 28.3°C (Griffiths mean 28.8°C at G = 0.50 K⁻¹; range 28.0–28.8°C across G = 0.25–0.50 K⁻¹), approximately 1.5–2.3°C warmer than ASHRAE Standard 55 predictions; the India Model for Adaptive Comfort (IMAC) and EN 16798-1 showed closer agreement. Principal component analysis revealed three perceptual axes (thermal load, air movement, humidity experience). K-means clustering (k = 3) tentatively identified three thermo-perceptual profiles, although moderate separation (silhouette = 0.235) suggests these should be treated as exploratory. Two groups at nearly identical operative temperatures (ΔT op = 0.17°C; Cliff’s δ = 0.14) differed substantially in thermal sensation (ΔTSV ≈ 1.03; δ = 0.43), associated with humidity and air-movement perception—revealing response-group divergence not captured by population-average regression. These patterns appear session-specific rather than stable occupant traits. Temperature-based comfort evaluation alone may overlook humidity- and air-movement-related perceptual heterogeneity in monsoon-season NV classrooms in BSh climates.

title: Toward sustainable student living: A systematic review of dormitory multi-domain environmental quality and energy performance
Prediction and causal-oriented interpretation of population activity intensity across function-dominated urban spaces under built-environment heterogeneity
The Impact of energy retrofit on indoor air quality in classrooms and offices
abstract: In Europe, buildings account for around 40% of total energy consumption. Improving the energy efficiency of the existing building stock is instrumental in achieving broader energy efficiency and decarbonisation targets. However, research has shown that energy efficiency measures implemented as part of retrofits can adversely affect indoor air quality, which is detrimental to occupant health and well-being. The impacts of retrofit measures in common office and classroom settings remain understudied with much of the existing literature concentrating on residential settings or constrained by limited sample sizes or monitored parameters. This study investigates the impact of energy-retrofit measures on indoor environmental quality in over 50 classrooms and offices in Ireland, pre- and post-retrofit. Week-long monitoring campaigns were conducted to measure carbon dioxide, fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ), nitrogen dioxide, volatile organic compounds (Benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, xylene, limonene, pinene, formaldehyde), temperature, and humidity. Changes following retrofit were assessed using Mann-Whitney U tests alongside linear mixed-effects models which controlled for meteorological covariates (outdoor temperature, relative humidity, windspeed, outdoor PM 2.5 ) and accounted for hierarchical data structures. Carbon dioxide concentrations in classrooms reduced by 28% (range: -65% to +17%). PM 2.5 decreased by 28-29% in both settings, with WHO daily average guideline exceedances reducing from 48% to 26% of monitored days. Temperature increases of up to 4.5°C were observed, while both speciated volatile organic compounds and total volatile organic compound concentrations showed variable changes across and within buildings. The findings highlight that acceptable indoor air quality can be maintained, and often improved following properly considered retrofit measures, though success depends on several factors including installation quality, commissioning, maintenance and ongoing monitoring.

title: POD-FNO for efficient and interpretable prediction of turbulent flow around bluff bodies
Thermal resilience and overheating risk in non-residential buildings in Ireland: Evidence from a field study of low-energy ventilative cooling strategies
abstract: As buildings in northern climates become more energy-efficient, and average ambient air temperatures increase, overheating is likely to become a more prevalent issue. This study investigates overheating risks in 30 non-residential buildings across Ireland, including office settings, healthcare facilities, and educational institutions, with data from over 287 individual spaces, collected between 2020 to 2024. Results show that over one fifth of rooms failed at least one overheating criterion, overheating occurred in all building types, with healthcare facilities being most affected (20–64% of rooms failing criteria), followed by offices/universities (11–26%) and schools (6–11%). Our resilience analysis highlights a weak relationship between excess heat indoors with outside conditions (overheating escalation factors < 1). Our correlation analysis, comparing building characteristics to overheating, suggests that zones that fail tend to have higher exposed area to floor area ratios and lower window opening area to exposed area ratios, smaller floor areas and have manual control over openings. Overall, this research highlights a need to update Irish design practice, particularly around the role of solar gain and occupant interaction with openings and controls on overheating. More research is needed in determining occupants’ interaction with ventilative cooling systems to determine the extent to which systems are being under-utilized and to what extent further cooling measures are required. Future work should consider these factors as well as the development of building and district level heat strategies to suppress overheating, improve energy efficiency and assess the likely risks that are present to vulnerable cohorts in society.

title: Piston ventilation modulates thermal comfort in subway hubs via a dual-path coupling mechanism: A field study in Nanjing, China
Editorial Board
Adjustable window-Trombe wall composite envelope for solar heating: A laboratory experimental study of thermal performance under different operating conditions
AI-driven HVAC control optimisation for enhancing energy efficiency and indoor environmental quality: A review of recent advances and emerging approaches
abstract: Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems are central to building decarbonisation, yet improving indoor environmental quality (IEQ) often increases energy demand. This paper presents a systematic literature review of AI-driven HVAC control optimization for jointly improving energy efficiency and indoor environmental quality across different building types and climatic contexts. Following a PRISMA-based screening process, the review synthesizes 143 recent peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025. The analysis revealed supervised learning as the dominant ML technique for prediction and surrogate modelling and is frequently embedded in model predictive control (MPC). Reinforcement learning and deep reinforcement learning are increasingly applied to multi-objective supervisory control of setpoints, airflow, dampers and HVAC components because they offer model-free adaptability. Hybrid and ensemble approaches are emerging to improve robustness and trade-offs between energy efficiency and IEQ. Across diverse building typologies and climates, the reviewed studies reported an average energy savings of 40% compared with baseline cases, with several studies achieving savings above 50% while maintaining excellent IEQ. Despite these promising results, real-world validation remains limited as only 8 of 130 studies progressed to field or testbed deployment, highlighting a concerning gap between simulation-based research and practical validation. This review provides a comprehensive, context-sensitive mapping of AI-driven HVAC applications for enhancing both energy efficiency and IEQ in buildings.

title: LES and RANS simulations of wind and dispersion in a complex urban environment: Comparison of momentum and scalar fluxes
abstract: Wind and dispersion in a complex urban environment have been numerically simulated with large-eddy simulation (LES) and Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) and compared to wind-tunnel measurements. This paper presents a systematic comparison of LES and RANS across mesh resolutions and turbulent Schmidt numbers, linking dispersion predictions to momentum and scalar flux modelling. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using several statistical metrics, including ‘factor-of-two’ (FAC2). The velocity magnitude showed excellent agreement (FAC2 0.94) between numerical and experimental data for both RANS and LES, regardless of the adopted mesh. For the turbulence kinetic energy (TKE), excellent agreement was found for the LES (FAC2 0.99), whereas RANS systematically underpredicted TKE (FAC2 0.90). Scalar concentration predictions were satisfactory for the LES (FAC2 0.85) but significantly poorer for RANS (FAC2 0.54). Notably, RANS required substantially higher mesh refinements to obtain mesh convergence, likely due to large scalar gradients near the point-like release source. Moreover, the RANS agreement with experimental data deteriorated with increasing resolution. Turbulent momentum and scalar (FAC2 0.53) fluxes computed from LES agreed well with the measurements. In contrast, the Boussinesq eddy-viscosity model and the gradient-diffusion hypothesis used in the RANS framework estimated less accurate momentum fluxes and very poor scalar fluxes (FAC2 0.30), respectively. In many cases, RANS predicted turbulent scalar flux in the opposing direction to the experimental and LES results. The results indicate that inaccuracies in RANS concentration predictions are dominated by limitations in scalar-flux closure assumptions, which highlights a RANS modelling limitation.

title: A geometry-aware multi-level optimization framework for enhancing range hood capture performance
How environmental conditions shape workload in hybrid work: a longitudinal mediation analysis
Experimental and numerical research on improving thermal and humidity conditions in a ventilated ice rink arena
Urban daylight model with open-source and GIS-based tools: A case study in Italy
abstract: This paper presents a detailed analysis of the daylighting performance of buildings in the centre of Catania, in southern Italy. The proposed methodology employs a set of ‘facade-room’ archetypes representing rooms with typical floor and window dimensions, adjacent to an external facade characterized by predefined features: orientation, sky view factor, presence of balconies, window to floor-ratio, building age, windows facing. These parameters are extracted from georeferenced datasets in QGIS, with geometries modelled in Blender and daylighting performance metrics calculated using the Radiance®-based VI-Suite plugin. The daylighting performance of each archetype is then linked to the corresponding building facades within QGIS, enabling rapid analysis of large urban areas. One hundred archetypes were defined and associated with 29’000 georeferenced facade planes. Focusing on the impact of urban densification on daylight, the study reveals an average Sky View Factor of 0.28 for the case study area, resulting in a 50% mean reduction in Useful Daylight Illuminance autonomy, a 40% decrease in Daylight Factor and a loss of 1’550 hours of daylight compared to scenarios without buildings obstructions. Conversely, urban dense environment reduces the probability of excessive sunlight and reflects sunlight towards buildings increasing daylight autonomy. The proposed methodology enables the assessment of likely daylighting performance for individual rooms in urban buildings, storing these data within a GIS framework to support urban planning, property valuation and urban energy assessment.

title: EEG applications in indoor environmental quality research: A methodological review with emphasis on machine learning approaches
Accommodation environment of a polar cruise ship: Stratified or mixing ventilation system
Torque-sensing damper with aerodynamic amplification for integrated airflow measurement and regulation in ventilation systems
Identifying ventilation corridors in a coastal mountainous city under multiple circulation scenarios: CFD-based mountain resistance parameterization and directional-consistency screening
Diffusion characteristics of horizontal multi-port buoyant jets in indoor ventilation under coupled effects of pulse frequency and density Froude number
Inter-device agreement and trend-monitoring utility of consumer-grade air quality monitors in a semi-open building environment
Socioeconomic factors shape urban heat island intensity: Evidence of Kuznets-type nonlinear dynamics from GAMs in Tianjin, China
Influence of local spatial information on CNN-based prediction of pedestrian-level percentile wind speeds around buildings
Modulating airborne transmission of respiratory diseases: Effects of saliva rheology on cough fragmentation and aerosol concentration
Data-driven characterization of spatio-temporal correlations between AC terminals and occupied zones for zone-based control in large built environments
Research on the form selection and configuration of manned lunar research stations under the influence of lunar surface thermal environment
Built environment associations with PM2.5 exposure in an arid high-density city: Seasonal response patterns and interactive associations
Impact of seasonal and climatic adaptations and individual differences on sleep thermal preferences based on large-scale thermostat data
ATLAS: A performance-based index for integrated evaluation and benchmarking of indoor environmental quality
abstract: Indoor environmental quality (IEQ) is a central determinant of occupant health, comfort, and well-being, and is closely intertwined with building energy use and operational performance. Yet, prevailing IEQ evaluation methods rely primarily on threshold-based criteria that inadequately capture the multidimensional and interdependent nature of IEQ and the variability in occupant perceptions. This study presents the ATLAS Index (Air quality, Thermal comfort, Lighting, and Acoustics Scale), a novel performance-based framework for integrated and continuous IEQ evaluation, developed for residential environments but readily adaptable to other indoor spaces. ATLAS integrates multiple parameters across four IEQ domains using a logarithmic aggregation method that prioritizes the lowest-performing domain, minimizes artifacts associated with rigid threshold cut-offs, and enables flexible domain weighting. Parameter selection and scoring criteria are grounded in internationally recognized guidelines and standards including WHO guidelines, ASHRAE standards, and EN standards, adapted to residential environments where relevant. Occupant perceptions were integrated by dynamically reweighting IEQ domains using Bayesian updating based on periodic surveys. The ATLAS index was demonstrated with 1.5 years of continuous IEQ measurements from 10 occupied apartments in Valencia, Spain. Results show that acoustic conditions frequently constrained overall IEQ scores, and that correlations between objective IEQ scores and self-reported satisfaction were weak, underscoring the complexity of interpreting residential IEQ based solely on physical measurements. An open-source web-based visualization tool is provided to facilitate practical deployment and benchmarking. The ATLAS index provides a flexible and scalable framework for next-generation IEQ assessment, adaptable to evolving emerging sensing technologies and diverse building contexts.

title: A template-based CFD simulation framework for ventilation design and environmental analysis in mechanically ventilated livestock buildings
The impact of roadside trees on pollutant dispersion for a single and infinitely repeated sources
abstract: Although trees provide shade for pedestrians, enhancing their thermal comfort, it is known that dense vegetation can remarkably hinder the ventilation efficiency of an urban area, resulting in greater pedestrian exposure to traffic-related air pollutants. In the present paper, an infinite network of street canyons containing intersections is analyzed for four wind directions (90°, 60°, 30°, 0°) via RANS CFD simulations. The investigated street canyons are of H/W = 0.5 aspect ratio and can contain three different tree arrangements (none, sparse, dense). The flow field is considered fully periodic in the x and y-directions, while dispersion is modelled in two ways: (1) by calculating the aperiodic concentration field of a single source, and (2) by taking periodically repeated sources into account. After optimizing the sand-grain roughness of the walls (Ks/H = 0.1) and the turbulent Schmidt number (Sct = 0.2), the velocity, TKE, and aperiodic concentration distributions show excellent agreement with previous wind tunnel results. When only a single pollutant source is considered, trees worsen the pedestrian exposure to traffic-related air pollutants for all investigated scenarios. Conversely, when the impact of infinitely many repeated street canyons and emissions is taken into account, trees have a ventilation-enhancing effect for the 0° and 30° wind directions. The wind direction-averaged mass transfer coefficient (mass Stanton number) is found to be decreased only by 6% and 16% by the sparsely and densely planted trees, respectively, which may be viewed as a trade-off worth considering when the beneficial aspects of urban trees are also considered.

title: Greenhouse gas emissions at construction sites: Lessons learned from Danish regulation
abstract: This study investigates how the introduction of life cycle assessment limit values for greenhouse gas emissions (GHGs) during the construction process stage (modules A4-A5) in the building industry shape organisational decision-making. Newly amended building regulation in Denmark is used for context with a focus on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). There is a risk that some building contractors do not possess requisite LCA knowledge/capacity-building to monitor their upfront GHG emissions in accordance with the limit values, particularly during the early stages of regulatory introduction. Six semi-structured interviews were conducted with six contractors operating in the Danish building industry in the months immediately following the regulation amendment. The results show that while contractors recognise the importance of industry-wide climate mitigation, their practice is shaped by limited data availability, methodological uncertainties, unclear requirements, and competing organisational interests within the industry. We argue that this organisational knowledge gap may manifest in competitive behaviours, rather than knowledge sharing. Through the lens of bounded rationality, knowledge gaps in the Danish building industry may already be shaping a tragedy of the commons system failure. We offer three potential learnings based on systems thinking and Ostromian institutional governance: 1) Rules should fit local circumstances, 2) Participation in decision-making is vital, and 3) Graduated sanctions for those who disregard the common collective decarbonisation efforts. Notwithstanding, LCA-based regulation remains a critical driver for decarbonising the building industry, provided it is supported by clear guidance, stronger data infrastructures, coordinated institutional support, and above all a systems thinking holism.

title: Coupled effects of temperature ramps and localized heating on thermal comfort responses and empirical modelling
Challenges and opportunities in air filtration for the control of infectious diseases
abstract: Air filtration is underutilized as a strategy to help reduce the control of airborne infectious diseases. There are many contributing factors including cost, secondary consequences (e.g., noise), and a variety of psychological and behavioural factors, as well as perceptions of building users. These factors also present opportunities to change the way that we use filters to have an additional layer of protection against infectious disease transmission. This commentary reports on two workshops where participants explored the challenges and identified opportunities for increased use of filtration.

title: Integrated effects of overhanging shading devices and aspect ratios on microclimatic performance in street canyons: Scaled outdoor experiments
Three-dimensional level set-based topology optimization using the adjoint method for a tee flow equalizer with a low-pressure-loss uniform air supply
Physics-aware POD–transformer surrogate modeling for building-resolved urban wind prediction using multi-GPU large-eddy simulations
Coupled impact of air-conditioning anthropogenic heat and building cooling energy consumption in high-density old urban neighborhoods
abstract: Air-conditioning anthropogenic heat (ACAH) accumulate in unregulated narrow street canyons of high-density old urban neighborhoods, forming a adverse loop between thermal environment degradation and energy demand growth. Therefore, this study systematically investigates the accumulation characteristics of ACAH and its coupled impact on building cooling energy consumption in high-density old urban neighborhoods. A typical high-density old neighborhood in Guangzhou was taken as the research object with full-scale numerical simulation. The heat accumulation effect caused by the ACAH under different ambient meteorology and spatial morphology was then evaluated. Nextly, the coupling effects between heat accumulation and cooling energy consumption were analyzed. Results showed that ACAH increased neighborhoods air temperature at 1.5 m (ΔTa) by 1.65 to 7.55 °C, with the most severe heat accumulation occurring under low wind speed and high ambient temperature. Spatial morphology factors analysis showed that building surface fraction exerted the strongest effect on ΔTa with β = 1.245, whereas sky view factor predominantly influenced subregion cooling energy consumption with β = 0.418. Under the ACAH-induced heat accumulation, the cooling energy consumption of individual air-conditioner rises by up to 44.58%, accompanied by a 17.42% reduction in COP and a 20.02% increase in exhaust air temperature. These results indicated that ACAH is a key driver of local thermal deterioration and cooling energy increase in high-density old urban neighborhoods. Mitigation measures should focus on improving ventilation and optimizing outdoor-unit arrangement. This study provides a scientific reference for spatial optimization, thermal environment improvement, and energy efficiency enhancement in high-density old urban neighborhoods.

title: Effects of spatial autonomy on sense of control and work-related outcomes in VR-simulated home-based work environments
abstract: Spatial autonomy—the opportunity to enact one’s spatial preferences in the physical environment—is an underexplored dimension of indoor environmental quality in home-based work (HBW) environments. This study examined how two forms of spatial autonomy, location control and configuration control, influence workers’ sense of control and work-related outcomes in virtual reality (VR)-simulated HBW environments. Using high-fidelity VR, two repeated-measures experiments compared autonomy-supported conditions with autonomy-restricted conditions. Study 1 focused on location control by comparing a self-selected preferred work location with an imposed least-preferred location. Study 2 focused on configuration control by comparing a self-configured furniture layout with an imposed layout that was incongruent with participants’ stated spatial priorities. Across both studies, autonomy-supported conditions increased participants’ sense of control and improved workspace satisfaction, inclination to use the same workspace, and self-rated performance. Configuration control generally produced stronger and more consistent effects than location control across subjective outcomes. By contrast, effects on objective cognitive performance were more modest and less consistent. The findings suggest that, in HBW environments, the benefits of spatial autonomy operate primarily through an enhanced sense of control and are especially pronounced when workers can meaningfully configure their immediate workspace. These results highlight the need for adaptable home workspace design and hybrid-work policies that recognize unequal opportunities for spatial autonomy in home-based work.

title: A hybrid physics-based and data-driven framework for spatiotemporal prediction of urban microclimate across climate zones
Mitigating pedestrian-level wind-speed amplification in orthogonal building arrays through stepped-height modulation
ReCliDaR: An open-source ML-based tool to identify representative climate days for urban environmental modeling
abstract: Building Energy Modeling and Computational Fluid Dynamics-based Urban Climate Modeling tools are essential environmental modeling tools for designers to make informed, climate-responsive design decisions. However, these tools are computationally intensive, particularly when applied at large spatial scales or within optimization workflows. Traditional approaches, such as simulating for solstice, equinox, or peak cooling days, often fail to capture the diversity of climatic conditions. This can lead to overestimation or undermining of urban environmental performance. The Representative Climate Days Recognizer (ReCliDaR) tool bridges this gap by utilizing unsupervised machine learning to identify representative climate days, condensing a typical meteorological year into a manageable subset of 24-hour profiles. The framework of the tool automates the data preprocessing, feature scaling, and dimensionality reduction before executing a comparative clustering analysis using k-means, Gaussian Mixture, and Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering. Evaluation of 108 global cities across 11 ASHRAE climate zones demonstrates that the k-means algorithm provides the most robust performance, achieving almost a 100% seasonal continuity rate in most regions while minimizing data loss. The results indicate that while temperate and high-latitude climates typically follow binary seasonal structures, tropical environments often exhibit complex ternary patterns driven by monsoon cycles. By providing a validated, user-friendly interface for extracting medoid-based representative days, the ReCliDaR tool empowers researchers and practitioners to perform accurate, long-term environmental assessments. The tool and its source code are openly available on GitHub to support reproducible research in climate-responsive urban design and energy-efficient building performance.

title: A data-driven approach for building energy efficiency of healthcare facilities in England and Wales using regulatory building energy datasets
abstract: Healthcare buildings are among the most energy-intensive and carbon-emitting building types. In the UK, healthcare buildings account for approximately 15% of the total carbon footprint of the National Health Service (NHS). Reducing energy consumption and carbon emissions in existing healthcare buildings through energy-efficient refurbishment is therefore a key strategy for achieving the NHS Net Zero targets. Data-driven approaches have been widely applied for the rapid and accurate assessment of building energy performance. However, their application at the building stock level remains relatively limited. This study investigates a data-driven approach for energy performance prediction and assessment, with a focus on primary healthcare facilities in England and Wales. A surrogate - residual machine learning model was developed based on regulatory building energy datasets and evaluated against measured energy consumption data. The results demonstrate robust predictive performance of annual gas, electricity and total energy consumption across the primary healthcare building stock. In addition, the model can be used for evaluating the energy saving potential of refurbishment measures for the entire stock. The proposed data-driven approach provides a computationally efficient solution that enables rapid energy performance evaluation across hundreds or thousands of buildings and multiple refurbishment scenarios by updating the values of input features to represent the intended measures. As such, it offers a scalable decision-support tool for large-scale healthcare building refurbishment planning and the implementation of strategies aligned with the NHS Net Zero targets.

title: Room-level overheating disparities and the limits of passive-design attribution in humid subtropical Australian homes: a year-long field study
abstract: Climate change has intensified residential overheating risks, yet field evidence on passive-design performance remains limited in humid subtropical climates. This study monitored 24 homes in Australia's humid subtropical Climate Zone 3 and quantified overheating using New Effective Temperature (ET*)-derived Degree of Discomfort (DD) metrics: Degree Hours of Discomfort (DhD), a cumulative severity-weighted measure of exceedance above adaptive comfort thresholds, and Maximum Degree of Discomfort (DD max ). Dwelling-level analyses compared living rooms and bedrooms, decomposed hourly DD variance, evaluated household-level grouped machine-learning models, and explored weather-adjusted residual associations with passive design features. Living rooms accumulated substantially greater overheating than bedrooms (mean DhD 2,309°C·h versus 563°C·h). Among 23 matched dwellings, living-room DhD exceeded bedroom DhD in 21 dwellings (median paired difference 1,769°C·h), and living-room DD max exceeded bedroom DD max in all matched dwellings (median difference 2.24°C). Between-dwelling differences explained only 9.0% of hourly DD variance in living rooms and 5.1% in bedrooms. Under household-level grouped validation, weather/time-only Random Forest models gave the strongest transferable hourly-DD prediction (R² = 0.346 living rooms; 0.282 bedrooms); passive-design-only models showed negative or near-zero R² and did not improve prediction. After weather adjustment, passive-design associations were limited. The clearest cohort-level signal was lower living-room residual overheating in larger dwellings (ρ = −0.496, p = 0.014), which may reflect lower external surface-area-to-floor-area ratios or correlated typological differences rather than a design effect. Binary feature signals were sparse and exploratory. Bedroom metrics carried greater comfort-model uncertainty. The findings distinguish temporal overheating prediction from cautious dwelling-level design attribution.

title: Urban windcatchers stabilise natural ventilation after energy modernisation
abstract: Natural ventilation is a key strategy for reducing energy demand and improving indoor air quality in residential buildings. Yet its effectiveness is often compromised following deep thermal modernisation, particularly in dense urban environments. Conventional ventilation solutions often rely on simplified aerodynamic assumptions and isolated-building analyses, limiting their applicability to real urban contexts. Here, we present a dual-scale experimental and numerical investigation comprising (i) microscale level - a controlled laboratory testing of a multidirectional eight-opening windcatcher to quantify its intrinsic aerodynamic and hydrodynamic performance, and (ii) macroscale level - atmospheric boundary layer wind-tunnel experiments on a representative five-storey residential building to resolve realistic roof-level pressure fields governing device placement. These complementary experimental campaigns, supported by computational fluid dynamics simulations, enable simultaneous characterisation of airflow capture efficiency, flow stability, and urban-induced pressure redistribution, providing a physically validated basis for assessing installation feasibility under realistic urban wind conditions. The results demonstrate relatively stable and predictable ventilation performance across a wide range of wind speeds (0.4-6.0 m s⁻¹) and angles of attack (0°-45°), with supply airflow rates reaching approximately 200 m³ h⁻¹ and limited sensitivity to wind direction. These findings indicate that multidirectional windcatchers can maintain effective wind-driven ventilation after deep residential retrofit and building adaptation interventions, providing a robust passive alternative to mechanical systems and supporting low-energy renovation strategies in compact urban areas for sustainable housing.

title: Nonlinear coupling mechanisms of multidimensional urban factors shaping satellite-derived diurnal thermal dynamics across spatially significant thermal backgrounds in a high-density inland city
Toward an evaluation framework for day-scale differential thermal adaptation in transient populations: Evidence from outdoor historic public spaces
Distinct prefrontal, autonomic, and subjective responses to built, ornamental, and natural virtual environments
abstract: Modern urban living increasingly confines individuals indoors, limiting access to restorative natural environments and contributing to cognitive fatigue and chronic stress. Although the psychological and physiological benefits of nature exposure are well established, the neural mechanisms underlying these effects remain insufficiently characterized, constraining evidence-based design. Here, we employed a multimodal neuroergonomic approach in high-fidelity immersive virtual reality (IVR) to examine brain-body responses across a continuum of built and biophilic environments. Thirty-two adults experienced five photorealistic IVRs derived from Longwood Gardens, including curated ornamental gardens, natural landscapes and a non-horticultural control. During exploration, prefrontal cortex (PFC) activity was measured using wearable functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), autonomic activity was assessed via electrodermal and cardiac wearable sensors, and participants reported perceived restorativeness and aesthetic engagement. The non-horticultural environment elicited the highest medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) activation, whereas both natural landscapes and ornamental gardens showed lower mPFC activation and were rated as more restorative and engaging. Ornamental gardens were additionally associated with the highest tonic electrodermal activity and greater perceived complexity. Together, these findings suggest that green environments can produce dissociable subjective, neural, and autonomic response profiles, rather than a single uniform restorative pattern. More broadly, the study demonstrates the value of combining IVR with mobile neuroergonomic methods to characterize how specific environmental features relate to human experience and may inform neuroarchitecture and digital nature interventions.

title: Effect of airflow rate difference on particle outflow during healthcare worker entry and exit in airborne infection isolation rooms
Reconciling technical compliance with lived experience: applying a mixed-methods approach to evaluate occupant satisfaction in a high-performance educational building
abstract: Evaluating the true sustainability of high-performance buildings requires expanding beyond technical benchmarks to capture occupant’s lived experiences. This study presents a longitudinal, mixed-methods post-occupancy evaluation (POE) of a Living Building Challenge (LBC)-certified university facility, integrating continuous environmental monitoring with 308 survey responses across three semesters. Point-in-time surveys were linked to sensor data using a uniform 20-minute pre-survey window, adopted as a practical, unvalidated compromise. A four-stage analytical framework evaluated benchmark compliance, ordered logistic regression sensor-satisfaction models, spatiotemporal mapping, and facility management triangulation. Results reveal a divergence between technical compliance and occupant satisfaction. Excellent air quality compliance aligned with low dissatisfaction (5.2%), whereas thermal comfort produced the highest dissatisfaction (15.3%) despite acceptable temperature compliance 96.3% of the time. Illuminance met high-performance thresholds only 8.3% of the time, but visual comfort remained the highest-rated factor. Building-wide averages and adjusted models did not explain these perceptual differences. After controlling for spatial and temporal context, no sensor-satisfaction pair remained statistically significant. This sensor-perception paradox suggests that, in tightly controlled high-performance buildings, measured values may carry too little variance to substitute for occupant feedback. Spatiotemporal mapping and operational triangulation contextualized the gaps, linking dissatisfaction to localized contexts, certification-mandated material constraints, and user-driven behaviors not captured by sensor values alone. These findings suggest that sustainable building rating tools could benefit from continuous occupant feedback to capture dynamic patterns missed by single-point evaluations. The study illustrates a candidate POE workflow linking technical compliance, human perception, and operational expertise. Future multi-building studies are needed to test its transferability.

title: Research on the impact of sweet odor on human thermal comfort in indoor environments
abstract: Buildings contribute substantially to global energy use, making it important to improve indoor thermal comfort in cold conditions without increasing heating demand. This study investigated the effects of a sweet odor on human thermal comfort and brain activity in a cold environment. The experiment adopted a two-stage design, with a no-odor condition followed by a sweet-odor condition. The sweet odor was a blended scent composed of strawberry, vanilla, and caramel aromas. Subjective evaluations of thermal comfort vote, thermal sensation vote, and smell pleasantness vote were collected by questionnaire in both stages. Simultaneously, electroencephalography (EEG) signals were recorded and analyzed using electroencephalographic equipment. The results showed that sweet-odor exposure improved both thermal comfort and thermal sensation. The mean TCV increased from −0.72 to −0.28, and the mean TSV increased from −1.33 to −0.61, indicating a shift toward a more comfortable and less cold perception. EEG analysis revealed that theta-band relative power increased by approximately 11.7% after sweet-odor exposure, whereas no significant changes were observed in the other frequency bands. The theta response was mainly distributed in the right frontal, left temporo-parietal, and occipital regions, with the right frontal showing the clearest association with changes in thermal comfort evaluation. No significant correlations were found between SPV and theta-band changes in subjective evaluations. These findings suggest that sweet odor may improve human thermal comfort in cold environments by modulating neural activities related to cognitive evaluation, emotional processing, and sensory integration, providing a new approach for low-energy indoor thermal comfort regulation in winter.

title: Investigating the aerosol removal efficiency of novel air curtain exhaust hood during the laser cutting process
Digital twin applications for indoor environmental quality in healthy building research: a systematic review of indicators, methods and computational paradigms
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital Twin (DT) technologies are increasingly adopted in Healthy Buildings research to monitor and optimise Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ). However, their implementation remains heterogeneous, with substantial variability in indicator selection, methodological configurations and computational architectures. This study presents a systematic review of 62 peer-reviewed contributions to analyse how DTs are operationalised across IEQ-domains and to identify structural integration patterns within the field. Through combined bibliometric mapping and qualitative content analysis, the review classifies DT-based IEQ applications according to three interconnected dimensions: (i) indicator typologies (dose-related, building-related and occupant-related), (ii) methodological approaches (quantitative, qualitative and hybrid), and (iii) computational paradigms, including scripting-based workflows, visual programming environments, machine-learning models, simulation-driven frameworks and semantic graph-based systems. Rather than ranking individual studies, the analysis examines dominant configurations and emerging trajectories of integration across these dimensions. The results reveal a strong prevalence of dose-related environmental indicators and quantitative sensor-driven methods, typically associated with monitoring-oriented and predictive architectures. In contrast, building semantics and occupant-centred variables remain comparatively under-integrated, limiting the representation of behavioural variability and long-term exposure dynamics. By systematically mapping how indicators, methods and computational architectures intersect, this review clarifies the current structural orientation of DT-research for IEQ and outlines research directions toward more integrated, interoperable and health-aware digital building ecosystems.

Effect of spaciousness-related indicators on the acoustic evaluation of modern theaters for Peking opera
abstract: Spaciousness is integral to the acoustic environment of Peking opera theaters, while the objective indicators underpinning this subjective perception have not yet been systematically elucidated. This study carried out two paired-comparison listening experiments. Experiment 1 (N = 33) evaluated three representative indicators (Glow, LFE4, and IACCE3) to identify which indicator dominates the evaluation of spaciousness. Experiment 2 (N = 35) further investigated its effect on overall acoustic preference under different reverberation time (T30) conditions. Results identified IACCE3 as the dominant indicator for spaciousness evaluation, with a larger effect size than Glow and LFE4. Its influence remained stable across different roles and tempos. Notably, a significant interaction between IACCE3 and T30 on acoustic preference was observed: Under short-reverberation conditions (T30-0.7 s), the impact of spaciousness variations on acoustic preference was minimal. Conversely, under long-reverberation conditions (T30-1.4 s), listeners exhibited heightened sensitivity to variations in spaciousness, with acoustic preference significantly increasing at higher IACCE3 levels. Within the evaluated range (0.232-0.667), it is recommended to keep IACCE3 above the optimal level of 0.379. This study provides practical guidance for the design of Peking opera theaters and other traditional theatrical performance spaces.

title: Estimating pollutant dispersion based on reconstructed mean flow field in a two-dimensional street canyon using two-step physics-informed neural networks
abstract: Urban environments exhibit complex physical phenomena involving multiple interacting and imbalanced variables, making high-resolution measurements challenging and expensive. This study aimed to reduce the measurement demand while accurately estimating the mean flow and pollutant concentration fields using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). To improve the robustness of and mitigate the difficulties faced by PINNs when handling imbalanced outputs, this article proposes a two-step framework in which the airflow and pollutant dispersion within a two-dimensional street canyon are trained separately. In the first step, a PINN reconstructs the mean flow field from sparse velocity data derived from a large eddy simulation and simultaneously estimates the eddy viscosity. In the second step, these results are imposed as fixed fields in the advection–diffusion equation, enabling estimation of the pollutant dispersion from a ground-level line source. By leveraging the accurately reconstructed flow field, the second-step PINN achieves reliable reconstruction of the mean concentration field and turbulent diffusivity. Incorporating the eddy viscosity as additional physical information not only reduces the training cost and improves the accuracy, but also substantially reduces the data requirements. The eddy viscosity data ensure system closure, enabling physics-driven concentration field estimation even in the absence of concentration measurements. Furthermore, a comparison of the optimization strategies shows that the L-BFGS is more effective than Adam because of its second-order characteristics, facilitating convergence in ill-conditioned residual loss landscapes. Overall, the proposed method demonstrates the strong capability of PINNs to handle multiple outputs with imbalanced scaling in urban environments, highlighting their potential for broader applications.

title: A computationally efficient and spatially transferable model for urban-scale facade solar irradiation prediction
Effect of supply conditions on turbulent jet self-oscillations in a room with an open side wall
Ten questions on digital twins of buildings for transforming building operations
abstract: Buildings are becoming ever more complex to manage during operations, driven by increasing dynamics in energy demand, intermittent on-site power generation, and distributed energy resources, compounded by variable grid pricing signals and the rising threat of extreme weather events causing large-scale power outages. To achieve optimal performance in energy efficiency, demand flexibility, energy resilience, and occupant comfort, new methods and tools are essential for transforming design and operations across a building’s entire life cycle. Digital Twins (DTs), enabled by recent advances in ubiquitous sensing, big data, cloud computing, and AI, offer a transformative approach to creating a real-time, bi-directional digital counterpart of a physical building. This paper presents ten critical questions highlighting the most foundational issues underpinning the successful deployment of digital twins of buildings. The questions are holistically structured around three core themes to provoke significant research and accelerate adoption. The paper first examines the Users and Business aspects, including use cases, stakeholder alignment, business models, and governance structures. It then dives into the Technology foundation, addressing key components, layered software architectures, data integration, semantic interoperability, and the critical issues of cybersecurity and privacy. Finally, it explores Application aspects, such as the role of AI, performance metrics and standards, and the current landscape of software tools. DT technology is still in the early stage of adoption in buildings despite successful pilot applications in preventive maintenance, FDD, and advanced controls to optimize building performance. Several barriers need to be addressed to scale up DT technology in buildings, including high development and maintenance costs, the lack of data-rich infrastructure in buildings, and a shortage of skilled workforce.

title: No evidence that short-term exposure to window views improved final exam performance: A three-year randomized controlled trial in a university lecture course
abstract: s Providing views is known to benefit occupants’ cognitive performance. However, it remains unclear whether having a view also improves learning outcomes. We investigated whether taking an exam in rooms with views leads to higher performance compared with taking an exam in a windowless classroom. We used the final exam scores from an undergraduate course, with 62 points and 37 points assigned to conceptual and calculation questions, respectively, to measure the outcome. Over three years, we randomly assigned students to rooms with and without views (171 vs 154 students). We found no evidence that having window views improved final exam scores (with view: median = 73.5; without view: median = 72; ΔMedian = +1.5, p = 0.27). We found the consistent results for each specific question type. Bayesian analysis further indicated that the observed data were 4.5 times more likely under the assumption of similar outcomes between the two conditions than under the assumption that performance would differ. As a post-hoc analysis, we built a linear regression model including two variables: the presence of window views as the primary variable and students’ previous achievement before the exam as an explanatory background variable. Pre-exam performance was calculated using scores from proctored quizzes, homework, activities, and attendance. We found that the benefit of having window views was negligible compared with the effect of prior achievement on final exam scores (+1.3 points with window view, p = 0.35). For now, it is difficult to suggest that having window views is associated with higher performance.

title: Ultraviolet germicidal irradiation in HVAC cooling coils: A literature review of design factors and system impacts
abstract: Cooling coils in air-conditioning systems are susceptible to biofouling because localized moisture accumulation and dense fin geometries can support microbial growth within narrow fin interstices. Biofilm formation, stabilized by extracellular polymeric substances, can create persistent microbial reservoirs and impose thermo-hydraulic penalties through reduced heat-transfer efficiency, increased airflow resistance, and higher maintenance demand. Continuous ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI) has been proposed as a proactive strategy to control coil biofouling; however, its engineering design remains constrained by complex microscale physical barriers. This review synthesizes 170 studies to clarify the interactions between UVGI systems and cooling-coil environments, linking microscale design determinants with building-level energy, maintenance, and health implications. The evidence indicates that coil disinfection performance is governed not only by nominal lamp power but also by fin-density-induced shadowing, low substrate reflectance, reduced lamp output under cold-airflow conditions, and optical attenuation by condensate films. To characterize these heterogeneous irradiance fields, advanced radiation modeling approaches, particularly Monte Carlo Ray Tracing, emerge as highly capable tools, though rigorous validation in true coil geometries remains critically needed. The review further proposes a comprehensive macro-evaluation framework that integrates operational energy recovery, maintenance savings, and health-related benefits for life-cycle assessment. While pure energy returns imply a payback of about five years, incorporating broader benefits can accelerate capital recovery to under one year; these financial outcomes are, however, context-dependent estimates rather than universal guarantees. This review provides a robust foundation for the precision design and performance evaluation of continuous UVGI interventions to maintain indoor air quality and cooling-coil energy efficiency.

title: Sex-specific thermoregulatory responses during 8-hour passive heat exposures to equivalent heat index conditions

Operationalising CIBSE TM59 for comparative overheating risk assessment in temperate climates: The dwelling overheating risk metric (DORM)
abstract: Overheating in dwellings is an emerging risk in temperate climates, yet existing assessment frameworks such as CIBSE TM59 produce room-level, pass/fail compliance outputs that are not suitable for stock-level comparative analysis. This paper introduces the Dwelling Overheating Risk Metric (DORM), a continuous, normalised indicator that aggregates TM59 exceedance criteria across all habitable rooms into a single dwelling-scale value, enabling consistent comparison across design configurations while preserving direct traceability to the underlying standard. To demonstrate the metric, a parametric simulation study was conducted using a middle-floor apartment typology representative of the Irish building stock. Dynamic building performance simulations were carried out across 288 configurations, systematically varying orientation, thermal mass, airtightness, wall U-value, window U-value, and window solar transmittance. Orientation-specific Random Forest surrogate models were then trained on the resulting dataset to enable rapid DORM prediction, achieving R² values of 0.92–0.98 and mean absolute errors below 0.11. Results show that around 5% of the parametric configurations exhibit high overheating burden (DORM >2), with 1% falling in the severe category (DORM >3). Following SHAP analysis, window solar transmittance and thermal mass were identified as the dominant determinants of overheating risk, particularly for west- and south-facing dwellings, while wall and window U-values exerted negligible influence under summer conditions. Airtightness was found to increase overheating risk when unaccompanied by controlled ventilation. The validated surrogate models are deployed in a freely accessible decision-support dashboard, enabling stakeholders to assess dwelling overheating risk and explore design alternatives without recourse to dynamic simulation

Generative artificial intelligence in building facade design: Models, applications, and future directions
abstract: Facade systems in buildings contribute significantly to buildings’ aesthetic qualities, performance, and occupants’ comfort. Recent advancements in generative artificial intelligence (AI) have created new opportunities for building design exploration. Despite the growing applications of generative AI in built environment research, a focused review study on its use in building facade research and design remains unexplored. Through content analysis and a critical review approach, this study examines the research landscape of generative AI in building facade design, with emphasis on model categories, data types, evaluation strategies, and application domains. The findings show that generative adversarial networks (GANs) remain the most widely adopted models in AI-related facade research. Also, image-based data type dominates both model input and output, while visual assessment and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) are the most frequently used evaluation methods. Furthermore, seven major application domains were identified, including facade restoration and reconstruction, design and visualization, sustainability-oriented investigations, human-centered evaluation, building and urban attribute analysis, facade deterioration and damage forecasting, as well as heritage and historic facade generation. Finally, the study identified several key research gaps, including the under exploration of autoencoder-based models, NeRF, and Gaussian Splatting, the need for more integration of generative AI with facade systems research and performance-driven design workflows, the development of architecture-specific generative AI tools, the limited adoption of geometry-aware and immersive workflows, and the underdeveloped area of human-centered facade evaluation. Overall, the review provides a foundation for advancing performance-oriented generative AI applications in facade design.

title: Urban-scale assessment of human thermal stress: A high-resolution framework incorporating intra-urban meteorological heterogeneity

Clothing-insulation diversity and shared thermal feasibility in Gulf cooling-dominated buildings
abstract: Cooling-dominated Gulf buildings routinely accommodate occupants wearing clothing ensembles with substantially different insulation levels, yet conventional thermal comfort methods evaluate only individual acceptability and provide no mechanism for assessing whether thermally diverse groups can simultaneously share the same indoor environment. This study introduces a shared thermal feasibility framework for clothing-diverse Gulf spaces. Five representative ensembles spanning intrinsic clothing-insulation values of I c l = 0.45 − − 1.27 clo were evaluated using PMV-based psychrometric analysis, and the Intersection Feasibility Index (IFI) was developed to quantify the normalized overlap between pairwise operative-temperature comfort bands. The framework included humidity and air-movement analyses, Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation, and parametric sensitivity analysis. Results showed reduced compatibility with increasing clothing-insulation divergence. A linear approximation suggested a preliminary, model-specific transition near Δ I c l = 0.73 clo (95% bootstrap interval: 0.60–0.81 clo), with a one-factor deterministic sensitivity range of 0.66–0.89 clo. The representative Western-light (W-Light) and Gulf female summer (GF-S) ensembles exhibited no shared feasible interval under the reference condition or across the evaluated humidity and air-speed ranges. Elevated humidity and increased air speed further reduced compatibility for selected ensemble pairs under the evaluated PMV assumptions. The framework formally distinguishes individual thermal comfort from shared thermal compatibility, highlighting a limitation of representative-occupant thermal design in clothing-diverse indoor environments. The study is simulation-based and uses published thermal-manikin data; field validation remains necessary.

title: Research on thermal design parameters of building walls in areas with intense solar radiation and large diurnal temperature range
Dynamic LCA of bio-based and mineral building materials: guidelines for time-explicit greenhouse gas inventories
abstract: This article aims to provide guidelines for a better understanding of dynamic climate change assessments (dCCA) by conducting reliable assessments for all types of building materials, discussing metrics and indicators, and supporting appropriate mitigation strategies. Building products emit different types of greenhouse gases (GHGs) over their life cycle, thus affecting the climate differently from short- to long-term perspectives. dCCA of product systems requires robust GHG inventories, i.e. transparent and science-based modelling hypotheses. This work focuses on temporally dynamic life cycle inventories of GHGs. Particular attention is devoted to bio-based materials and biogenic carbon, with an important distinction between agricultural and forestry products. As a matter of fact, they exhibit different GHG absorption and release dynamics, particularly with regard to end-of-life scenarios. We show that dCCA well depict the influence of one hypothesis or another on climate impacts. The dynamics of carbonation of mineral products are also carefully studied. A case study illustrates the potential of dCCA to combine the dynamics of biogenic carbon, carbonation, and process inventories in order to consider all types of products. This study concludes with guidelines for default inventory modelling to facilitate the use of dCCA.

title: Ten questions concerning stack effect issues in high-rise buildings
A human–shading interaction approach for deriving personal vertical illuminance setpoints for shading control in shared offices
abstract: The increasing adoption of shared and open-plan offices has introduced challenges in maintaining visual comfort due to variations in occupants’ daylight sensitivity and the shared consequences of shading adjustments, where one occupant’s operation may influence neighbouring users. However, empirical evidence capturing real-world daylight exposure, shading interactions, and subjective comfort responses in shared offices remains limited. This study investigates human–shading interaction as a promising approach for developing learning-based control thresholds. The Personal Vertical Illuminance Threshold (PVIT) is identified as a daylight tolerance boundary at which occupants adjust shading devices in a shared university office in Brisbane, Australia. These occupant-derived thresholds can subsequently be integrated into automated shading systems as adaptive setpoints, enabling personalised and behaviour-responsive daylight management. Data were collected over 16 working days during summer (December 2024–January 2025), with 16 participants occupying four workstations under different daylight conditions. Continuous daylight measurements from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, daily questionnaires, and direct observations of shading interactions were collected. The results reveal substantial inter-individual variability in visual comfort, demonstrating the limitations of uniform illuminance criteria in shared offices. Human–shading interaction is demonstrated as a viable alternative to conventional voting-based approaches for identifying personalised visual comfort thresholds. Despite the presence of an engaging window view, occupants tolerated only up to 20% above their preferred visual comfort thresholds, while 67% of shading adjustments occurred within 2 minutes after discomfort onset. Overall, this study provides rare real-world evidence and establishes an empirical framework for occupant-centric daylighting and personalised shading control strategies.

title: Perforated plate rectification for uniform air supply in the sudden-expansion structure of slot air terminal devices
Assessing indoor heat strain through occupant language: A framework for building thermal resilience
A dynamic stock-level life cycle assessment framework integrating material, energy, climate change scenarios, and grid decarbonization in urban commercial buildings
abstract: This study develops a dynamic building-stock life cycle assessment (LCA) framework to evaluate the temporal evolution of greenhouse gas emissions under climate change and electricity-grid decarbonization, demonstrated for 200 commercial buildings in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (USA). The time-resolved framework jointly represents material stock evolution, cyclic renovation flows, end-of-life processes, and climate-driven operational energy demand. It couples urban building energy modeling with material stock analysis and uses Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) climate projections across four Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5) together with grid-decarbonization trajectories. Foreground flows are linked to ecoinvent v3.10, and climate impacts are reported as global warming potential. Projected warming modestly reduces total energy demand because declining heating loads outweigh rising cooling requirements. Operational energy remains the dominant contributor to cumulative emissions, but grid decarbonization reduces cumulative operational emissions by ∼43% across SSPs. Construction material supply emissions are dominated early by mineral and cementitious materials, while insulation contributes an increasing share later; renovation emissions are primarily driven by plastic and bituminous materials. The framework identifies which life-cycle phases, material categories, and operational energy uses dominate emissions over time, enabling prioritization of electrification, renovation scheduling, low-carbon material procurement, and circular end-of-life strategies for long-term building-sector decarbonization.

title: Turbulence enhancement of indoor human thermal plumes under low‑Frequency pulsed ventilation: A 2D chamber study
