Leveraging Digital Twin to achieve healthy built environments: A systematic review
abstract: Digital Twin (DTw) technology creates a virtual representation of a physical environment, wherein data exchange between the physical and virtual domains supports performance-based decision-making such as targeting healthier built environments. Despite its growing adoption, how existing academic research operationalizes DTw to achieve healthy built environments has not been systematically synthesized. Adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, this study undertakes a review to examine the deployment of DTw in fostering healthier built environments. It delineates the health-related topics, spatial contexts, and core DTw layers evident in the selected literature. Based on the limitations and trends identified in the current literature, this review outlines several pivotal avenues for future investigation. These include: (1) direct human health data integration; (2) spatial context diversification; (3) advancement toward more reliable and real-time data processing; (4) deeper human-DTw integration; (5) AI-empowered DTw capabilities; and (6) evolution from Digital Models (DMs) or Digital Shadows (DSs) toward true DTws. These directions are expected to advance the development of more comprehensive and human-centric DTw for healthy built environments.

title: Dual mode thermal regulating materials for building envelopes: A review of mechanisms, performance and applications
abstract: Dual mode thermal regulating materials have emerged as a promising strategy for reducing the seasonal mismatch of conventional building envelope materials, which often provide cooling benefits in summer but cause heating penalties in winter. This review systematically examines dual mode thermal regulating materials for building envelopes from the perspectives of mechanisms, performance evaluation, climate applicability, durability, environmental impact, and practical implementation. Based on 126 peer reviewed articles, the reviewed systems are classified into passive stimulus responsive materials, active regulation systems, and hybrid systems. Active regulation includes both externally controlled chromic materials and structurally switchable systems. Their working principles are discussed in relation to solar absorptance, solar transmittance, longwave thermal emittance, and envelope heat transfer. Particular attention is given to the different evaluation requirements of opaque envelopes and transparent envelopes, as well as the climate dependence of annual heating and cooling performance. The review shows that current studies have progressed from material level optical switching to building oriented energy assessment, but standardized parameters, long term outdoor durability, environmental safety, and construction scale validation remain insufficient. Future research should prioritize climate specific design criteria, comparable performance reporting, and integration strategies that connect material functionality with realistic building operation.

title: A comprehensive framework for automatic labeling and fault detection in chillers under steady and transient states
abstract: Vapor compression chillers are important parts of HVAC systems, and their reliable operation is critical due to their high energy use and cost. Automatic Fault Detection and Diagnosis (AFDD) supports preventive maintenance by identifying and isolating faults early, helping mitigate performance issues and energy waste. Many studies assume that chiller systems work under steady state conditions and fault-free data are already known for developing an unsupervised method such as PCA. In practice, however, operational datasets are often unlabeled, and chillers frequently operate under dynamic conditions due to load variations, which are largely overlooked in most existing approaches.This study proposes a two-step methodology to address these issues. First, DBSCAN combined with Kernel PCA (DBSCAN-KPCA) is used to label unlabeled data and identify normal operating conditions even when faulty samples exist in the dataset. DBSCAB clusters similar operating conditions, and KPCA applied to each cluster to distinguish fault-free from faulty data with the help of Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA). The labeled fault-free data are then used to train an Unfold PCA (UPCA), which incorporates time-lagged variables to capture temporal dynamics and detect faults under both steady-state and dynamic conditions. The methodology was evaluated on two benchmark datasets: the ASHRAE RP-1043 chiller system with three fault types (refrigerant leakage, refrigerant overcharge, and condenser fouling) at four severity levels, and an ammonia (R-717) chiller dataset with refrigerant leakage faults.The results showed that DBSCAN-KPCA can successfully separate fault-free and faulty patterns when data is unlabeled, and UPCA achieved good fault detection accuracy at low severity levels under both steady and dynamic operation. The proposed approach also has low computational cost compared to kernel methods, which makes it more practical for online fault detection in real-world applications.

title: Dynamic audio-visual preference in waterfront walking environments: Effects of distance-layered spatial structure and soundscape
Field-informed reinforcement learning for multi-objective indoor air quality control in naturally ventilated buildings
abstract: Indoor air quality (IAQ) control in naturally ventilated buildings involves a trade-off between ventilation-driven carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) reduction and particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) infiltration from outdoor environments. This study proposes a physically consistent control framework integrating a physics-informed neural network (PINN) surrogate environment with deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for multi-objective IAQ management under stochastic field conditions. The surrogate environment was constructed from long-term measurements in an occupied office, capturing site-specific pollutant dynamics, occupant behavior, and meteorological conditions. A DRL agent then derived Pareto-optimal policies coordinating natural ventilation and air purification under practical constraints. Multi-seed uncertainty analysis evaluated policy robustness, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) interpreted decision mechanisms. During a 30-day validation period, Pareto policies outperformed measured operation and rule-based baselines. The ventilation-oriented policy eliminated CO 2 violations and reduced mean CO 2 from 776 to 619 ppm, while the purification-oriented policy reduced PM 2.5 violations from 1063 to 83 and mean PM 2.5 from 17.1 to 6.3 µ g/m 3 . Simple baselines remained constrained by the CO 2 –PM 2.5 trade-off: ventilation-only control still produced 902 PM 2.5 violations, whereas rule-based CO 2 –PM 2.5 control produced 495 CO 2 and 267 PM 2.5 violations. In contrast, the intermediate RL-derived Policy 14 achieved 70 CO 2 and 152 PM 2.5 violations. These results demonstrate that physically informed, data-driven control can bridge simulation-based optimization and real-world building operation, providing an interpretable decision-support framework for IAQ management. Its scalability should be interpreted at the methodological-workflow level rather than as direct transferability of the quantitative results or calibrated model parameters.

title: Spatiotemporal and occupant-centered assessment of circadian-effective daylight exposure in a single-sided window room in Sapporo
Indicator bias in overheating assessment: Implications for building performance simulation outcomes
abstract: With climate change, indoor overheating has become a key aspect of building performance simulation and design. Numerous indicators exist to assess overheating, each embedding different assumptions regarding temperature thresholds, exposure duration, or occupancy patterns. Practitioners thus implicitly make several methodological choices when selecting an indicator, yet the extent to which these choices influence overheating evaluation and decision-making remains largely unexplored. To that end, this study investigates how different indicators influence overheating assessments and exhibit biases towards certain housing characteristics. First, a comprehensive literature review is conducted, from which a general mathematical framework for the categorization of overheating indicators is derived. This framework introduces five key characteristics, resulting in 108 distinct indicator variations. These indicators are then applied to 10,000 variations of a Dutch terraced house, simulated via EnergyPlus. Our results reveal that the choice of threshold value (above which a room is considered overheated) is the most influential aspect and can introduce small to moderate biases in design outcomes. In particular, filtering or optimization procedures based on overheating can yield different “preferred” housing characteristics depending on the indicator used. The most affected housing characteristics are typically those that change the amplitude of indoor temperature variations, such as the floor type (thermal mass) or insulation level. Overall, this study provides critical insights for practitioners regarding overheating indicator selection, highlighting potential biases in thermal comfort assessment and decision-making.

title: Unraveling the impacts of 2D/3D urban morphology on thermal discomfort: Bridging objective and subjective perspectives under the LCZ framework
Climate-adaptive winter design day reconstruction and Variable Refrigerant Flow thermal response evaluation in severe cold climate: A PI-LSTM co-simulation framework
Evaluating the practicality of a Prandtl mixing-length model for urban airflow: Predictive fidelity vs. computational economy
abstract: Neutral urban mean-wind simulations are essential for pedestrian-level wind assessment and early-stage urban planning, but the computational cost of conventional turbulence closures often limits their use in large-scale analyses. This study evaluates the practical utility of a Prandtl mixing-length model (MLM) within a time-dependent Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) framework. MLM’s performance is validated against wind-tunnel measurements across five benchmark cases, ranging from isolated buildings to a realistic urban district (Niigata City), and compared with the standard k–ε (SKE), RNG k–ε (RNG), and large-eddy simulation (LES) models. Model performance is assessed for key mean-flow features, including windward stagnation, wake recirculation, canyon vortices, and pedestrian-level strong-wind zones. A vector accuracy score (VAS), an extension of the conventional hit-rate concept, quantifies local mean-flow agreement, while an accuracy–cost trade-off metric (TOM) summarizes computational efficiency. Results demonstrate that MLM reproduces major flow structures, including several pedestrian-level strong-wind zones, with competitive accuracy. While showing limitations in resolving fine-scale rooftop vortices, MLM yielded favorable TOM values in selected mean-flow-dominant regions. In terms of computational cost, MLM required only 2,345 core-min, representing just 15% of the cost of LES (15,746 core-min) and 70% of two-equation RANS models. These findings position MLM as a cost-effective first-pass screening option for neutral, mechanically driven urban mean-flow assessment within the tested validation envelope, rather than as a replacement for higher-fidelity RANS or LES.

title: Sensory influence and overall comfort: Combined effects of thermal, acoustic, and visual stimulus intensity in office environments
abstract: Most published research has studied the effects of poor indoor environmental quality (IEQ) conditions – such as elevated temperatures, excessive noise, visual glare, and poor air quality, in isolation, failing to account for the inherently multisensory nature of human perception. This study aimed to evaluate the independent, cross-modal, combined, and hierarchical effects of concurrent thermal, acoustic, and visual stimuli on subjective IEQ assessments. A simulated office (field-lab) experiment was conducted with 29 participants exposed to controlled variations in temperature (23°C vs. 28°C), noise (quiet vs. noisy), and lighting (glare absent vs. present) for a duration of 70 minutes. Data were analyzed using Cumulative Link Mixed Models (CLMM). Results showed that while fundamental sensory ratings remained largely independent, significant cross-modal interactions emerged during higher-order comfort evaluations. Stimulus potency analysis revealed that temperature exerted the strongest per-unit influence on overall comfort. While modeling overall comfort based strictly on physical parameters yielded only simple additive effects, modeling it based on subjective domain-specific comfort votes revealed significant interactions, including ceiling effects under multi-domain discomfort. These findings caution against simplistic linear IEQ models, emphasizing that future building design and assessment tools must account for non-linear integration mechanisms and context-dependent sensory dominance.

title: Spatial variability of indoor particle dynamics induced by the human thermal plume
abstract: The human body influences indoor particle transport through the generation of a buoyancy-driven thermal plume that modifies near-body airflow and particle dynamics. This study experimentally investigated the influence of the thermal plume on particle transport and apparent removal using a full-scale female thermal manikin (MONICA) instrumented with particulate matter sensors. Experiments were conducted in a 40 m3 controlled chamber (IRINA) under both well-mixed and non-mixed initial conditions, combining a size-resolved reference instrument with a distributed sensor network positioned on and around the manikin. At the chamber scale, size-resolved deposition loss coefficients derived from the reference instrument showed only minor differences between heated and unheated conditions, indicating a limited influence of the thermal plume on room-averaged deposition rates. In contrast, spatially resolved measurements revealed substantial local increases in apparent particle removal, particularly above the manikin, with enhancements reaching 25%. Transient experiments further showed that heating reduced particle detection times in the near-body region by 35–50%, while far-field measurements remained largely unaffected. Complementary CFD simulations were performed to visualise the flow field surrounding the manikin and support interpretation of the observed transport behaviour. Overall, the results demonstrate that the human thermal plume has a limited effect on bulk room deposition but significantly alters near-body particle transport dynamics. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for occupant-generated airflow in indoor aerosol transport, exposure assessment, and ventilation design, particularly in weakly mixed indoor environments.

title: The impact of three-dimensional spatial structure of urban block land units on carbon emissions: The case of Zhengzhou city, China
How building façade geometry and protrusion depth of external AC outlets shape anthropogenic heat dispersion: A large-eddy simulation study
abstract: Due to global warming, buildings increasingly rely on air‑conditioning (AC), whose anthropogenic heat release elevates near‑façade air temperatures and degrades outdoor thermal environments. Existing studies simplify façade geometries and overlook AC outdoor unit configurations. This study uses large-eddy simulations (LES) to examine AC-induced heat dispersion around an idealized high-rise residential building under a perpendicular approaching wind and a typical AC operating condition without solar-radiation effects. Results show that, within this setting, subtle façade-scale geometric variations markedly alter the intensity and distribution of AC-induced heat accumulation. Increasing protrusion depth of AC outlets promotes plume detachment from façades and reduces near‑wall heat accumulation. When protrusion depth increases from 0.00 m, i.e., flush with the façade, to 1.00 m, the area‑averaged mean façade temperatures ( T s ) decrease by up to 1.6 °C and 1.0 °C on windward and leeward façades, respectively. External shading affects near-wall heat transfer, particularly on the windward façade. For AC outlets flush with the façade, horizontal shading has the best heat removal effect, reducing the area‑averaged T s by 1.0°C and 0.4°C on windward and leeward façades, respectively. At a 0.5 m protrusion depth of AC outlets, the heat removal benefit of shading becomes limited, and egg-crate shading increases T s . Increasing parapet‑wall height intensifies heat accumulation and increases T s . Pedestrian-level air temperature fields are influenced by façade geometry: deeper protrusion enlarges leeward hot air zones; vertical shading intensifies them on both windward and leeward sides. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for understanding façade-scale AC heat dispersion in residential contexts.

title: Rethinking adaptive thermal comfort: The overlooked role of rooftop solar photovoltaic systems in office buildings
A visual field light distribution model for enhanced visual comfort
At the human-biodiversity interface: Experimental evidence on human well-being in semi-outdoor environments
abstract: Evidence linking nature and human well-being is compelling, yet the specific role of biodiversity remains unclear. The aim of this research is to evaluate the impact of biodiverse greenery on the design of semi-outdoor environments to enhance psychological, cognitive, physiological, and social outcomes. We conducted a within-subject experimental study on a semi-outdoor terrace in Sydney, Australia. 35 participants were exposed to two contrasting biodiversity scenarios (high vs. low). We collected data through surveys, performance tests, physiological monitoring (blood pressure, heart rate, skin conductance level, and electroencephalography), and interviews. Compared with the low biodiversity condition, the high biodiversity condition resulted in higher perceived biodiversity (d = 0.91) and naturalness (d = 0.54), greater perceived restorativeness (d = 0.41), more positive mood states (r = 0.55), and improved cognitive performance (d = 0.79). There was a significant relationship between perceived biodiversity and perceived naturalness, and both variables were strong predictors of perceived restorativeness, mood, and perceived social comfort. We observed no consistent differences in physiological outcomes between biodiversity levels. Interview responses showed that participants experienced stronger feelings of restoration, emotional relief, and connection to nature in the high biodiversity setting. These findings suggest that increasing biodiversity in semi-outdoor environments may facilitate subjective restoration, affective benefits, and attention recovery, although short-term physiological responses are less evident. The study highlights the importance of incorporating diverse vegetation communities with greater species richness, varied plant forms, layered planting structures, colours, and multisensory experiences rather than relying solely on overall green coverage to foster restorative built environments.

title: Impact of conduction and convection approaches for urban microclimate assessment: from surface temperatures to outdoor thermal comfort
abstract: Urban surface temperature is key to microclimate simulations. It has a significant impact on both outdoor comfort and building energy consumption. However, surface temperatures are particularly complex to simulate, since they require adequate consideration of radiative, conductive, convective and evaporative (in the case of porous surfaces) exchanges between the surface and its environment. Many urban microclimate models exist, based on a wide variety of conduction and convection models. The aim of this study is to assess the influence of these models on the prediction of urban surface temperatures using the SOLENE-Microclimat model. Three conduction models and four convection models are compared across three case studies with different morphologies, each subjected to summer conditions. The study includes several pavements located in France, a street canyon in an industrial district of Singapore and a typical theoretical European neighbourhood under the context of hot clear-sky summer and low wind speeds conditions. The choice of conduction and convection models influences the daily amplitude and the temporal dynamics of the evolution of the surface temperatures. Simulated results are compared with on-site measurements, where available. For the conduction model, the 3R4C model is a good compromise between accuracy of results and complexity, on a neighbourhood scale. It is more complex to conclude which convection model is most suitable, as recommendations vary according to urban surfaces – roof, wall or ground – and the time of day. In addition, a sensitivity analysis carried out on the Mean Radiant Temperature and the Universal Thermal Climate Index highlights the non-negligible influence of the conduction and convection models’ choice while assessing the outdoor thermal comfort of pedestrians.

title: Multi-objective thermodynamic optimization of indoor air distribution: entropy generation minimization integrated with ventilation effectiveness
abstract: This study presents a multi-objective thermodynamic optimization framework for indoor air distribution using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and the second law of thermodynamics. The framework minimizes total entropy generation rate ( S ˙ gen ) while simultaneously maximizing air change efficiency (ACE) and contaminant removal effectiveness (CRE), subject to thermal comfort constraints (PMV and DR). Useful Energy Loss (UEL) metric based on Tu & Chen’s approach is also examined for comparison with entropy generation minimization (EGM). Results show that single-objective EGM favors stratified displacement-like flows. However, a deliberately constructed short-circuiting configuration illustrates that entropy generation and ventilation effectiveness are not always aligned (ACE as low as 33.4%). Two-objective optimization (minimizing S gen and maximizing ACE) resolves this fundamental trade-off, improving ACE from 65.8 % to 72.7 % in side-supply configurations and reaching an ACE of 65.1 % in floor-supply modes at a lower S gen . Incorporating CRE as a third objective further identifies Pareto-optimal solutions quantifying the inherent conflicts among thermodynamic efficiency, global air renewal, and local pollutant removal in occupied zones. Optimized configurations effectively resolve the inherent trade-offs, improving ACE by 6–32% while maintaining near-minimum entropy generation. Optimized configurations consistently feature lowered or laterally offset exhausts that better exploit buoyant plumes from internal heat sources. A two-source case further shows that a contaminant source without an accompanying heat plume requires higher-momentum supply and a greater entropy-generation cost to remove. The proposed physics-based approach provides practical design guidelines for balancing second-law energy efficiency with indoor air quality in sustainable buildings.

title: Healthy and energy-efficient building retrofits: A systematic review of CFD, digital twins, and occupant-centred intelligence
abstract: Building retrofits are essential for reducing carbon emissions, improving energy efficiency, and upgrading ageing building stocks. However, interventions such as insulation, airtightness improvement, glazing replacement, and HVAC modernisation can also modify airflow, pollutant transport, thermal comfort, moisture balance, overheating risk, and occupant health. This systematic review examines the role of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), Digital Twins (DTs), occupant behaviour modelling, and machine learning in supporting intelligent, health-centred retrofit strategies. Using a PRISMA-informed methodology, studies applying CFD, DTs, or hybrid approaches to retrofit performance assessment were synthesised. The findings show that conventional energy models are useful for estimating annual energy demand but often fail to capture local airflow patterns, contaminant hotspots, thermal stratification, ventilation effectiveness, and occupant exposure risks. CFD provides detailed insight into airflow, heat transfer, pollutant dispersion, moisture transport, ventilation performance, and airborne infection transmission. Occupant behaviour, including walking, window opening, door use, and occupancy schedules, strongly influences airflow and contaminant pathways, especially in airtight retrofitted buildings. DTs further enhance retrofit assessment by integrating sensor data, predictive simulation, and adaptive control for continuous performance optimisation. Machine learning methods are increasingly used to accelerate CFD predictions, reconstruct indoor environmental fields, and support near-real-time decision-making. Although retrofits can improve winter comfort and reduce heating demand, they may also increase overheating, CO₂ concentrations, VOC accumulation, moisture-related problems, and infection vulnerability when ventilation is inadequate. To address these trade-offs, this review proposes a Retrofit Suitability Index (RSI) integrating energy efficiency, indoor air quality, thermal comfort, health protection, affordability, and user acceptance for healthier, resilient, occupant-centred retrofits.

title: Exploring indoor olfactory environments through multimodal neurophysiological responses and emotion recognition: A controlled laboratory study
Multi-objective optimization and decision-making in building retrofits: A systematic review of frameworks, trends, and research gaps
abstract: In this study, a systematic literature review is presented on optimization-based building retrofits, with an emphasis on how recent studies structure and use decision-support frameworks. The reviewed studies, published between 2020 and 2026, were classified according to the following criteria: retrofit strategies, objective functions, optimization algorithms, computational tools, climatic contexts, and the integration of Sensitivity Analysis (SA), Machine Learning (ML), Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO), and Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM). The findings show that envelope-related measures, including insulation, window, airtightness, and shading upgrades, remain the most frequently optimized strategies, followed by HVAC improvements and renewable energy integration. The dominant GA-based algorithm is NSGA-II due to its robustness in handling nonlinear, simulation-coupled, and conflicting objectives. However, the primary contribution of this review lies in identifying the fragmented but emerging integration of optimization, SA, ML, and decision-making frameworks. Recent studies have increasingly combined SA for parameter prioritization, ML for surrogate prediction and computational acceleration, MOO for Pareto-front generation, and MCDM for final solution ranking. Despite this progress, integration remains limited by insufficient surrogate-model validation, inconsistent reporting of computational costs, and inadequate assessment of uncertainty effects on Pareto-front accuracy and decision rankings. Economic and life-cycle carbon assessments also remain simplified through the use of static energy prices, fixed emission factors, and inconsistent LCA boundaries. Climatic analysis indicates a dominant focus on cold and multiple or mixed climatic contexts, whereas future climate scenarios remain insufficiently incorporated into the retrofit planning process. The most important gaps in optimization and decision-making frameworks for building retrofits include dynamic carbon and cost modeling, embodied carbon assessment, uncertainty quantification, future climate resilience, and stakeholder-informed decision-making. This review highlights the need for transparent, data-driven, and integrated assessment frameworks to support both resilient and implementable retrofit decisions.

title: Outdoor thermal comfort differences among orthopedic, oncological and chronic-disease patients in cold-region hospital spaces
CFD modeling of particle distribution in a living room for varying source locations: Impact of air-change rate and ventilation configuration
abstract: Particulate matter is a primary indoor air pollutant. A well-mixed condition for room air and particles is often employed to calculate indoor air quality and occupant exposures. However, perfect mixing (uniform concentrations) is generally difficult to achieve in practice. This implies that for example source location and ventilation configuration can influence particle distribution within indoor environments. Therefore, this study systematically investigates the impact of source locations on particle distribution in a living room using experiments and CFD simulations. The analysis considers a total of 118 source locations, three air-change rates (ACH = 1.0, 2.0, and 6.0 h -1 ), and three ventilation configurations (3 inlets and 3 outlets, Case_3I3O; 1 inlet and 3 outlets, Case_1I3O; and 3 inlets and 1 outlet, Case_3I1O). First, the CFD results of velocity and temperature are validated with experimental results. Next, the validated CFD setup is used to investigate the impact of source locations on particle distribution under different ACH and ventilation configurations. The results show that variations in source locations have a pronounced impact on particle distribution. For Case_3I3O under ACH = 2.0 h -1 , the normalized surface-averaged concentration ( C a v g * ) at the breathing plane (1.2 m height) increases by approximately 215% when comparing the source location yielding the largest C a v g * to the one yielding the lowest. For the cases studied, increasing ACH is generally a more efficient method for decreasing C a v g * than altering the ventilation configuration. This study contributes to the understanding of indoor particle distributions, providing knowledge for designing healthy indoor environments.

title: Physics-guided multimodal deep learning for thermal performance prediction of green building envelopes
Personalized or pragmatic? A critical review of machine learning and metric-based models for indoor thermal comfort estimation
Are building embodied emissions aligned with future climate pathways? A method for measuring building-sector performance and defining science-based targets
abstract: Research has made huge progress in measuring and benchmarking embodied emissions at the building level. But gaps remain in our understanding of how changes in technologies, socioeconomic pathways and construction trends could influence future embodied emission trajectories at a national and regional level. This research presents a novel methodology to measure whole of life greenhouse gas emissions of building sectors using prospective life cycle analysis (pLCA). The method provides a comparison with emissions pathways to limit global warming and establish science-based embodied emission targets to meet these pathways at the national level. This is demonstrated on the office building sector in Australia, from 2024-2049. Results show total emissions of 137.8 Mt CO2e by the end of 2049, with 45% of this from embodied emissions. A gap of 79.7 Mt CO2e is found with a < 1.5 °C emissions pathway, and 56.9 Mt CO2e to a < 2.0 °C pathway. Technological and sufficiency strategies were able to close these gaps by up to 47.1 Mt CO2e, but not completely. Upfront embodied emissions would need to reduce 37% annually to meet the 2.0 °C pathway, requiring targets of < 10 kg CO2e/m2 by 2032. If new office construction activity is halved, such drastic targets would not be required until 2046. This study shows widespread use of low carbon technologies such as mass timber are not enough to adequately reduce emissions in the Australian office sector, and sufficiency measures such as mass refurbishment and reducing new construction are essential.

title: Fungal growth on a hemp-flax-cotton biobased insulation materials and their potential to emit microbial volatile organic compounds (mVOCs)
abstract: Bio-based insulation materials contribute to building decarbonization and good hygrothermal performance. However, in humid conditions, they can promote fungal growth and the emission of mVOCs, affecting indoor air quality. The aim of this study is to assess the influence of aging on the susceptibility of bio-based materials to promote fungal growth and VOC emissions, and to investigate potential mVOC emissions. To this end, a hemp-flax-cotton insulation material was subjected to a 3-month accelerated aging process under alternating humidity cycles. The material was exposed to weekly dry (11± 4%) and humid (60± 2%) conditions at 25± 0.8°C. Native and aged materials were inoculated by fungal spores using dry aerosolization system and incubated at 95 ± 1% for 30 days. Fungal development was quantified using the cultured cell method. VOCs and SVOCs were characterized for both native and aged materials, whereas mVOC emissions were monitored from inoculated native materials on days 1, 7, 9, 15 and 30. All compounds were identified and quantified using TD-GC-MS/FID and HPLC. Results showed strong fungal proliferation on both native and aged materials, with spore concentration reaching 100–1000 times the initial inoculum. The material was identified as very low VOC emitter in its native state. Aging did not significantly modify the overall VOC emission profile. During 30 days of incubation, emissions of 74 VOCs decreased, whereas 10 newly detected compounds (1–13 µg m −2 h −1 ) appeared between days 7 and 9, peaked on day 9, and then progressively declined, suggesting fungal metabolic degradation of the material.

title: A physics-guided multi-task framework for joint forecasting of heating load and return temperatures at building-side district heating substations
Multimodal fusion-based dynamic thermal comfort prediction for cross-subject generalization
A physics-informed framework for physically stable reconstruction of indoor wall jet ventilation flow fields via finite-volume weak constraints and physics-guided regularization
Washbasin hygiene trap: quantifying droplet inhalation risks during near-facial respiratory proximity behavior
Street space as health infrastructure: diagnosing uneven street support for exercise through the spatial triad
Multi-objective optimization for multi-zone HVAC system via physics-integrated predictive control framework with CFD-assisted visualization
From omnidirectional to directional SVF: Summer day–night thermal characterization in high-density residential blocks
Scenario-based dynamic life-cycle assessment of large-space public buildings using a dual-functional unit approach: Gymnasium cases across climate zones in China
Field measurement and numerical simulation of turbulent dispersion effect of wind-driven rain on a building in an urban street canyon
Information entropy-guided fast dimensionality reduction CFD-TRNSYS coupling for piston wind and phase change material (PCM) energy saving in subway stations
Evaluation strategy of human thermal comfort in ship cabins considering vibration: Integrating human exergy model, heart rate and SHAP analysis
The associations between non-acoustic temporal factors and subjective evaluations of sound perception in the built environment: A systematic review
abstract: Non-acoustic factors in subjective evaluations of sound perception often exhibit temporal characteristics. Evidence on associations between such non-acoustic temporal factors and perception remains fragmented, and the role of these factors in human–sound environment interactions has yet to be systematically understood. Based on 107 studies, this systematic review develops a classification scheme and synthesizes evidence with bias assessment. The main findings are as follows: (1) A taxonomy classifies 4 perceptual dimensions (Perceived Acoustic Attributes, Noise Annoyance, Perceived Quality, and Soundscape Assessment) and 10 factors (categorized into personal and situational domains). The former domain reflects individual temporal characteristics and the latter comprises subdomains of exposure time and temporal positioning. (2) Evidence with acceptable bias indicates the following significant patterns. For exposure time, evidence of short-term exposure (typically minute-scale) consistently shows longer experimental stimulus duration is associated with higher annoyance, whereas evidence of medium- and long-term exposure (hour- and month-scale) shows a longer average time spent and time elapsed since an event link with lower annoyance in some instances. For temporal positioning, season could link with Noise Annoyance and Perceived Quality, day of the week with Perceived Quality, and time of the day with Perceived Acoustic Attributes, Noise Annoyance, and Perceived Quality. However, the predominance of non-significant results suggests practical relevance of temporal positioning warrants cautious interpretation. (3) Preliminary evidence suggests acoustic or visual environmental factors could moderate associations between exposure-time-related factors and Noise Annoyance. This review proposes a framework to integrate non-acoustic temporal factors into sound environment research and practice.

title: Influence of pressure wave characteristics induced by two high-speed maglev trains intersecting in a tunnel
Built environment constraints on well-being in resource-based cities
abstract: Natural resources have long supported economic development, yet cities dependent on resource extraction often face persistent challenges in urban livability. While literature has largely focused on macroeconomic outcomes, less attention has been paid to residents’ everyday experiences and the environmental pathways through which resource dependence shapes well-being. This study examines how resource dependence is associated with subjective well-being through residents’ perceptions of the built environment in resource-based cities (RBCs). Using a large-scale national survey dataset from China, we apply an XGBoost–SHAP framework to identify built-environment predictors of happiness in RBCs and non-RBCs. The results reveal a clear divergence between economic performance and well-being. At the micro level, happiness in RBCs is more strongly associated with basic environmental conditions—particularly safety, infrastructure reliability, and environmental risks—than with consumption-oriented amenities. Heterogeneity analyses further show that this pattern is consistent across social groups but places disproportionate constraints on vulnerable populations, including low-income residents, migrants, and older adults. By foregrounding the built environment as a key mediating pathway, this study shifts attention from production-oriented development to the environmental conditions of everyday urban life, offering a more grounded perspective on the well-being implications of resource dependence and informing policy efforts aimed at improving livability in resource-dependent cities.

title: Addressing data sparsity in thermal comfort evaluation: A dynamic constraint relaxation framework using large language models
Geometric, subjective, and model evaluation of design indoor environmental quality in residential buildings
abstract: Buildings’ indoor environmental quality (IEQ) influences occupants and sustainability by multiple interacting aspects. Therefore, this research introduces a methodology for assessing design-related aspects of IEQ (design-IEQ) and how they are perceived by users. It expands beyond traditional physical-IEQ (thermal, visual, acoustic, and air quality) to include sufficiency-related aspects like size, openness to the outdoors and flexibility. In two stages a total of 74 participants rated their IEQ perception at Living Lab NRW in Wuppertal, using seven model houses with varying sustainable design features. Design-IEQs were quantified through geometric methods including area proportions, areas, or numbers. Participant perceptions of both physical and design-IEQs were captured via repeated questionnaires that extended standard physical-IEQ evaluations to incorporate design aspects. The association between objective and perceived IEQ was analysed using cumulative link mixed models including ceiling effects. Results of this exploratory analysis suggest relationships between geometric measures of design-IEQs and surveyed perception for selected design-IEQs. Specifically, increased openness to the outdoors had a positive association with size perception despite no increase in area resource demand, while flexibility was negatively associated with size perception but allowed more efficient use of available space through adaptable furniture. A multidomain analysis further revealed associations of these design elements with visual, thermal, and privacy perception. The proposed approach streamlines measurement and comparison of design-IEQs alongside physical-IEQs, providing an integrated framework for linking user perception with building design characteristics. The results could support methods aiming at the optimization of space sufficiency in residential buildings by addressing design and physical-IEQs.

title: Airflow acceptability and thermal comfort of neck-side ventilation as a wearable personalized ventilation strategy
Morphology–crowd coupling and mitigation of pedestrian-level PM2.5 exposure in summer night markets: interpretable machine learning and CFD across compact LCZs
Ventilated solar façades in multi-storey buildings: natural ventilation with flow confluences
abstract: Effectively utilising solar facades combined with natural ventilation is vital for future zero-carbon buildings. However, the thermal-flow coupling and natural convection mechanisms in multi-inlet vertical airflow networks remain unclear, obstructing ventilation designs and energy consumption evaluations. To address this gap, we investigated the inter-storey flow interference within multi-storey solar facades. A numerical model validated using existing results and Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) experiments analyses the vertical cavity flow field. The result illustrates a non-linear impact of the flow confluence on the ventilation performance at different floors, with a flow area contraction of 41%, 58%, 66% and 74% on the 2nd to 5th floor, respectively. A mathematical model was hence developed to estimate the dynamic discharge coefficient ( C d _ m ) of multi-storey NVDSF. Based on the derived coefficients for multi-storey buildings, we proposed to establish a ventilation satisfaction rate based on the air change rate (ACH). Through the analysis of annual climate data from two cities,we obtained ventilation satisfaction that is jointly influencedby floor-wise confluence coefficients and outdoor solar radiation intensities, thereby providing a more accurate analytical basis for assessing the natural ventilation potential and energy saving rates for multi-storey buildings.

title: Evaluating passenger pressure comfort inside the train under pressure change: Mechanistic analysis and thresholds determination based on multi-source data
Impact of wind on pedestrian comfort in the urban environment: wind discomfort, heat stress and rain exposure
abstract: ABSTRACT This study addresses the interaction between pedestrian wind, thermal, and rain exposure comfort in a high-rise urban environment, using Geneva, Switzerland, as a case study. Multiscale simulations with urbanMicroclimateFoam and w indDrivenRainFoam are used to quantify wind comfort, heat stress during heatwaves, and annual rain exposure. The results show that high-rise induced downflow, corner streams and channeling flows generate localized wind acceleration, increasing wind discomfort and rain exposure in exposed street corridors while simultaneously improving thermal conditions during heatwaves through enhanced ventilation. In contrast, thermal discomfort concentrates in sun-exposed courtyards and near south-facing façades with limited shading, whereas sheltered zones such as building wakes reduce wind and rain exposure. For this specific case study, wind discomfort affects 39% of the pedestrian area, strong and very strong heat stress together cover 91.5%, and 97% of the domain exhibits rain exposure values above 0.9, indicating generally high exposure conditions across most pedestrian spaces. Wind and thermal discomfort overlap in only 8% of the study area, indicating that wind-exposed discomfort zones are generally associated with comparatively more favorable thermal conditions. The overlap regions of wind discomfort, excessive heat stress, and high rain exposure are limited but spatially concentrated in key pedestrian areas, where multiple stressors coincide. These findings highlight the multidimensional and sometimes conflicting nature of pedestrian comfort, where mitigation of one stressor may exacerbate another. Although case-specific, they indicate that priority should be given to these overlapping high-stress zones, particularly in areas of intense pedestrian activity such as waiting areas, and resting spaces.

title: Omnidirectional terrain category determination and refined wind field assessment in island cities based on UAV aerial photography and image recognition
Experimental and numerical analysis of evaluating the cooling potential of a green wall in a controlled chamber
Comfort-constrained zonal temperature control for subway platforms under train-induced piston airflow
abstract: Train-induced piston airflow in subway tunnels can cause spatially non-uniform airflow on platforms, leading to localized variations in transient passenger thermal comfort. This study proposes a comfort-constrained zonal temperature control strategy for an overtaking subway station with adjustable platform screen door vents. A validated three-dimensional unsteady CFD model with dynamic mesh is developed to reveal platform airflow characteristics. The Relative Warmth Index (RWI) is used to quantify transient thermal comfort in different platform zones, followed by temperature sensitivity analysis to determine appropriate zonal setpoints. The energy-saving potential is then evaluated by comparing the sensible cooling loads under different control strategies. The results show that the acceptable thermal comfort ratios at the arrival end, middle section, and departure end are 92.4%, 90.0%, and 67.6%, respectively, identifying the departure end as the most unfavorable zone. Among the five proposed zonal air temperature control schemes, Scheme C achieves the best overall performance, by setting the arrival end, middle section, and departure temperatures at 25.4 °C, 25.7 °C, and 24.1 °C, respectively. This scheme increases the average acceptable thermal comfort ratio from 83.3% to 86.2% and reduces the maximum inter-zone difference from 24.8% to 3.3%. Under the same departure-end comfort constraint, Scheme C increases the equivalent platform temperature by approximately 1 °C and reduces the outdoor-air sensible cooling load by about 2.26 kW, while recirculated-air sensible cooling load remains unchanged. The theoretical electricity-saving potential is approximately 1080-2430 kWh per platform.

title: Radar‑based breathing detection towards emotion‑responsive lighting: Laboratory studies with robot simulations and human occupants under varied occupancy
abstract: The built environment plays an important role in human well-being, performance, and daily activities. Lighting, one of the primary indoor environmental quality factors, not only influences vision but also physiological and psychological processes associated with autonomic regulation, with respiration frequency serving as a measurable indicator. The feasibility of using millimetre-wave radar for 1) occupancy detection, 2) respiration frequency estimation, and 3) exploration of respiration frequency as an indicator for emotion-aware systems was investigated using two experimental frameworks. First, a controlled setup using two custom-built Controlled Airflow Thorax robots (CAT-bots) simulated consistent chest movements to systematically evaluate occupancy detection and respiration frequency estimation across scenarios with zero, one, or two occupants at varying distances from the radar. The second experiment included human participants (individually or in pairs) seated at different distances from the radar, watching emotion-evoking videos. Radar performance was evaluated with real occupants and examined whether radar-estimated breathing frequency varied across different emotional states (high/low valence/arousal). The results showed reliable occupancy detection, with weighted F1-scores of above 0.90 for both experiments. Respiration frequency estimation achieved 80% within a clinically meaningful tolerance of ±3 bpm. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed that radar respiration frequency was significantly different for high versus low arousal videos, while no significant differences were observed across valence conditions. The findings demonstrate the feasibility of radar-based occupancy and respiration monitoring in indoor environments with varying occupancy; however, the small arousal-related differences relative to the estimation accuracy indicate that further investigation is required before respiration frequency can support emotion-responsive lighting systems.

title: Editorial Board
Higher chroma, not hue, may elevate attentional load during continuous reading: A factorial EEG study under near-neutral chromatic illumination
Wind’s dual influence on user comfort in pocket parks: A threshold experiment on mechanical and thermal effects
One heatwave, many definitions: Implications for global building performance analysis
Ankle draft risk model under winter clothing conditions
abstract: The ankle draft model in ASHRAE Standard 55 was derived from studies where participants mainly wore summer clothing with exposed ankles (∼0.6 clo), potentially leading to overly conservative perimeter heating or facade insulation requirements in winter conditions where occupants typically wear long trousers, socks, and closed-toe shoes (∼0.75 clo). We evaluated thermal comfort responses to ankle-level draft under these conditions in controlled laboratory experiments with 51 participants. In a within-subjects repeated-measures design, participants were exposed to nine conditions varying in ankle-level air temperature (17–20 °C) and air speed (0.1–0.7 m/s), simulating window downdraft. The existing ankle draft model systematically overpredicted dissatisfaction across all conditions. While prior studies with exposed ankles reported dissatisfaction rates of 23–57%, we observed only 6–20%, with the existing model overestimating by an average of 2.3 times and by as much as 30% at high air speeds. We developed separate generalized linear mixed-effects models for covered- and uncovered-ankle conditions from this and prior studies. The covered-ankle model showed lower baseline dissatisfaction risk and reduced sensitivity to air speed. Only whole-body thermal sensation and ankle-level air speed were significant predictors; ankle-level air temperature and room temperature were non-significant within tested ranges. These results are subject to a 20-minute exposure duration and the exclusion of radiant asymmetry from cold window surfaces. These findings support differentiating ASHRAE Standard 55 ankle draft criteria by clothing level. Adopting a covered-ankle criterion could enable meaningful reductions in perimeter heating and facade insulation without compromising occupant comfort, with benefits for energy use and carbon emissions.

title: Ventilation and air conditioning design for interconnected large-space underground pumped storage power stations and prediction method for spatial temperature distribution
Urban heat mitigation assessment based on surface unsealing potential and microclimate modelling
abstract: Global climate change causes rising temperatures and more frequent heat waves in Central European cities. Combined with ongoing urban densification, this exacerbates the urban heat island (UHI) effect. Consequently, city residents are increasingly exposed to heat stress and related health risks. Climate change adaptation measures, such as unsealing impermeable surfaces, are required to reduce heat loads in the urban fabric. To our knowledge, the cooling performance of unsealing measures at the neighborhood scale - based on an assessment of potential areas suitable for unsealing - has not been previously analysed. To fill this research gap, we developed a mixed-method approach consisting of (a) a scoring framework to identify areas with unsealing potential, and (b) a sensor-validated microclimate model (ENVI-met) to simulate the cooling effects. Analyses were performed for two 16-hectare urban study areas in Cologne, Germany, both significantly affected by the UHI effect. Three model scenarios of low, medium, and high unsealing potential were simulated in each study area to investigate the heat mitigation performance compared to the status-quo. We found a statistically significant mean cooling effect of up to -1.28 K on for temperature at pedestrian height during a simulated 3-day heat event. The mean physiological equivalent temperature (PET) was reduced by up to -4.91 K. The findings highlight the effectivity of unsealing in the urban fabric and demonstrate the relevance of this combined assessment approach to support strategical decision making in urban planning.

title: Thermal sensation differences among BMI groups
Constraint-aware generative operation strategy for multiple AHUs using graph recurrent forecasting
Size-resolved airborne particle control in a dental operatory: field comparison of window opening, portable air purifier, and UV air disinfection
How do heated and ventilated seats affect the driving experience: A vehicle case study
High-resolution urban air temperature mapping and interpretable multi-scale built-environment analysis for climate adaptation in a severe cold-region city
Full-scale experimental assessment of a radiant-capacitive cooling system driven by nocturnal and diurnal radiative cooling
abstract: ABSTRACT We demonstrate a full-scale radiant-capacitive cooling system (RCCS) capable of maintaining continuous thermal comfort during hot summer conditions without using mechanical refrigeration, thanks to a combination of sky radiators with water-filled radiant-capacity ceiling panels. Tested in twin full-scale cells under clear-sky conditions, the RCCS maintained operative temperatures within the adaptive comfort limit for 94% of the monitoring period when uncoated and for 100% when the radiators were coated with a commercial passive daytime radiative cooling (PDRC) material. The experimental cell exhibited temperatures on average 6–7 K cooler than the control cell, with peak daily reductions in indoor maximum temperature up to 12 K. Sky radiators produced a median cooling potential of about 56 W m⁻² (43–74 W m⁻² across the series), while the ceiling panels removed an average of 2.8–3.2 kWh per day (432-494 Wh/m 2 ∙day), depending on configuration. Applying the PDRC material extended effective cooling by 2–4 hours per day and increased daily delivered cooling energy by more than 10%. Multiple-regression models based on climatic and operational variables explain the observed temperature reductions and cooling potential of the sky radiators. These results indicate that a low-complexity, water-based radiative cooling system built from widely available components can significantly improve thermal comfort in well-insulated buildings during extreme heat without mechanical refrigeration.

title: Physics-informed deep learning model for predicting outdoor temperature field incorporating building anthropogenic heat emission
Field evaluation of dynamic bedroom air-temperature control for sleep in real homes: implementation fidelity and exploratory sleep outcomes
Predicting public building energy consumption in the early design stage using a multi-agent LLM for occupant behavior simulation
abstract: Accurate building energy prediction at the early design stage is essential for low-carbon design decisions, but its reliability is often limited by incomplete design information and simplified assumptions about occupant behavior. This study proposes a design-stage energy prediction framework for hospital outpatient buildings that integrates BIM-based layout information, scenario-based environmental variables, AI agent-generated occupant behavior data, and data-driven prediction models. Three outpatient campuses in Wuhan, China, were used as case studies. A multi-agent simulation process was developed to generate occupant behavior logs under outpatient service scenarios, from which temporal, spatial, service-process, interaction, and energy-related behavior variables were extracted. Four benchmark models selected from representative recent building energy prediction studies, namely multiple linear regression, TLBO-ANN, Transformer, and temporal fusion transformer, were then compared under a unified evaluation setting. The results show that the temporal fusion transformer achieved the best overall performance, with an MSE of 69,400, an MAE of 181, a MAAPE of 0.052, and an R^2 of 0.933. Incorporating AI agent-generated behavior variables improved all benchmark models, reducing MSE by 19.1--19.8% and increasing R^2 by 1.97--3.53%. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further indicate that temporal occupancy features, HVAC usage duration, zone-level occupancy, and service-process variables are key drivers of prediction performance. The proposed framework provides a practical way to incorporate simulated occupant behavior into early-stage energy prediction and offers decision support for low-carbon hospital outpatient building design.

title: Urban microclimate-soil thermal interactions in high-altitude construction zones: Coupled modeling and observational evidence from Nagqu City, Tibetan Plateau
Experimental assessment of the CO2 phytoremediation efficiency of living walls in indoor environments
abstract: Living walls (LWs) are bio-based systems with potential to improve indoor air quality (IAQ) by mitigating carbon dioxide (CO2) accumulation. This study experimentally assessed the CO2 phytoremediation performance of two passive LWs installed in a full-scale climatic chamber (4.3 × 3.3 × 2.7 m) and composed of the species Spathiphyllum, Philodendron hederaceum, and Epipremnum aureum. Tests were performed at 20 °C and 24 °C under three lighting levels (LED OFF, LED ON 50 %, and LED ON 100 %) using decay and pulse protocols. Decay tests quantified intrinsic CO2 removal through the decay constant k, half-decay time t1/2, cumulative exposure M, and equivalent airflow rate Q. Under illumination, k increased from 0.00566 min-1 (OFF) to 0.00816 min-1 at 20 °C and 0.01105 min-1 at 24 °C, reducing cumulative exposure by up to 44 %. The equivalent airflow rate increased from 13.0 m3 h-1 (OFF) to 18.8 m3 h-1 and 27.6 m3 h-1 at 20 °C and 24 °C, respectively. Pulse tests simulated the CO2 production of approximately three school-age children and were evaluated relative to the LED OFF condition. The final CO2 increase was reduced by 20% to 27% and 35% to 39% at 20 °C for 50% and 100% LED intensity, and by 26% to 27% and 33% to 37% at 24 ◦C. Under full illumination, the apparent respiratory load decreased from 3.3 to 2.1 occupants. Overall, passive LWs provide a measurable contribution to indoor CO2 mitigation and can complement hybrid ventilation strategies.

title: High-fidelity spatiotemporal prediction of thermal environments in hybrid HVAC-conditioned open-plan offices using a coupled BES–CFD framework
Energy-saving performance of a temperature-adaptive thermally activated wall integrated with solar photothermal utilization and radiative cooling

GFNO: A generalized Fourier neural operator framework for wind flow field reconstruction from sparse observations
abstract: This study proposes the Generalized Fourier Neural Operator (GFNO), a modular framework for reconstructing high-resolution wind fields from sparse sensor observations. GFNO decouples sparse flow reconstruction into an embedding stage that transforms irregular observations into latent grid representations and a Fourier-based operator stage that reconstructs the full flow field.The framework systematically combines four representative embeddings with three Fourier kernels under a unified physics-informed objective. GFNO is evaluated on two complementary datasets, including Dataset I containing 2,000 transient flow snapshots under fixed sensor locations and Dataset II containing 3,360 mean flow fields with varying building layouts, inflow directions under various sensor placements.Results reveal that the optimal embedding strategy depends strongly on dataset characteristics. For Dataset I, multilayer perceptron (MLP) embeddings outperform alternatives because geometric information provides no additional discriminative signal under fixed configurations. In contrast, for Dataset II with varying layouts and sensor placements, graph neural network (GNN) embeddings consistently achieve best performance, highlighting the importance of geometric priors in cross-configuration reconstruction.Across all datasets, U-Net-augmented FNO (U-FNO) consistently delivers best performance, indicating the importance of recovering localized flow structures in sparse reconstruction. Sensor counts from 4 to 32 are systematically investigated, revealing that reconstruction accuracy in Dataset I saturates beyond 16 sensors, whereas GNN-based models in Dataset II maintain near-saturated accuracy with as few as four sensors.Complementary out-of-distribution evaluations assess robustness under unseen inflow conditions and limited training data. The proposed framework provides an efficient data-driven evaluation tool for urban flow reconstruction under complex interference configurations.

title: Strategic decarbonisation of Norwegian non-residential buildings: life-cycle, energy and circularity evidence with Danish and German comparators
abstract: Public evidence on low-carbon non-residential buildings is expanding, yet it remains fragmented across life-cycle assessment (LCA), operational energy, reuse, recycling, transport, design for disassembly and digital documentation. An auditable synthesis is developed for six Norwegian flagship projects and their interpretation against selected Danish and German policy, certification and practice comparators. The reframed scope is Norway-centred, with Denmark and Germany used as contextual comparators rather than as equal statistical samples. The method comprised a review of 156 sources, including 84 peer-reviewed journal and conference papers, together with structured case selection, module-based LCA coding, energy-performance interpretation, circularity assessment and ordinal evidence-visibility scoring. The Norwegian cases are Powerhouse Kjørbo, Powerhouse Brattørkaia, Kristian Augusts gate 13, HasleTre, Zero Emission Buildings (ZEB) Laboratory and Ruseløkka School. Danish and German comparators include Green Solution House 2.0, EDGE Südkreuz Berlin, Alnatura Campus Darmstadt and the wider Danish and German regulatory and certification systems. The resulting synthesis is primarily qualitative, as only Powerhouse Kjørbo and Ruseløkka School provide open module-or category-level carbon indicators, and these indicators use different boundaries and reporting categories. A key cross-case insight is that sustainability labels and pilot status do not guarantee reproducibility: underlying quantities, product-to-EPD mappings, transport assumptions and post-occupancy data are often restricted by ownership, confidentiality, fragmented responsibility or communication-oriented reporting. The strongest documented strategies are combinations of retention or material efficiency, verified low-carbon products, reuse, recycled content, short logistics, reversible connections, material passports, low operational demand and renewable energy. Reported indicators include 70% greenhouse-gas reduction and almost 80% material reuse at Kristian Augusts gate 13, about 60% lower emissions reported for HasleTre, about 485,000 kWh yr -1 photovoltaic generation at Powerhouse Brattørkaia and about 60–61% total greenhouse-gas reduction in the as-built Ruseløkka School climate account. AI-supported BIM-to-LCA matching, early carbon prediction, energy surrogate modelling and circular logistics are discussed as an auditable decision-support layer derived from the wider literature, rather than as workflows already implemented in the nine cases.

title: Deep learning based determination of thermal-optical and light transmission properties of complex fenestration systems for high throughput applications
abstract: Physically detailed thermal–optical models for complex fenestration systems (CFSs) are computationally expensive, particularly when evaluating glazing and shading systems with strong angular dependence. This limits the practical use of ISO 15099-based calculations in large-scale design exploration, optimisation, and building-performance simulation workflows. This study investigates whether a physics-informed neural surrogate can reproduce ISO 15099-derived thermal-optical response fields while retaining sufficient fidelity for building-scale simulation. A TabNet-based surrogate was developed using 5,760 ISO 15099-compliant façade configurations and trained to predict 145-dimensional SHGC distributions together with directional-hemispherical visible transmittance. Results show that the surrogate reconstructs these high-dimensional response fields with substantially lower error than an interpolation-based k-nearest-neighbour benchmark, reducing SHGC RMSE from 0.0372 to 0.0074 and visible-transmittance RMSE from 0.0423 to 0.0075. Relative to deterministic ISO 15099 calculations, evaluation time decreases from 57.78 s to 2.25 × 10⁻⁴ s per façade configuration. Learning-curve analysis indicates stable convergence, limited evidence of overfitting, and robust performance across different training-data fractions and random initialisations. An ablation study further demonstrates that physics-informed weighting of physically sensitive and energetically relevant angular regions improves prediction accuracy compared with a conventional loss formulation. To assess downstream applicability, surrogate-predicted SHGC fields were propagated into annual TRNSYS simulations for Stuttgart and Doha climates. For both locations, more than 92% of configurations remained within 5% deviation of ISO 15099 reference results and more than 98% remained within 10%, indicating that local prediction errors are largely attenuated at building scale. The results demonstrate that physics-informed surrogate modelling can extend detailed fenestration analysis to high-throughput façade design, optimisation, and building-performance simulation workflows.

title: AI agent-enhanced energy-use behavior detection in residential buildings

Creating thermal refuges with low‑energy cooling: effectiveness of evaporative coolers
abstract: Heatwaves increasingly endanger public health, underscoring the urgent need for low-energy cooling strategies suitable for emergency use. Among them, evaporative cooling (EC) systems represent a promising solution to create temporary thermal refuge areas with minimal energy and infrastructure requirements, especially under hot and dry conditions. However, experimental evidence on their real cooling potential, particularly under different ventilation and boundary conditions, remains limited. This study investigates the thermal performance of two EC systems, a whole-room unit and a personal-scale device, through laboratory tests in a controlled climate chamber (5 × 5 × 2.53 m) set at 32°C. We assessed: (i) indoor air temperature and humidity offsets, (ii) spatial airflow and turbulence distributions, and (iii) cooling effects (CE) measured using a thermal manikin. We found that the whole-room EC reduced air temperature by up to 2.8 K and increased relative humidity from 15-20% up to 52%, while producing an average CE of 3 K on the manikin and over 5 K in upper body regions. When combined with a personal EC, the CE rose to 6 K, despite limited additional air temperature reduction. Spatial mapping revealed heterogeneous airflow and turbulence, which enhanced convective heat transfer. Energy demand was small (220 W and 10 W for the whole-room and personal ECs, respectively), while water consumption averaged 2.6 L/h (0.034 L/h⋅m³). These findings show that evaporative cooling can provide rapid, effective thermal relief with low energy use, offering a scalable solution for protecting vulnerable populations during extreme heat events.

title: Ventilation-driven removal of laser-cleaning-generated submicron aerosols in confined built environments: Effects of source material, airflow characteristics, and internal structures

Machine learning surrogate models for moisture-risk prediction in cross-laminated timber wall assemblies under wind-driven rain leakage
abstract: Numerical hygrothermal simulations are widely used to assess the moisture durability of mass timber envelopes, but their computational cost limits their use in large-scale probabilistic assessments. Machine learning surrogate models offer a faster alternative, yet their reliability for predicting the nonlinear moisture response of cross-laminated timber (CLT) wall assemblies under wind-driven rain (WDR) leakage remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates Random Forest (RF), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models for predicting temperature, relative humidity (RH), and moisture content (MC) at the exterior surface of CLT panels. The models were trained and tested using DELPHIN-generated data covering four CLT wall configurations, four orientations, 17 Canadian climates, and two moisture-loading scenarios: no leakage and 1% WDR leakage applied to the CLT surface. Under no-leakage conditions, all models predicted temperature accurately, with R 2 values greater than 0.99. For RH and MC, LSTM and CNN outperformed RF, while LSTM achieved high accuracy with shorter training time. Under WDR leakage, LSTM and CNN reproduced the main moisture response trends for assemblies with vapor-permeable exterior insulation. However, prediction accuracy decreased substantially for assemblies with vapor-impermeable exterior insulation, where leakage caused localized water retention, high moisture accumulation, and delayed drying. In these cases, MC predictions showed R 2 values below 0.60. The results indicate that LSTM-based surrogate models can support efficient simulation-based hygrothermal assessment of CLT wall assemblies under normal moisture loading and WDR-leakage conditions with sufficient drying potential, but physics-informed models are needed for restricted-drying conditions dominated by liquid-water transport and moisture storage.

Accounting for female thermal requirements in ISO 7730: Biophysical modelling for equitable HVAC control
abstract: HVAC setpoints in European offices follow ISO 7730, whose metabolic input is calibrated to a male reference morphotype and applied uniformly across the workforce. It does not account for sex differences in body composition and basal metabolism, which may contribute to female thermal dissatisfaction. To quantify this bias, a stochastic biophysical pipeline ( per cohort) was evaluated against the CBE Thermal Comfort Database II (within-building analysis, office observations, buildings). Heat production integrates the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, a bounded body composition model, and DuBois body surface area. Two clothing scenarios were simulated: S1 (identical clothing, ) and S2 (asymmetric seasonal clothing). Under S1, basal metabolic dimorphism yields a baseline of (parametric interval about the quadrature central value of : ; ), an age-dependent shift in neutral skin temperature calibrated on the SWAN menopausal cohort ( ). Under S2, clothing asymmetry amplifies from (winter) to (summer). The ISO 7730 input exceeds the simulated female surface metabolic flux by . Within buildings, women exhibit a higher neutral temperature than men ( , interval excluding zero), as predicted. At the standard setpoint, of female occupants fall outside their summer comfort band, against of males. A building-management control law is discretized at . At parity ( ), S2 yields ; S1 a biophysical target of under clothing convergence. Both are deployable as software-only updates aligned with European energy-sufficiency objectives.

abstract:  Probabilistic GHG displacement factors developed for timber frame wall systems. Monte Carlo captures uncertainty in EPD data and national End-of-Life scenarios. Whole life cycle displacement factor mean of +0.33 kgCO2e/kgCO2e biogenic, with 95% uncertainty interval -0.15 to +0.99. The mean share of displacement factor contribution is 70% for module A, 22% for module C, and 8% for module D.  Main influencers of displacement for module A are masonry and insulation emissions, for module C-D are wood product and masonry EOL pathways.
