Minimum Viable Data (MVD) for digital twinning: Underserved community energy representation in data scarcity scenarios
abstract: Underserved communities often face disproportionately high energy burdens, yet lack access to detailed audits and sensor-based data collection networks that conventional energy studies require. This paper proposes and evaluates a “Minimum Viable Data” (MVD) framework for community-scale digital twinning under conditions of data scarcity. Using electricity billing data, appliance-level consumption records, and publicly available property assessment records for 17 single-family homes in Atlanta, we identify which minimal inputs are sufficient to generate actionable insights to alleviate energy cost burdens. Findings show that monthly billing data combined with assessor records can reveal household vulnerability and risk profiles, with assessed property value emerging as a stronger predictor of proxy energy burden than physical building attributes. Spatial mapping within the digital twin identifies geographic patterns of energy disparity that are less apparent in tabular datasets. This visualization allows for the differentiation between building-related energy losses and household economic constraints. Although appliance-level disaggregation validated consumption patterns, the results demonstrate that high-frequency monitoring is not essential for effective intervention planning. The study concludes that the MVD framework can effectively isolate high-priority households. Specifically, k-means clustering identified a high burden outlier group comprising 17.6% of the sample (n=3), with proxy energy burdens ranging from 24.8% to 36.7% and energy intensities up to 1.99 kWh/ft2. These findings demonstrate that MVD based digital twins can differentiate between structural inefficiencies and economic vulnerability without the need for invasive sensor based audits.

title: Advancements in occupant-centric comfort using artificial intelligence
abstract: Universal comfort standards provide baseline guidance but fail to capture individual variability. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based personalised comfort models (PCMs) address this gap by modelling complex, context-dependent responses. However, methodological fragmentation, spanning feature selection, comfort integration, outcome definition, and evaluation, along with the lack of standardised benchmarks and deployment frameworks, continues to limit reproducibility, comparability, and practical deployment. To address these research gaps, a PRISMA-based systematic review of 92 AI-driven PCM studies was conducted, supported by sensitivity analyses across the reviewed literature and a random-effects meta-analysis of 7 eligible studies. This review synthesises thermal perception outcomes and correlations in PCMs, reviews sensing, data collection, modelling and evaluation practices, and consolidates guidance for reproducible, scalable PCM modelling. Findings indicate that thermal comfort is multifaceted, requiring outcome-driven models. Correlation analysis confirms this, identifying environmental and physiological variables as key drivers whose associations vary by prediction index. Air temperature best predicts most comfort indices, while skin temperature strongly correlates with thermal sensation (r≈0.66). Sensing strategies and study designs vary widely, driving heterogeneity in intrusiveness, sample size, and data density. Model performance evaluation is largely classification-based, although inconsistent rankings across performance metrics demonstrate that accuracy alone is inadequate. Despite methodological variation, deep-learning, random-forest, and boosting models consistently achieve high predictive performance (>80% accuracy), with meta-analytic evidence confirming the robustness of ensemble approaches under substantial heterogeneity. In conclusion, AI-based PCM models demonstrate strong predictive capability, but effective deployment depends on outcome-aligned design, appropriate sensing choices, and evaluation frameworks that reflect the multidimensional nature of thermal comfort.

title: Task-dependent effects of dynamic daylight on alertness and cognitive control in a university multimedia classroom
Provincial heterogeneity in carbon mitigation potential of lightweight modular integrated construction for urban housing in China: A scenario-based LCA study
Combined effects of cool material coatings and vertical greening on pedestrian thermal comfort in street canyons
abstract: Urban overheating has intensified pedestrian heat exposure in street canyons, while the combined effects of cool material coatings and vertical greening remain insufficiently quantified. This study developed a three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics framework coupling radiation, species transport, porous media, and canopy evapotranspiration models to evaluate wind speed, air temperature, water vapor mass fraction, and the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI). The constituent submodels were validated separately against relevant experimental or benchmark data. The effects of mitigation strategy arrangement, canyon aspect ratio, solar radiation, background temperature, relative humidity (RH), leaf area density, and minimum stomatal resistance were systematically examined. The simulated field patterns showed limited airflow and humidity changes in the cool-material-only case, whereas cases containing vertical greening exhibited lower air temperature, higher humidity, and modified pedestrian-level airflow. Under the baseline hot-weather conditions, with an aspect ratio of 2, direct and diffuse solar irradiance of 800 and 150 W m -2 , an air temperature of 318.15K, and a relative humidity of 20%, the configuration combining equal façade areas of cool material coatings and vertical greening reduced path-average UTCI by 1.65K on the leeward side and 2.27K on the windward side compared with the untreated canyon. Decreasing leaf area density increased path-average UTCI, whereas decreasing minimum stomatal resistance reduced it. The findings are conditional on the tested steady state conditions, perpendicular inflow, and fixed solar configuration.

title: Effects of indoor temperature cycles on human subjective thermal perception, physiological responses and cognitive performance under flexible air-conditioning operation

A dual approach to window view dynamism using subjective and image-based measures of variation
abstract: Dynamic attributes in window views, such as shifting light patterns across the day, shape how people experience indoor environments. Previous research suggests that variation in outdoor scenes can enhance preference and perceived restoration, yet the relationship between image-based measures of variation and subjective impressions remains unclear. This exploratory study examines that relationship by comparing perceived dynamism in window views with image-based measures of variation in lightness. Perceived dynamism ratings were obtained from a previous Virtual Reality (VR) experiment in which participants viewed time-lapse videos of outdoor scenes. Variation in lightness (L*) was quantified in MATLAB using two complementary approaches: cosine similarity, capturing temporal variation in spatial lightness patterns across the image sequence; and a Regions of Interest (ROIs) method, identifying clusters of variation across Non-Porous, Porous, and Sky regions. Scenes rated as highly dynamic often exhibited highly stable lightness patterns, indicating a mismatch between self-reports and cosine similarity. ROI analysis showed that variation in Porous and Sky regions corresponded closely with perceived dynamism: scenes with extensive sky exposure were rated most dynamic, while enclosed scenes were rated least dynamic, even when variation in lightness was present. These findings suggest that perceived dynamism depends not only on measurable variation but also on the salience of specific regions. Although cosine similarity did not track perceived dynamism, it confirmed that scenes changed little overall, providing a stable baseline for interpreting regional variation. Together, the two methods offer a replicable workflow, with cosine similarity screening for stability and ROI analysis locating perceptually relevant variation.

title: Transient thermal sensation of pedestrians at sun-shade boundaries: response patterns, predictive factors, and process modeling
Applicability of SET and PMV in prefabricated offices at tunnel construction sites in high-altitude cold regions of Southwest China: a four-season field study
Systematic review and empirical assessment of submodels of physical processes in low-order gray box energy models of commercial buildings
abstract: : Low-order gray-box building energy models (GBBEMs) enable rapid district-scale simulation but often simplify or omit key physical subprocesses (e.g., occupancy gains, infiltration/ventilation, latent loads, and convection), with uncertain consequences for predictive accuracy. This shortcoming was identified in multiple recent review articles. To fill this gap, this study conducts a systematic review of the methods for including physical sub-processes in GBBEMs, then empirically evaluates the methods most commonly used for five sub-processes found to be under-investigated, using chilled water data from 66 buildings located on Ohio State University campus collected in 2022. The literature review showed solar radiation is well studied in the literature, but the effects of submodels of convective heat transfer on external surfaces, internal gains from occupants and occupant activities, internal gains from electrical loads, ventilation and infiltration loads, and latent loads associated with people, their activities, and infiltration/ventilation are not well understood. Results show that using optimal occupancy, internal load, and infiltration/ventilation load models-something that is rarely done in typical practice today- has the potential to reduce model error (CVRMSE) by 55%, 25%, and 20%, respectively. Inclusion of convection modeling or explicit modeling of latent loads showed no statistically significant improvement in model predictions, suggesting they may be neglected moving forward. Results also show that data-driven parameter calculation of submodels outperforms the use of pre-calculated parameters.

title: Airflow redistribution and optimization of a vertical single-row inclined slit ventilation system via splitter plates
Improving architectural design to enhance natural ventilation in a high-rise residential building: A case study in New Zealand
abstract: Urban expansion and increasing residential energy demand, particularly in New Zealand, triggers a need to improve indoor air quality without excessive energy use. This study evaluates natural ventilation performance in a high-rise student dormitory through three design configurations: the original building (Case 1) and two modified designs: partially replacing the façade with a balcony (Case 2) and further creating opposite passageways by removing two envelope segments (Case 3). Wind tunnel tests were conducted to investigate ventilation performance across five selected rooms at different plan locations. Three floor levels were selected: ground, mid-centre, and top. Pressure-differentials between the building openings and room interiors were sampled at varying wind directions, accounting for nearby buildings and the atmospheric boundary layer. Flow visualisation analysis presented the wind interaction with the building and its openings, providing an understanding on how macroclimatic conditions influenced the ventilation flows through the building. The results showed that the design modifications enhanced ventilation from single-sided (Case 1) to cross-ventilation (Cases 2 and 3), with optimal performance when windows faced windward winds. However, Cases 2 and 3 showed negligible differences, suggesting that minimal design modifications (Case 2) could provide the most cost-effective solution.

Performance of hybrid cooling control for the thermal storage effect of PCM-integrated floor in hot-humid climates
abstract: Phase change materials (PCMs) integrated into building constructions with night ventilation have been shown to be effective for cooling indoor spaces during the daytime owing to the thermal storage effect; however, they have limited applicability under high nocturnal temperature conditions. Therefore, this study proposes a hybrid cooling mode that uses control logic to switch between night ventilation and mechanical cooling, which supplies adequate cooling capacity to enable nighttime heat discharge of PCMs. A PCM-integrated floor system equipped with hybrid cooling was designed for indoor thermal comfort and cooling energy savings considering the lifestyles of Indonesian residents. The switching setpoint (27.0°C) was determined based on a comprehensive analysis, involving PCM phase change, resident thermal comfort, and local typical meteorological year data. Field measurements were conducted in apartment units in Tegal, Indonesia to evaluate system performance and hybrid cooling effectiveness. Relative to the non-cooling mode, the system under forced night cooling reduced the peak floor surface temperature by up to 0.6°C and extended the average daytime comfort duration by 231 min, with the effect significant in low-height zones below FL+1.1 m. Relative to AC-only mode, the hybrid cooling mode consumed 29.3% less energy. Although its daytime comfort was slightly lower under hotter measurement conditions, hybrid cooling is essential for sustaining PCM nighttime heat discharge, because most nights in the local climate are too warm for night ventilation alone. Hybrid cooling therefore provides a reliable and energy-saving strategy for PCM-integrated floors in hot-humid climates with high nocturnal temperatures.

title: Indoor air quality in long-term care facilities: A scoping review of particulate matter, volatile organic compounds, and mitigation strategies
abstract: Indoor air pollution is an environmental health concern in long-term care (LTC) facilities, where residents have prolonged exposure and may be particularly vulnerable. This scoping review mapped particulate matter (PM), volatile organic compound (VOC), formaldehyde, and complementary indoor air quality (IAQ) evidence, together with reported determinants, activity-related peaks, and mitigation strategies. Following PRISMA-ScR, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for English- or German-language peer-reviewed research published from 2000 to the family-specific final search dates in July and August 2026. Seventy-five publications were included: 41 informed observational IAQ evidence and 36 informed mitigation evidence, with two contributing to both evidence families. The 36 mitigation reports represented 32 distinct studies or campaigns; 28 were classified as core LTC-specific evidence and eight as supportive evidence. PM2.5 concentrations were commonly 5–30 ug/m3, whereas higher concentrations and short-term peaks occurred during traffic or wildfire episodes, cooking, occupancy, movement, or ventilation-related conditions. PM10, total VOCs, formaldehyde, and complementary indicators also varied by facility, room, season, activity, and measurement approach. Mitigation evidence covered filtration and air purification, natural and mechanical ventilation, fresh-air and pressure-control retrofits, germicidal ultraviolet and air-sterilization technologies, physical barriers, green infrastructure, and LTC-specific modelling. Particle-focused filtration generally reduced measured particle concentrations in the settings studied, while ventilation interventions increased air exchange or improved CO2-related and modelled outcomes under specific conditions. Evidence was heterogeneous, several studies were short-term or model-based, and VOC-targeted mitigation remained sparse. Standardized, activity-resolved monitoring and real-world evaluations integrating IAQ, thermal comfort, energy, humidity, and acceptability are needed.

title: Optimizing dynamic lighting for visual and non‑visual impact with emphasis on power efficiency
abstract: Light perception is a fundamental aspect of human sensory experience and lighting a key element of building design. However, light’s effect goes beyond vision - illuminance is the primary external driver of melatonin suppression. The discovery of intrinsically photoreceptive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) shifted attention toward spectral composition beyond the simple 3 cone model. The 24‐hour solar cycle remains the benchmark, providing strong midday suppression, mild evening suppression, and no suppression at night. Advances in LED technology have enabled dynamic lighting systems to replicate these non‐visual effects. However, despite extensive work, energy efficiency, in particular, melanopic efficacy, has not been addressed—a critical omission given the demand for sustainable, cost‐effective building solutions. Spectral power distributions were synthesized utilizing combinations of commercial LED strips, including warm‐white (WW), ice‐blue (IB), cool‐white (CW), cyan, and RGB, with the three objectives: (1) maximize melanopic illuminous efficacy (for daytime lighting), (2) maximize melanopic efficacy of luminous radiation (m-ELR) tunability, and (3) maximize photopic illuminous efficacy at low m-ELR(for evening lighting); under the constraint of high colour fidelity (CRI > 95, Duv|<0.001, CCT<6500 K). Results show that a four‐LED system (WW, IB, red, green) achieves high melanopic illuminous efficacy (daytime), broad m‐ELR tunability, and strong photopic illuminous efficacy at low m‐ELR. Incorporating Cyan LEDs offered negligible gains. Amber extended the m‐ELR range for improved nighttime performance. Considering the North American Electrical Codes (96 W/circuit maximum) and simplicity of installation, we recommend a streamlined three‐strip configuration (WW, IB, RAG) for 24 hr dynamic white lighting.

Ten questions concerning the future of intelligent buildings
abstract: Buildings face growing pressure to reduce energy use and carbon emissions while maintaining healthy, resilient indoor environments. Conventional automation often optimises isolated functions and cannot coordinate environmental, operational, and occupant requirements across building systems and lifecycles. Intelligent buildings (IBs) can address these limitations through integrated sensing, analytics, adaptive controls, and responsive materials, but effective implementation remains essential. This paper examines how IBs address these pressures and identifies the conditions required for responsible building intelligence. The ten questions are organised into four thematic clusters covering foundations, technologies, performance, and ethical and social implications. The paper examines these questions across building information modelling and digital twins, ubiquitous technologies, smart materials, operational systems, grid flexibility, Industry 5.0, and data responsibility. The discussion demonstrates that these technologies can improve coordination, energy flexibility, maintenance, indoor environmental quality, and lifecycle decision-making. However, technology alone does not make a building intelligent or guarantee measurable environmental and human outcomes. Effective IBs require interoperable systems, reliable data, clear performance objectives, cybersecurity, maintainability, accountable governance, and meaningful occupant participation. Neighbourhood coordination is important because shared energy assets, local grid constraints, and environmental exposures cannot always be managed by individual dwellings. Accordingly, IBs should be assessed through measurable outcomes, including comfort, health, safety, energy flexibility, resilience, privacy, and long-term value. The resulting research agenda supports human-centred, low-carbon, grid-responsive, resilient, and ethically governed intelligent residential buildings.

title: Multi-objective evaluation of urban greening strategies in high-density tropical cities: an integrated framework for environment, energy, emission and economy
Built-environment modulation of urban tree transpiration during summer heat–humidity extremes
Real-time dimming control of integrated daylight and electric lighting systems using a multimodal generative surrogate model
Contaminants of emerging concern in dust from different indoor microenvironments
A flow conditioned infiltration metric for traffic-related air pollution ingress and indoor air quality in naturally ventilated buildings
abstract: The indoor-outdoor pollutant concentration relationship in naturally ventilated buildings is commonly studied by means of the indoor/outdoor concentration ratio. This metric provides information on instantaneous exposure levels relative to the outdoor environment but does not account for the local air flow condition that govern pollutant transport through the building opening. This work aims at developing a flow conditioned ingress parameter that complements the indoor/outdoor concentration ratio to physically describe the indoor-outdoor relationship. Simultaneous field measurements of indoor and outdoor NO 2 concentrations, traffic flow and wind conditions were performed in a single-sided ventilated office building located in a high aspect-ratio street canyon in Gżira, Malta. The proposed metric is compared with the conventional indoor/outdoor ratio. A low-frequency domain analysis of both parameters showed the conventional indoor/outdoor concentration ratio closely followed the dominant traffic frequencies irrespective of varying wind conditions. On the other hand, the newly proposed metric also showed dependence on wind conditions, which altered its frequency response. Furthermore, the conventional indoor/outdoor ratio showed high scatter during low outdoor concentration events and showed no clear dependence on local flow conditions. The proposed metric demonstrated a clear sensitivity to local flow conditions with its polarity indicating whether favourable or unfavourable ventilation states prevail. The proposed parameter was therefore shown to provide a physically interpretable metric that links gaseous pollutant transport processes with indoor pollutant concentrations that addresses the limitations of conventional metrics used in the design of naturally ventilated buildings exposed to polluted outdoor environments.

title: Refined local-to-overall thermal sensation modeling for young and older people under non-uniform thermal environments
Experimental study on surveillance video-based indoor occupancy measurement for occupant-centric control
abstract: Accurate occupancy information is essential for closed-loop occupant-centric control (OCC) in smart buildings. However, existing vision-based occupancy measurement methods often struggle to provide stable and accurate measurements in real indoor environments, and their implications for downstream HVAC control remain insufficiently studied. To achieve Net Zero emissions by 2050, this paper presents an experimental study of large language models (LLMs)-enhanced vision-based indoor occupancy measurement and its impact on OCC-enabled HVAC operation. Detection-only, tracking-based, and LLM-based refinement pipelines are compared under identical conditions using real surveillance data collected from a research laboratory in China, with frame-level manual ground-truth annotations. Results show that tracking-based methods improve temporal stability over detection-only measurement, while LLM-based refinement further improves occupancy measurement performance and reduces false unoccupied prediction. The best-performing pipeline, YOLOv8+DeepSeek, achieves an accuracy of 0.8824 and an F1-score of 0.9320. This pipeline is then integrated into an HVAC supervisory model predictive control framework in OpenStudio-EnergyPlus. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework can support more efficient OCC operation, achieving a substantial HVAC energy-saving potential of 17.94%. These findings provide an effective methodology and practical foundation for future research in AI-enhanced smart building operations.

title: Restorative benefits of campus window views: Evidence from an orthogonal experiment
Combined effects of face mask blocking, filtration, and ventilation strategy on exhaled air transmission and infection risk
abstract: Face masks reduce airborne transmission by filtering particles and by redirecting exhaled air through facial leakages, the blocking effect. Whether blocking enhances protection beyond filtration alone depends critically on its interaction with the ventilation strategy. Two heated, cyclically breathing thermal manikins were employed in a full-scale climate chamber to quantify this interaction. A medical mask, two FFP2 mask types at two fit levels each, and a face shield were tested under mixing and displacement ventilation at and , with masking applied to the source, the recipient, and both simultaneously. CO 2 tracer gas yielded the local ventilation effectiveness (LVE) at the recipient’s breathing zone, which was combined with particle reduction rates from a dedicated filtration study in two complementary infection risk models. Under displacement ventilation, source masking increased LVE from 0.97 without masks to between 1.39 and 1.91, and up to 2.55 when both manikins were masked, consistent with an enhanced upward redirection of exhaled air. Under mixing ventilation, LVE remained between 0.78 and 0.97 for all mask configurations, so that no blocking-related enhancement was detectable and the mask effect there is attributable to filtration. No distance effect was resolvable within the measurement uncertainty. Risk models assuming ideal mixing overestimated the relative risk of masked configurations by up to a factor of 2.3, showing that ventilation effectiveness measurements are essential in stratified environments. Both models agreed on intervention rankings, with FFP2 masks under displacement ventilation yielding the greatest risk reduction.

title: From cabin thermal exposure to safety-related driver burden: Quantification using multidimensional subjective burden indices
High-resolution multi-summer simulation of urban heat island and heat stress across local climate zones in a megacity in Central China
Retraction notice to “Energy optimization strategies for high-rise buildings: A simulation-driven approach” [Building and Environment 298 (2026) 114625]
Vertical wind profiles and urban morphology effects on nocturnal urban heat islands from Doppler LiDAR observations and machine learning
abstract: Nocturnal urban heat islands (UHI) in high density cities are influenced by local morphology and vertical atmospheric structure. Most UHI assessments have relied on near-surface measurements and the interaction between vertical wind profiles and heterogeneous urban morphology is insufficiently explored. This study investigates how vertical wind pattern is associated with nocturnal UHI during summer months in Hong Kong. High-resolution Doppler LiDAR wind profiles are integrated with surface meteorological observations, ERA5 reanalysis data and urban morphology across multiple Local Climate Zones (LCZs). The Self-Organizing Map method (SOM) is used to classify hourly vertical wind profiles into four wind patterns. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) performs best among the tested models and is used to interpret the interactions between weather conditions and localized morphology. Thermal differences are found within the same LCZ types and vary under the vertical wind structure. Pattern 2 shows the weakest ventilation and strongest nocturnal stability with wind speed of 1.97 m s -1 at 50 m at the urban core site and boundary layer height of approximately 230 m. Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and building density have their greatest relative predictive importance under this pattern. Pattern 4 is associated with the deepest boundary layer and lowest nocturnal UHI among all patterns, although lower-level wind speeds at the urban site remain lower than those at the exposed site. Incorporating the structural variations of the atmospheric boundary layer into spatial assessments may provide a physical foundation for heat resilience and climate-sensitive design in urban planning.

title: Range-dependent performance of alertness indicators reveals cyanopic modulation under indoor lighting
Evaluation of a POD-ANN surrogate model for electric vehicle cabin thermal environment prediction: Accuracy, computational speed, and data efficiency
Physics-informed AI-integrated digital twin framework for early and real-time prediction of mould growth in buildings
abstract: Indoor air quality issues, particularly mould and dampness, remain persistent public health concerns in residential buildings despite improvements in building standards and energy performance regulations. In current practice, mould management is largely reactive and relies on occupant complaints and visual inspection after mould has already become visible, at which occupants may have already experienced prolonged exposure to unhealthy indoor environment. To address this limitation, this study proposes a Digital Twin–based framework for continuous monitoring and predictive assessment of mould risk in buildings. The framework combines continuous environmental monitoring using an Internet of Things (IoT) sensor network with a calibrated Building Energy Model (BEM) that synchronizes real-time sensor data with simulation outputs to estimate surface hygrothermal condition across both monitored and unmonitored locations. These hygrothermal conditions are then used to evaluate mould development using the VTT mould growth model. Building upon this physics-based representation of mould dynamics, a Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) model based on Extreme Gradient Boosting is developed to forecast mould growth across prediction horizons ranging from 1 hour to 1 week. The proposed framework was implemented and validated on a sensor-instrumented residential building case study located in Syracuse, New York, achieving high prediction accuracy of up to R² of 0.99 for short-term forecasts and approximately 0.90 for longer horizons up to one-week-ahead mould index prediction. The findings demonstrate reliable prediction of mould development under dynamically changing indoor environment. The framework provides a scalable approach for real-time monitoring and proactive mould risk assessment in new and existing building to improve operation and add a new automated layer for maintenance, enabling early smart decision-making and intervention.

title: Exploring effects of temporal perspectives on life cycle climate impact and costs in building renovation
abstract: Life cycle (LC) building renovation studies typically present aggregated results that cannot capture the accumulation of emissions and costs over time, particularly in future scenarios. This study explores the influence of temporal perspectives on life cycle assessment (LCA) and whole life costing (WLC) outcomes for envelope and ventilation renovations of a multi-residential building in a subarctic climate. Cumulative climate impact and costs are evaluated over a 100-year period, enabling comparison of time-resolved and aggregated results while also testing sensitivity to four key temporal parameters related to future energy systems, technological development, and cost escalation. Although not a dynamic LC study per se, it incorporates dynamic elements through time-resolved results and temporal developments. Time-resolved LC analysis provides greater nuance than aggregated assessments by revealing when and why the relative performance of renovation packages changes over time. Comparing the rate and direction of climate impact and cost trajectories clarifies long-term renovation performance and illustrates how rankings depend on the selected analysis period. Furthermore, temporal parameters influence renovations’ long-term climate and cost performance. Energy mix decarbonisation strongly influences climate-impact trajectories, shifting the burden towards embodied emissions, especially in regions with low-emission energy supply. For WLC, higher cost escalation rates increase the relative importance of operational savings, but investments are rarely fully recouped. While temporal perspectives do not necessarily alter the relative performance of different renovation strategies, their inclusion enables more robust evaluation over long time horizons by clarifying future uncertainties and revealing strategies that align long-term climate mitigation with economic constraints.

title: Corrigendum to “Are present microclimate assessments valid in future changing climates? A case study from Hong Kong” [Building and Environment, Volume 290 (2026), Article 114131]
Scaling response and spatial heterogeneity of wind-driven rain on building facades: Hierarchical explicit modeling based on symbolic regression
Nonlinear relationship between urban form and heat resilience: An empirical study of Seoul

Mitigating extreme heat stress for heat-vulnerable children under hot-humid summer conditions: A cross-scale assessment of meso‑scale local climate zones and micro-morphology

Citywide assessment of perceived window view openness using photorealistic 3D model imagery and automatic machine learning
City-scale 3D radiative transfer simulation of urban canopy albedo over complex urban geometry
Experimental validation of a CFD model for an ultra-clean ventilation system in a UK operating theatre under HTM-03-01
abstract: Ultra-clean ventilation (UCV) systems are used in operating theatres to reduce airborne contamination associated with surgical site infection risk by supplying downward unidirectional airflow over the surgical zone. In the UK, UCV commissioning is assessed against Health Technical Memorandum (HTM) 03-01 Part A (2021), with acceptance criteria defined for airflow velocity and particle entrainment. However, these tests rely on discrete probe locations and limited sampling heights, providing limited insight into the three-dimensional flow structures that govern velocity distribution and particle transport beneath UCV canopies. This study combines full-scale HTM-compliant measurements with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to examine the relationship between HTM acceptance criteria and underlying airflow behaviour. Experimental testing was conducted beneath a Howorth UCV canopy in a UK operating theatre, including velocity mapping at 1 m and 2 m above floor level and particle entrainment testing using 0.3 µm aerosols released at prescribed HTM challenge positions. A CFD model was developed to reproduce the same commissioning conditions and simulate three-dimensional airflow and Lagrangian particle transport. The model showed close agreement with measured velocity data and consistently reproduced particle penetration trends across the HTM challenge positions within experimental uncertainty. The UCV system satisfied all HTM acceptance criteria. This study demonstrates how validated CFD can reveal flow mechanisms underpinning commissioning metrics and provides a reproducible HTM-aligned benchmark dataset for future UCV model development and performance assessment.

title: Heating performance analysis of an air source heat pump heating system with different heating terminals under frosting conditions
Do confined transportation cabins require joint illuminance–air-temperature evaluation? Evidence from comfort, physiological, workload, and performance responses
A method for measuring and quantifying body-part-level quilt coverage state in sleep thermal environment research
From numerical attribution to semantic interpretation: environmental associations of noise perception with LLM and Geo-XAI
Characteristics and dynamic benchmarks for embodied carbon emissions of educational buildings based on Bayesian inference and probabilistic regression approaches
Ventilation trade-offs and air-volume allocation for post-blasting CO control in multi-branch construction tunnels: Dimensionless relationships and a constraint-aware framework
Multimodal responses to low-frequency-enriched floor-impact noise in multi-family housing: annoyance, autonomic responses, and EEG network patterns
Humidity-prioritized positive-pressure fresh-air retrofit for a permeable heritage building in a hot-humid climate: moisture, comfort, IAQ, and energy assessment
Beyond mass and concentration: Spatiotemporal evolution and influencing factors of damage-oriented environmental performance for air pollution and greenhouse gases
Uncovering nested thermal landscape connectivity in megacities: A multi-level recursive decomposition framework for heat island mitigation
Colour rendition quality evaluation for artificial and natural lights based on a spectral simulation pipeline
Ten questions concerning air movement as a primary cooling strategy: “Fan-first” cooling
abstract: Conventional cooling assumes that indoor air must be both cooled and kept still. While effective for maintaining thermal comfort and protecting occupants from heat stress, this approach is highly energy-intensive and costly. Raising air speed while allowing a higher air temperature can produce the same cooling sensation as still air at a lower temperature, with all other environmental and personal factors held constant, at only a fraction of the energy demand. Here, we argue for a “fan-first” approach that prioritises air movement as the primary cooling mechanism, applying mechanical cooling only when necessary, across mechanically conditioned, mixed-mode, and naturally ventilated buildings. We propose ten questions addressing the benefits and challenges of this approach across thermal comfort, energy efficiency, visual comfort, and indoor air quality, synthesising current evidence and identifying critical gaps for future research. Across these questions, evidence indicates that “fan-first” strategies can maintain thermal comfort at indoor temperatures of , deliver cooling-energy savings of , and reduce zone-level Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) construction costs by up to , while also supporting indoor air quality through improved room-scale mixing. While ceiling fans receive the most attention given the breadth of available evidence, the underlying principles apply to any device that elevates air speed across the body, including desk, pedestal, and portable fans. Aimed at researchers, practitioners, and policymakers, this article encourages broader adoption of air movement as a viable, sustainable cooling strategy, reducing reliance on energy-intensive mechanical systems.

title: Shared window control in open-plan offices: Linking perceived drivers and observed actions in a mixed-methods case study
abstract: Occupant window behaviour affects indoor environmental quality and building performance, yet it is often modelled mainly through environmental and temporal predictors. This approach is less suited to open-plan offices, where operable windows function as shared environmental controls and occupants’ ability to act may depend on their spatial position and social context. This study investigates how social and spatial conditions mediate window-opening behaviour by comparing interview-derived themes with observed behavioural patterns. Semi-structured interviews with 30 occupants from multiple shared offices identified motivations, contextual influences and decision processes. These findings then informed a 41-day field study involving a separate occupant group in one naturally ventilated office at the same university in Tianjin, China. Structured observation and environmental monitoring were combined with window-specific generalised estimating equation models accounting for temporal dependence. Indoor temperature showed window-specific associations, with positive but uncertain estimates for W1 and W3 and a clear negative association for W2. Window proximity and adjacent-seat occupancy showed the clearest convergence across interviews and observations. Occupants near windows operated them more often, while non-adjacent occupants did so mainly when adjacent workstations were unoccupied. Fresh-air preference and habitual routines were supported mainly by qualitative and case-specific evidence. Perceived hierarchy was prominent in interviews but was not associated with overall operation frequency in observation. These findings suggest that window behaviour in open-plan offices should be understood as a socially and spatially mediated form of shared environmental control, where room-level evaluations may obscure uneven access to control and comfort within the same space.

title: Fast adaptation for cross-climate building HVAC and window coordinated control with Wasserstein-guided meta-reinforcement learning
Effects of rooftop parapet walls on airflow and dust deposition on photovoltaic arrays: A CFD–DPM study
abstract: Rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems are increasingly deployed in dense urban environments, where parapet walls are common architectural features that alter rooftop airflow patterns. However, the resulting effects on particle transport and dust deposition, which can significantly reduce PV energy yield, remain insufficiently understood. This study employs three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) coupled with a discrete phase model (DPM) to investigate airflow characteristics and first-contact particle capture on individual rows of rooftop PV arrays with parapet walls. The airflow model is assessed against wind-tunnel measurements of the approach flow and of surface pressures on the PV array. Results show that parapet walls significantly alter rooftop airflow by reducing near-surface velocity, displacing the separated shear layer, and modifying recirculation around the PV array. The effect of parapet height is conditional rather than monotonic, and the influence of wind speed is strongly particle-size dependent. The particle diameter associated with the highest capture varies with operating conditions, with peaks near 100 μm at U He = 1.3 m/s, 150–200 μm at U He = 2.6 m/s, and 200–300 μm at U He = 3.9 m/s. Capture is highly non-uniform across the PV rows: upstream rows intercept particles with greater inertia, whereas medium-sized particles bypass the front rows and show enhanced capture on downstream modules at higher wind speeds.

title: Dual-objective turbulent topology optimization with vorticity modification term under developing flow: Application to ventilation tee
Evaluating the microclimatic and thermal comfort impact of high-reflective pavements across different urban canyon settings in a tropical city
abstract: Urban heat islands (UHIs) pose major challenges in tropical cities, where elevated temperatures intensify thermal discomfort and environmental stress. The effectiveness of mitigation strategies, however, depends strongly on urban morphology. This study investigates how contrasting urban canyon configurations influence the microclimatic performance of reflective pavements (RP) and pedestrian thermal comfort in a tropical city. Representative vertical and horizontal urban canyons, characterized by distinct socioeconomic conditions and urban forms, were evaluated using high-resolution ENVI-met simulations under baseline and RP scenarios. Results showed that high-albedo pavements (α = 0.5) reduced surface temperatures by up to 9.6°C and air temperatures by 1.7°C during peak solar hours, but simultaneously increased mean radiant temperature by approximately 13°C. The cooling efficiency of reflective pavements was not uniform and depended critically on urban canyon geometry. Low-rise urban canyons exhibited higher temperatures than verticalized areas due to limited shading and restricted airflow. In contrast, vertical canyons reduced the overall effectiveness of RP through radiative trapping and multiple reflections. Furthermore, the conventional UTCI classification tended to overestimate thermal stress, whereas locally adapted UTCI thresholds provided a more realistic assessment consistent with residents’ thermal perception. These findings demonstrate that urban form plays a decisive role in modulating the benefits and trade-offs of reflective pavements and highlights the importance of context-sensitive UHI mitigation strategies for tropical cities.

title: Comment on “Evaluating ASHRAE Standard 241: Toward realistic indoor environments and airborne infection risk assessment” by Sedighi et al. (2025)
Editorial Board
Urban outdoor artificial light at night: A scoping review of assessment approaches from environmental light to person-referenced biologically effective exposure
A carbon-conduction model for quantifying cascading replacements in renovation embodied carbon assessment
Acoustic performance of educational buildings using raw-earth construction systems: An in-situ comparison of different techniques
abstract: This study presents an in situ acoustic assessment of five earthen school buildings in north-west France, comparing construction techniques such as cob, wattle and daub, light earth, and raw earth brick. The analysis addresses both airborne sound insulation between classrooms (in three of the five schools) and, more extensively, room acoustics in all cases. The latter was evaluated using standardised indicators such as sound pressure level, reverberation time, and the Speech Transmission Index (STI). It was further complemented by an in situ characterisation of acoustic absorption properties in four schools using a pressure–particle velocity (PU) probe.,The results indicate that global acoustic indicators are useful for assessing classroom quality. Reverberation times (0.39–0.49 s) comply with standards and speech intelligibility (STI) is generally good to excellent. In addition, sound insulation between classrooms highlights limitations related to construction details and earth shrinkage. Despite the usefulness of these global indicators, it remains difficult to isolate the specific influence of raw earth on the acoustic performance of the spaces. For this reason, in situ absorption coefficients were determined. The results highlight a strong dependency on the construction technique and surface finish, with values exceeding α > 0.7 for systems such as light earth and α < 0.2 for more homogeneous and less porous techniques such as cob. Overall, these findings demonstrate that the acoustic performance of raw earth depends largely on the construction technique and surface condition rather than on the material itself.

title: Do spectral power distributions beyond correlated colour temperature affect occupants’ thermal sensation?
Image-based method for estimating vertical solar irradiance on building windows under tree shading
abstract: In hot environments, tree shading is widely recognized as an effective way to reduce solar heat gain through building windows. Accurate estimation of window solar irradiance under various tree-shading conditions is important for thermal environment assessment and building energy analysis. However, this remains challenging because tree shadows are spatially non-uniform across the window surface, and sky-diffuse radiation is directionally distributed and changes with sky conditions. To address these challenges, this study proposes an image-based method for estimating vertical solar irradiance on a tree-shaded window. Using one panoramic image taken from the window exterior, global horizontal irradiance data, and basic geometric information, the method estimates the direct, sky-diffuse, and ground-reflected irradiance components on the window surface. A window direct solar access ratio is defined to account for partial tree shading. The sky-diffuse radiance distribution is estimated based on the Perez model. The method was validated using a mock-up house under unshaded and tree-shaded conditions, covering different tree species, tree–window distances, and tree azimuth positions. After cloud filtering, the proposed method showed high accuracy under both unshaded and tree-shaded conditions, with R 2 reaching 1.0 in the unshaded case and remaining above 0.94 in all tree-shaded cases. Accounting for the non-uniform distribution of tree shading across the window surface made a larger contribution to improving prediction accuracy. Overall, this study provides a practical tool for estimating window solar irradiance under tree shading with relatively low input requirements, supporting tree-shading impact assessment, vegetation design around buildings, and building energy analysis considering surrounding environments.

title: Temporal regime diagnostics of dining-space CO2 under occupancy loading: A long-horizon operational study with dense-grid seed evidence
Neighbouring-building effects on high-rise façade convective heat transfer and energy response: A coupled CFD–BES study
abstract: High-rise buildings in dense urban districts experience exterior convection governed by local airflow fields that are strongly shaped by surrounding buildings. However, most building energy simulations still rely on empirical exterior convection algorithms developed for simplified exposure conditions. This study investigates how neighbouring high-rise buildings modify facade convective heat transfer coefficients (CHTCs), and how these local changes propagate through outside surface temperature, wall heat balance, and whole-building energy demand. An external quasi-dynamic computational fluid dynamics-building energy simulation (CFD-BES) workflow couples EnergyPlus and ANSYS Fluent through BCVTB and MATLAB at 10 min intervals. A 36-storey office tower is analysed as both a stand-alone building and within a symmetric array of eight neighbouring towers at various spacings. Selected summer conditions in Hong Kong and winter conditions in London and New York are evaluated, and CFD-derived CHTCs are compared with the DOE-2 exterior convection algorithm. The results show that neighbouring buildings reorganise facade exposure through shielding, wake interaction, gap channelling, and partial flow recovery. At narrow spacing, facade-mean CHTCs are strongly reduced relative to the stand-alone tower. In New York winter, north and west facade-mean CHTCs decrease from 28.55 and 27.34 W/m²·K for the isolated tower to 17.10 and 13.32 W/m²·K at 1W. For the isolated tower, CFD-derived CHTCs substantially exceed DOE-2 values, whereas urban shielding reduces the discrepancy and can reverse its sign. Across neighbouring-building cases, mean absolute facade-mean CHTC differences between the coupled method and DOE-2 are 18–31%, while absolute whole-building load differences are 0.31–2.14% (median damping index 2.23%). This damping results from adjustments in surface temperature, conduction, and long-wave radiation. For the investigated five-day periods, DOE-2 produces comparable period-integrated loads in sheltered, sealed configurations, but this does not imply local physical equivalence. CFD-BES remains more informative for exposed towers and facade-level assessment.

title: Toward interoperable indoor thermal physiology research in the built environment: An interpretive framework for physiological measurement and metadata architecture
abstract: Physiological measurements are increasingly incorporated into indoor thermal comfort research, yet the field lacks shared documentation structures capable of making datasets from heterogeneous laboratories mutually interpretable. Fragmentation across mechanistic, measurement, descriptive, integrative, reproducibility, and cross-domain layers limits cross-study comparison and constrains cumulative physiological evidence generation. This paper diagnoses the structural sources of that fragmentation and proposes a framework for methodological coherence in indoor thermal physiology research. An empirical metadata analysis of 273 published indoor thermal physiology studies (295 unique experiments) tests these fragmentation types directly and provides the basis for the framework design. Across the literature, reporting was substantially more consistent for the existence of measurements than for the contextual, anatomical, temporal, and analytical information required for physiological interpretation. Key descriptors including session timing, participant modifiers, anatomical specificity, and data accessibility were inconsistently documented. In response, a structured framework is proposed comprising three complementary components: physiological signal documentation addressing mechanistic rationale, sensing principles, anatomical specification, cross-method comparability, biological modifiers, and data handling; an interpretive interoperability infrastructure comprising harmonised notation, standardisation of derived metrics, controlled vocabulary, and anatomical reference taxonomy; and a hierarchical metadata architecture separating experiment-, participant-, session-, and sensor-level descriptors into tiered structures. The framework is accompanied by a version-controlled open repository designed for iterative refinement and stable citation. The objective is not methodological standardisation through uniform protocols, but documentation alignment that makes heterogeneous practices interpretable. By consolidating established physiological knowledge into structured and explicitly reasoned form, the framework aims to support cumulative, interoperable physiological evidence generation for indoor environmental research.

title: Reliable leakage detection for district heating infrastructure in the built environment using physics-consistency-filtered latent diffusion
Whole building HVAC diagnostic Bayesian networks for comfort-related fault detection and diagnosis: Application, evaluation and operational testing
abstract: Automated fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) can support building energy performance and predictive maintenance by leveraging the vast amounts of data generated by building management systems. However, most work on FDD for HVAC systems focuses on individual components, neglecting complex system interactions and the cascading effects of component faults. Diagnostic Bayesian Networks (DBN) offer a particularly promising approach for whole-building FDD due to their robustness, flexibility and scalability. This paper presents the development of a DBN for whole-HVAC FDD and its application in an office building in the Netherlands. The DBN uses aggregated representations of all major building systems to detect which faulty components need further investigation and uses knowledge-based and data-driven methods for parameter estimation. The DBN’s performance and the effects of input parameter assumptions are assessed using historical data as well as experimental data obtained by introducing simultaneous faults into the air handling unit (AHU) controls. Although fault injection was restricted to AHU controls due to safety concerns, the model architecture represents all major HVAC systems and simultaneously diagnoses their faults. The results using historical data identified persistent sensor-related anomalies in the building, as well as possibly associated system and control faults. Despite these sensor issues, the evaluation using experimental data showed that the DBN achieved a classification rate of 87.8% for AHU faults while maintaining a low false alarm rate (3.8%). However, the miss rate was high, exceeding 25% in all cases. Finally, the DBN is demonstrated through its application to diagnose a suspected fault during operation.

title: A coupled network framework for street-scale urban ventilation analysis
Upper temperature limit in office environments with air movement: insights from psychophysiology and cognitive performance
Experimental Performance Evaluation of Directional, Ceiling, and Desk Fans in Heat Stress Recovery
Pressure-constrained coordinated demand-controlled filtration strategy for environmental control in an industrial cleanroom
Heating in human-HVAC interaction for smart homes: An interdisciplinary overview
abstract: As part of HVAC systems, residential heating provides foundational infrastructure for human habitation in cold weather. However, research on how residents interact with HVAC systems, particularly heating systems, remains fragmented across architecture, engineering, informatics, physiology, psychology, sociology, and design. Based on 541 studies from these fields, this review integrates interdisciplinary research on Heating in Human–HVAC Interaction in smart homes. The resulting synthesis is conceptualized through the Situated Interaction Dynamics of control and feedback between users and systems. User-initiated interactions involve monitoring past and present system performance and planning future operation, while system-initiated interactions rely on sensor networks to trigger automation or provide information enabling user action. These interaction dynamics connect Residents’ Experience and Practices with Heating in HVAC System Mechanics. Residents’ Experience and Practices include thermal comfort and energy management, where thermal comfort involves both individual physiological and psychological experiences of indoor climate and social practices shaped by norms, empathy, and negotiation among cohabitants. Heating in HVAC System Mechanics includes thermal conditions and energy performance. Thermal conditions concern the regulation of air temperature, mean radiant temperature, air velocity, and relative humidity, while energy performance concerns efficiency and environmental impact. This overview highlights four interdisciplinary tensions: sensed versus lived conditions, personalization versus negotiation, efficiency versus health, and automation versus agency. The resulting framework offers a conceptual lens to interpret heating interactions and design Human–HVAC Interaction that balances IEQ-driven healthy thermal conditions, affordability, and sustainability.

title: Detecting tourists’ overheating exposure risk in pedestrian district: An integrated framework for UGC-driven ABM and MRT modeling
Determining feasible design parameter domains of impinging jet ventilation and passive chilled beam combined systems using an integrated CFD-data-driven framework
Linking spatial cognition to perceptual anticipation in indoor sports environments: A multimodal virtual reality framework
A controlled chamber study of sensor placement and personalized modeling for breathing-zone CO2 and particle detection in offices
abstract: Accurately and practically estimating breathing-zone pollutant concentrations remains a key challenge for personal inhalation exposure assessment in office environments. We conducted controlled human-subject experiments in a climate chamber configured to simulate a mechanically ventilated shared office with HEPA-filtered supply air and no outdoor air infiltration under multiple indoor air quality and thermal conditions. Minute-resolved measurements of CO₂, PM₂.₅, and PM₁₀ were collected simultaneously at the breathing zone and at several practical sensor locations around the workstation and room. Using these data, we systematically evaluated sensor relevance and redundancy through correlation analysis and complementary linear and nonlinear modeling. The results showed clear pollutant-specific differences in sensor placement performance within the tested chamber configuration: breathing-zone CO₂ could be reasonably estimated using a single desk-level sensor placed above the laptop, whereas PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀ required a combination of room-center and desk-left-side measurements, reflecting stronger spatial heterogeneity under the tested low-source, filtered-air conditions. Models trained on the selected sensor sets generalized well across participants and controlled environmental conditions. Compared with conventional room-level sensing, using the selected sensor configurations improved overall breathing-zone estimation by approximately 14% for CO₂, 17% for PM₂.₅, and 3% for PM₁₀. Personalized residual modeling then provided additional individual-level improvements by approximately 38%, 5%, and 11%, respectively. These findings provide controlled experimental evidence for pollutant-specific sensor placement and personalized modeling strategies to support practical breathing-zone exposure estimation in office environments.

title: Combined green-roof and night-ventilation cooling across multiple thermal positions and roof heat-flux reduction: An interpretable machine-learning study
Investigating indoor CO2 heterogeneity: The impact of sensor location on CO2-based IAQ classification and presence detection in Brazilian educational buildings
abstract: Indoor carbon dioxide (CO2) distributions are spatially non-uniform, yet most monitoring and occupancy sensing applications rely on single-point measurements. This study examined the impact of sensor placement on CO2-based Indoor Air Quality (IAQ) assessments and data-driven presence detection in two Brazilian educational buildings. Multi-point CO2 measurements were combined with Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations to characterize spatial CO2 distributions. Stacked ensemble and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) presence detection models were trained repeatedly for each sensor location and feature combination and statistically compared using Welch's ANOVA and Games-Howell tests.In the purely naturally ventilated open-plan office, low CO2 levels prevailed at all positions, and sensor placement had a negligible practical effect on IAQ assessment. In rooms with natural ventilation combined with air conditioning, persistent vertical CO2 gradients made sensor height the dominant factor. This produced differences of up to 18 percentage points between heights. For presence detection, sensor location had a statistically significant effect in all rooms. Top-mounted sensors outperformed lower-mounted ones in the room with purely natural ventilation. The most important feature was the vertical CO2 gradient, and dual-sensor configurations improved model performance, consistent with prior observations in a German school. However, these advantages did not generalize to the air-conditioned rooms. Active recirculation disrupted vertical stratification, reversed the height advantage, and diminished the value of gradient features.These findings demonstrate that the practical relevance of sensor placement depends on whether the ventilation configuration produces spatial CO2 heterogeneity and that placement guidance must be adapted accordingly.

Selective real-time monitoring of respiratory droplets for indoor air safety in educational environments
abstract: Respiratory aerosol transmission represents an important pathway for the spread of infectious diseases in indoor educational environments. Real-time monitoring of respiratory droplets was performed using the AeroDrops respiratory droplet detector in multiple educational settings, including kindergarten and a primary school classroom, a university lecture hall, and experimental chemistry workshops. Measurements were conducted under different environmental conditions, including different ventilation regimes, seasonal conditions, and groups of preschool children, school children, and young adults. The detector selectively detected respiratory droplets while remaining insensitive to particulate matter and other non-respiratory aerosol sources. Distinct temporal variations in droplet concentrations were observed which correlated with participant activities, occupancy levels, vocalization, and movement. The results demonstrate that selective real-time monitoring of respiratory droplets provides information unavailable from conventional indoor air quality indicators and offers a promising approach for ventilation management and indoor air safety assessment.

Characterizing layout-dependent breathing-zone contaminant concentration in office spaces with mixing ventilation using an occupant-to-exhaust distance index: a parametric CFD study
abstract: Office layouts are an important factor in controlling exposure to human-generated contaminants, yet their effects across diverse occupant layouts and inlet/outlet arrangements remain insufficiently characterized using simple geometric descriptors. This study aims to characterize layout-dependent variations in indoor ventilation performance using an occupant-to-exhaust distance index. We analyzed CFD results from 198 cases across different room sizes, ventilation configurations, ventilation airflow rates, and desk arrangements per room to investigate how the combination of ventilation opening placement and occupant positioning affects ventilation performance. Using previously validated steady-state CFD dataset[A. Takii et al., Results Eng., 2026] as background velocity fields, we newly solved the passive scalar transport equation to generate contaminant concentration fields and evaluate ventilation performance indices. The contaminant concentration distributions varied widely with the layout, affecting the magnitudes of ventilation indicators and their sensitivity to ventilation conditions. The introduced occupant-to-exhaust index captured the layout-dependent variations in breathing-zone concentration and served as a first-order geometric proxy. In particular, layouts with the normalized index greater than 0.3 tended to exhibit higher concentrations, suggesting that this value can serve as an empirical threshold for screening potentially unfavorable occupant--ventilation layouts. Through detailed analysis, we also identified cases where the proposed index could not fully explain the results. These deviations were associated with wall proximity and occupant clustering, which promote the formation of recirculating or stagnant regions and elevated breathing-zone concentrations. These findings provide valuable insights for screening office layouts and developing indoor ventilation strategies in typical enclosed office rooms equipped with ceiling-mounted mixing ventilation systems.

Equipment, affordability and occupant control as mechanisms of winter thermal inadequacy in non-housing dwellings
abstract: Warmth in winter is ordinarily treated as a function of two conditions: heating equipment must be present, and the household must be able to pay for its operation. A third is seldom examined because in conventional housing it is satisfied by default, namely that the occupant must be able to operate the system. Using two waves of a national survey of households outside the statutory housing stock in the Republic of Korea (2017, n = 4,272; 2022, n = 9,350 dwellings with heating equipment), we sequentially examine heating-equipment availability, thermal adequacy among equipped dwellings, and the primary reported reason for inadequacy. Thermal deprivation affects 19.1% of households. Equipment absence accounts for 13.7% of it, whereas 47.2% selected inability to adjust central heating as the primary reported reason; 15.7% of households whose heating is installed and in use remain deprived, and no eligible respondent cited equipment breakdown. Control deprivation is concentrated in small, centrally served units, declines sharply with floor area, and was not reported in units of 36 m² or more. Its share does not follow the ranking of prevalence: it dominates in commercially operated micro-units but is absent from self-built shacks, where deprivation is most widespread. An auxiliary 2022 analysis found bundled utility billing associated with heating equipment reported as unused (odds ratio 1.68, p = 0.003), an indirect cross-wave convergence rather than a direct measure of control. Thermal adequacy standards for dense residential micro-units should address operational control alongside equipment and fabric.

title: Odor annoyance, sensory irritation or relaxation: Acute effects of pinewood-derived VOC mixtures at indoor-relevant concentrations
abstract: Abstract Wood is commonly used in the building sector, emitting volatile organic compounds (VOCs) contributing to indoor air quality. These VOC profiles can have a pleasant smell and positive effects e.g., induce relaxation. Contrarily, VOCs can have adverse health effects in higher concentrations. Therefore, some VOCs are regulated by guide values (GV). Potentially positive and negative effects of pinewood emissions, ranging from 0.2 mg/m 3 (German GV I for bicyclic terpenes) to 2.0 mg/m 3 (GV II) were investigated in an experimental 2 h exposure study using a within-subject design. Thirty-two healthy participants rated the perception, pleasantness, symptoms of irritation, and indicators of well-being. During a demanding working memory task (n-back) and a resting period, heart rate (HR) and HR variability (HRV) changes were measured. Before and after each session physiological markers of sensory irritation were assessed. Ratings indicated that the exposure to GV I and GV II were not perceived as more intense or pleasant. Mostly concentration-independent effects were revealed, indicating that inter-individual factors influenced the ratings rather than the VOCs. The pinewood odors during the n-back task did not cause distraction nor did it facilitate performance as previously suggested. HR/V changes indicated that pinewood odors during and after the n-back tasks did not induce relaxation. Only symptoms of nasal irritation showed some weak concentration-dependency, not supported by physiological markers or comparable ratings of sensory irritation. In conclusion, the fact that no distinct odor is detected suggests that interfering factors potentially prevent the regulation of odors at relevant indoor air concentrations. Highlights Successful exposure to realistic indoor pinewood VOCs No effect on ratings of indoor air quality, performance or sensory irritation No induction of relaxation during or after stressful tasks Short-term exposure to concentrations between GV I and II are non-effective
