Are expensive sensors necessary for assessing indoor environmental quality? A data-driven approach using minimal sensing
abstract: Modern, highly glazed buildings often suffer from excessive daylight and solar heat gain, leading to visual glare and thermal discomfort. Measuring the indoor environmental quality (IEQ) factors quantifying these conditions traditionally requires intrusive and expensive equipment, such as high dynamic range (HDR) cameras and black globe thermometers, making real-time control of automated shading systems impractical. Therefore, this study proposes minimal, low-cost sensing to predict two solar-affected IEQ metrics directly related to thermal and visual comfort, Daylight Glare Probability (DGP) and the globe-to-air temperature differential as a proxy for the radiant environment, leveraging a data-driven model. Experiments were conducted in two unoccupied environmental chambers with fully automated roller shades. Over four months, minimal sensor measurements, including indoor illuminance, approximated outdoor solar irradiance, solar angles, and shading positions, were paired with target DGP values and measured globe-to-air temperature differentials. Random Forest models mapped minimal sensor data to the IEQ metrics. Models achieved median coefficients of determination ( ) between 0.70 and 0.85. Permutation feature importance showed that indoor illuminance is the most critical predictor for glare, while a combination of solar irradiance, shading position, and solar positions contributed most strongly to the radiant-environment proxy. Given their strong predictive power with the IEQ metrics in question, these low-cost environmental variables demonstrate the potential to serve as practical inputs for estimating comfort-related IEQ conditions in real-world settings. This suggests that expensive equipment is unnecessary for estimating complex comfort conditions, supporting the scalable deployment of automated, occupant-centric shading controls.

title: Dynamic climate resilience of Mediterranean educational buildings: A multidimensional assessment of resilient cooling strategies under future extreme heat conditions
abstract: Energy efficiency has been positioned as a central response to climate change mitigation in the building sector. However, Mediterranean warming is intensifying the combined impacts of heatwaves and urban heat island (UHI) effects. This context reveals the limitations of energy efficiency in addressing overheating risk and exposes a critical gap in the climate-adaptation capacity of educational buildings, an underrepresented typology. This paper presents a multidimensional approach for assessing building climate resilience through resilient cooling strategies. The approach is applied to a university building in Terrassa, Spain, under four climate scenarios: present conditions (TMY2020), mid-future conditions (RCP8.5-TMY2050), the most severe/longest and the most intense future heatwaves (HW), including UHI effects. Dynamic indicators are used to quantify the effectiveness of cooling strategies in contributing to climate resilience under extreme heat conditions. The results for energy performance and thermal comfort under typical-weather scenarios showed that, under TMY2050, Exterior Blinds and Natural Ventilation-24h reduced cooling demand by 8–15% and increased comfort hours by 9–35%. However, under heatwaves, resilience was determined by temporal performance. During the most severe/longest HW, the Base case required about 21 kWh/m² of cooling in only 29 days, while Natural Ventilation-24h delayed critical overheating by 9 days and reduced recovery to 2 days. Under the most intense HW, recovery reached 35 days in the Base case but decreased to 1–2 days with Combined scenario and Natural Ventilation-24h. The proposed multidimensional methodology captures complementary resilience dimensions, providing a framework for resilience-oriented retrofit assessment under representative climates and future heatwaves.

title: Elderly thermal sensation: Determination of the optimal measurement method and establishment of a CatBoost-HHO prediction model
The relationships of indoor thermal and luminous parameters with self-reported dry eye symptoms: a quantitative cross-seasonal field study
Large language model agents capture heterogeneous occupant behaviors in building energy simulation of shared office spaces
abstract: Occupant behavior is a major source of uncertainty in building energy simulation, yet existing models struggle to effectively capture the behavioral diversity within shared office spaces. Specifically, traditional probabilistic models fail to characterize individual differences, while large language model agents lack sufficient exploration in multi-occupant social contexts. To bridge this gap, this study couples physics-based building energy simulation with large language model agents to represent heterogeneous occupants with distinct thermal comfort preferences, psychological expectations, and energy-saving intentions. A closed-loop framework links environmental sensing, agent reasoning and control actions in real time. Tested through a four-person shared office scenario, the simulation successfully demonstrates the technical feasibility of this framework, which yields profile-dependent behavioral dynamics. Quantitative analysis reveals a highly concentrated distribution of operational authority, where one dominant occupant executed 62.1% of all control actions, whereas the least active occupant contributed only 1.3%. Within this simulated case, this study observes a sequential propagation chain from individual differences through group interactions and action execution to energy consumption feedback. Furthermore, the proposed framework provides a computational basis for investigating socially mediated occupant behavior in human-centric building operations.

title: The hidden heatwave: Thermal hazards in the New York City subway system
abstract: Underground transit systems (Subway) are susceptible to frequent heat waves, which pose serious health and safety risks to commuters and transit workers. Yet, the patterns and extent of temperature changes within the subway system remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we conducted a study of thermal variability across 112 subway stations in New York City. Temperature and relative humidity were measured at both platform and street levels. Results show that during the summer, 70% of subway stations had platform heat index higher than street level heat index. We also developed a machine learning forecasting model to predict platform-level temperatures. The model achieved strong predictive performance of (R² = 0.85 at platform-level). These findings highlight stations where heat management is most needed and demonstrate the potential for predictive tools to inform targeted interventions that improve the resilience and safety of urban transit systems.

title: Too high to cool? Reference-surface and solar-exposure effects on extensive green roof cooling at two rooftop elevations
abstract: Comparing green-roof temperature advantages between rooftop sites requires separating the behaviour of the vegetated assembly from that of its local reference. This study quantified these components using paired field measurements at two extensive Eco-pillow (ECP) green roofs in central Auckland, New Zealand, approximately 50 m (ENG50) and 18 m (LIB18) above street level. Both roofs contained ECP and stone-ballast/bark-mulch (SBB) assemblies; ENG50 also had an asphalt reference (AST). Surface-level temperatures were monitored at 10-min intervals during December 2024–February 2025. Under high-solar conditions, the ENG50–LIB18 SBB temperature contrast was −2.67°C (95% CI: −3.79 to −1.59°C), whereas the ECP contrast was +1.80°C (95% CI: +1.11 to +2.52°C). Together, the cooler reference and warmer ECP yielded a 4.47°C smaller SBB–ECP temperature difference at ENG50. ECP nevertheless remained 14.15°C cooler than local AST under the same high-solar conditions, demonstrating the reference dependence of the reported temperature advantage. As a supporting sensitivity check, screening for small modelled within-roof ECP–SBB shade-fraction (SF) differences changed the cross-roof contrast from −4.47 to −4.39°C. This check concerns built-obstruction shading, with leaf-canopy radiation outside the model. The observations establish how two distinct surface responses combine in the measured contrast; identifying their physical causes requires further evidence. Reporting both assembly temperatures and their difference supports thermal appraisal against locally relevant roof-cover alternatives on elevated buildings.

title: Soundscape evaluation of urban street canyons: Effects of height-to-width ratio and nature-based interventions
abstract: The present study aimed to investigate the effects of height-to-width ratio (H/W) geometry, nature-based sound interventions, and presentation modality on soundscape perception in urban street canyons within the pleasantness-eventfulness framework. A total of 40 participants were exposed to 69 stimulus cases representing three H/W levels (0.5, 2, and 4), 11 scenarios incorporating trees, flower beds, water features, and the tested birdsong stimulus, and three presentation modalities (visual-only, audio-visual, and audio-only). Pleasantness, eventfulness, and overall impression were assessed via the ISO 12913 framework. Repeated-measures ANOVA revealed that H/W was a significant determinant of pleasantness and overall impression in the visual-only and audio-visual conditions (ηp² = 0.328-0.449) but had no main effect on soundscape evaluation in the audio-only condition. The tested nature-based sound interventions produced differential effects on eventfulness, although the two directions were not equally well supported: the water stimuli consistently reduced eventfulness, an effect that survived both Holm–Bonferroni and false-discovery-rate correction, whereas the birdsong stimulus increased eventfulness only under the more permissive false-discovery-rate correction and most consistently at H/W = 2. Across all modalities, a direct regression confirmed that overall impression was more strongly predicted by pleasantness (standardised β = 0.78, p < .001) than by eventfulness (β = -0.01, p = .944). These findings indicate that H/W geometry’s influence on soundscape evaluation is contingent on the availability of visual information, and that the tested birdsong and water stimuli generate soundscape profiles that are qualitatively distinct – robustly so for the water stimuli, and tentatively for the birdsong stimulus – and that cannot be distinguished by a single valence-based measure alone.

Multi-field coupled optimization of an air-purifying BIPVT system with thermal–UV synergistic disinfection: A CFD–Bayesian optimization approach
abstract: The use of renewable energy to reduce building energy consumption has become a major trend, while indoor bioaerosol control has received increasing attention in the post-pandemic era. Air-purifying building-integrated photovoltaic/thermal (BIPVT) systems can provide power generation, space heating, and air purification without additional energy input, offering a pathway to integrate building energy efficiency with indoor health. In this study, a thermal–UV synergistic inactivation mechanism is introduced to enhance the bioaerosol control capability of such systems. However, the highly non-uniform temperature, UV radiation, and flow fields, together with multi-dimensional structural parameters, make the coordinated optimization of power generation, heating, and air purification challenging. To address this issue, Bayesian optimization is introduced for the first time into BIPVT system optimization through a coupled CFD–Bayesian optimization framework. The results show that: 1. Bayesian optimization rapidly identified high-value regions within the first 20 iterations and increased the optimal scalarized utility to 2.068, representing a 19% improvement. 2. Under equal weighting of heat gain, power generation, and air purification, high-value designs were mainly associated with moderate PV coverage and upper-channel UV lamp placement. 3. Compared with random and uniform sampling, Bayesian optimization achieved 5.1% and 15.6% higher optimal scalarized utilities under comparable sample sizes. 4. Parametric analysis further confirmed its stability and effectiveness under different UV wavelengths, channel depths, and lamp numbers, while increasing UV lamps showed limited marginal benefits beyond two lamps. The results provide insights for controlling indoor airborne disease and offer a new approach for optimizing BIPVT systems.

title: Evaluating outpatient medical-technical layouts in large comprehensive hospitals: A dynamic-static combined framework for patient visit efficiency
Beyond leaf traits: context dependent particulate matter accumulation across outdoor, indoor and active green walls
abstract: Improving air quality in cities is a social challenge related to human health. Nature-based Solutions (NbS) have been shown to effectively remove air pollutants such as particulate matter (PM) from the atmosphere, with the PM removal capacity appearing to be largely dependent on the species morphological traits. However, other factors, such as chemical interactions and atmospheric and microclimatic parameters, can also affect the PM removal efficiency. To test this hypothesis, we compared the PM accumulation in five plant species with different morphological traits (Chlorophytum comosum, Hedera helix, Monstera deliciosa, Nephrolepis exaltata, Tradescantia zebrina) upon their installation in three different green walls (GWs) located outdoor (OGW), indoor (IGW), and in a closed chamber with a forced ventilation (active green wall - AGW). Leaf surfaces were analysed through Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) to characterise their micromorphological features associated with PM accumulation. The deposited PM load was estimated by combining gravimetric and conductimetric approaches, and the PM chemical composition was assessed by Microwave Plasma Atomic Emission Spectroscopy (MP-AES). Statistical differences between species in PM capture were observed. Species exhibited distinct PM accumulation patterns across the green walls, with notable species-specific affinities for certain potentially toxic elements, demonstrating that PM retention is not driven by leaf morphology alone. Among species, Chlorophytum comosum best performed in OGW and IGW while Tradescantia zebrina in AGW. In AGW, the presence of the plants reduced PM concentration by approximately 50% and high humidity enhanced wet deposition and increased fine-particle capture, confirming the relevance of microclimatic factors for air-purification.

title: Seasonal reversal and nonlinear thresholds: Interactive mechanisms of blue-green space, urban morphology, and human activities on urban thermal environments

A multi-domain scoring framework for solar accessibility at the neighborhood scale
abstract: The concept of solar neighborhoods as communities that prioritize sunlight for energy production and thermal and visual comfort has emerged as a solution toward energy and emission targets, while also contributing to more livable urban environment. Building on this premise, the present study introduces a novel multi-domain scoring framework to evaluate solar accessibility at the neighborhood scale and demonstrates practical examples of its applications. The framework converts early-stage solar metrics into 12 performance indicators across the often-disconnected urban spatial domains of outdoor, envelope, and indoor. A set of acceptability thresholds, derived either through site-specific statistical analyses or from established literature, are applied to develop a comparable, six-classes scoring framework. A weighting mechanism is also developed to allow flexibility according to different urban planning priorities and objectives. The framework was applied on 44 neighborhoods in the city of Trondheim (Norway). Results indicate generally favorable solar conditions, especially for the indoor domain. The envelope domain presents the greatest variability, while the outdoor domain seldom exceeds moderate performance levels. Further analyses showed that density indicators (i.e., building coverage and envelope-to-plot ratio) explain nearly 80% of the observed variation in solar accessibility across neighborhoods. The proposed framework has the potential to support municipalities and urban stakeholders as a decision-making tool to shape comfort- and energy-related policies and strategies. Potential applications include: (i) evaluating the impact of future or alternative urban design scenarios on solar accessibility, (ii) supporting local governance in planning processes, and (iii) estimating energy production potential at both neighborhood and city scale.

title: Pathway-specific CFD investigation of ventilation, thermal stratification, and local discomfort in a full-scale smart house
abstract: Occupant-controlled ventilation can influence retrofit performance by altering airflow pathways, heat distribution, vertical stratification, and local thermal comfort. This study investigates these effects using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) in the University of Huddersfield Smart House, an IoT-monitored residential research facility. A three-dimensional model developed in Autodesk Revit 2026 was simplified for CFD analysis and evaluated against monitored temperatures under a representative winter condition. A deterministic 2⁴ full-factorial design comprising sixteen steady-state scenarios examined the combined effects of window state, internal-door position, radiator operation, and outdoor relative humidity (70–80%). Temperature, air velocity, relative humidity, predicted mean vote (PMV), predicted percentage dissatisfied (PPD), vertical temperature difference, and dimensionless response indicators were evaluated using domain-averaged outputs and occupant-relevant sampling locations. Radiator operation and window state were the dominant thermal drivers. Radiator activation increased mean indoor temperature by 12.5°C, whereas window opening reduced it by 4.4°C; outdoor relative humidity had only a minor effect. Sealed heated scenarios provided the most favourable mean conditions, with temperatures near 24.6°C, PMV of approximately −0.33, and PPD near 7%, although vertical stratification remained pronounced. Door-mediated ventilation maintained temperatures near 22.1°C with PPD around 28%, whereas window opening and combined window–door through-flow reduced temperatures to 16–17°C and increased PPD to 90–95%. All unheated scenarios were thermally unacceptable. The results demonstrate that lower heating-demand indicators under highly ventilated conditions can reflect underheating rather than energy savings, providing pathway-specific guidance for retrofit ventilation and comfort assessment.

title: Evaluating the potential to achieve life cycle net-zero emissions in an educational building under northern and southern European conditions using multi-objective optimisation
abstract: In line with the building stock decarbonisation targets set by the European Union, this study examines the feasibility of achieving life cycle net-zero emissions (LCNZE) in a public educational building in Sweden and Spain, focusing on a typology remaining underrepresented in the life cycle assessment literature. A multi-objective optimisation (MOO) approach based on the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II, calibrated and validated against measured data, was applied to investigate this feasibility, followed by uncertainty analyses considering uncertainties related to climate change and ongoing emission reduction efforts in the materials and energy sectors. MOO was adopted primarily for its ability to address trade-offs among competing objectives, particularly between embodied and operational emissions, and to identify optimal solutions capable of achieving life cycle net-zero emissions. The findings indicate that, although LCNZE performance remained unattainable for the Swedish case, the optimisation approach enabled offsetting approximately 45% of total life cycle emissions under typical climatic conditions. In contrast, the Spanish case not only achieved LCNZE performance but also net-negative emissions, primarily due to lower operational energy demand, higher renewable energy generation, and a more carbon intensive energy system, which together enabled greater carbon offsets than in Sweden. Similar outcomes were obtained under climate change and emission reduction scenarios for the materials and energy sectors, with the Swedish case remaining unable to achieve LCNZE performance. Nevertheless, up to 82% of life cycle emissions could be reduced for the Swedish case under a scenario with a 60% reduction in material embodied emissions and no change in the carbon intensity of the energy sector. These findings underscore the critical role of the materials sector and reductions in embodied emissions in countries with already low-carbon energy systems, such as Sweden.

Evaluation of individual-level uncompensable heat stress in dynamic outdoor environments
abstract: Extreme heat is a growing public health concern that contributes to heat exhaustion, heat stroke, and other heat-related illnesses. Understanding the physiological limits of human thermoregulation under extreme conditions is therefore essential. In this study, we evaluate heat-health impacts at the individual level in outdoor conditions. This is achieved using high-resolution environmental and physiological data collected from participants exposed to real-world thermal variability. We examine how steady-state physiological models (e.g., the HEAT-Lim model) perform under transient outdoor conditions and assess the uncertainty introduced by simplified assumptions. Results show that applying constant inputs underestimates both the frequency and magnitude of uncompensable heat stress. Incorporating time-varying environmental inputs, particularly mean radiant temperature and wind speed, shifts compensability thresholds and reveals the onset of heat storage at substantially lower air temperatures than predicted by simplified models. Sensitivity analysis indicates that radiative load, airflow, and individual physical characteristics strongly influence heat storage and heat tolerance, whereas variability in skin temperature has a comparatively limited effect. Refining key parameters improves the representation of individual heat strain and leads to revised liveability and survivability thresholds. An unsteady exergy-based analysis further reveals rapid fluctuations in thermodynamic strain during sun–shade transitions, highlighting the limitations of steady-state approaches in capturing short-term physiological stress. These findings demonstrate that individual heat stress is governed by dynamic environmental forcing, physiological variability, and transient thermodynamic processes. The proposed framework advances personalised heat-health assessment and supports wearable monitoring systems, adaptive warning strategies, and climate-resilient urban design to protect human health in a warming world.

Localised cooling for spatial alliesthesia: Is more better?
abstract: Localised thermal stimulation is widely used in personal comfort systems and offers a flexible and energy-efficient approach to improving occupants’ thermal comfort and pleasure. This study examined whether combining multiple localised cooling produces additive effects on thermal pleasure. A total of 27 participants (14 female, 13 male) completed five single- and dual-site cooling configurations at a segmentally equivalent homogeneous temperature of 24°C in a 30°C ambient condition, while a subset of 12 participants (6 female, 6 male) also completed the same configurations at 21°C and 27°C. Thermal pleasure, thermal sensation, and skin temperature were monitored during exposure. Thermal pleasure did not differ significantly between configurations or intensities at the end of the 15-minute cooling session. Cluster analysis identified distinct thermal pleasure response profiles. During exposures, larger increases in thermal pleasure were generally accompanied by faster declines in mean skin temperature, while the group exhibiting the largest increases in thermal pleasure tended to maintain higher skin temperatures at unstimulated proximal sites throughout the cooling period. These findings suggest that the magnitude of thermal pleasure resulting from localised cooling is influenced not only by the local thermal effects at the stimulated site but also by its broader impact on whole-body thermal state. This is consistent with the alliesthesia framework of thermal perception. Findings from this study offer an explanation for why combining multiple localised stimuli or applying more intense stimulation does not necessarily elicit higher thermal pleasure.

title: Behavior-resolved bioaerosol exposure modeling reveals scale-dependent occupational risk in pediatric wards
Ten questions concerning the integration of edge data centers in buildings
abstract: This ten-question paper examines the integration of edge data centers into buildings, considering both design and operational aspects. It provides a structured overview of techno-economic, environmental, and operational aspects of deploying edge data centers within the built environment. The paper begins by clarifying definitions, sizing, and operational characteristics of edge data centers, along with the key drivers for their adoption, including latency, data security, and resilience. Subsequent questions examine cooling technologies suitable for building integration, comparing their performance, reliability, and implications for waste heat recovery and utilization. Such analysis considers temperature levels, temporal load matching, and synergies with building energy demands and local thermal conversion and storage technologies. Environmental performance is assessed using key performance indicators that extend beyond energy efficiency to include carbon impacts and system-level sustainability considerations. A central contribution of the paper is to address how edge data centers can be incorporated into building energy system planning, accounting for multi-vector interactions across electricity, heat, and renewable energy sources. The roles of advanced energy system modeling, optimization methods, energy management systems, and digital twins are critically reviewed, highlighting their current capabilities and limitations. Control strategies are discussed in terms of operational priorities between building services and data center requirements. Design guidelines and practical insights derived from pilot implementation provide empirical grounding and actionable recommendations. Finally, the paper explores scalability, replicability, and associated business models, identifying pathways to wider deployment of low-carbon, efficient, and resilient building energy systems.

A virtual reality study on the influence of indoor visual quality on thermal comfort perception
abstract: Improving thermal comfort while reducing building energy demand represents a key challenge in the transition towards more sustainable and occupant-centred buildings. Although previous research demonstrated that individual visual stimuli influence thermal perception, the effect of the overall visual quality of an indoor environment remains poorly understood. This study investigates the influence of indoor visual quality on thermal comfort perception using an immersive Virtual Reality experimental approach. Thirty participants were exposed to three distinct representations of the same office environment (named Base, Cozy, Industrial) while seated inside a controlled environmental chamber maintained at 17°C and 50% relative humidity. Subjective thermal responses, environmental conditions and physiological parameters were recorded throughout the experiments. Results showed that participants exposed to the Cozy scenario reported significantly higher Global Comfort Vote (p=0.022) and warmer Thermal Sensation Vote (p=0.026) compared to Base and Industrial environments, despite identical physical conditions and no significant differences in skin temperature or heart rate. Thermal sensation progressively increased throughout the exposure period only in the Cozy scenario, suggesting that visual indoor quality influence may strengthen over time. Qualitative analysis further revealed that warm colours, natural materials, domestic features, and perceptions of inhabitation were frequently associated with enhanced comfort. These findings provide experimental evidence that, in the tested indoor environment, indoor visual quality can influence thermal comfort perception independently of the physical thermal conditions, supporting a broader understanding of thermal comfort as a multisensory phenomenon and highlighting the potential for integrating architectural and interior design strategies to support energy reduction in buildings.

title: Wind tunnel experimental study on wake–rotor aerodynamic coupling: Impact of building geometry on UAV flight stability
A digital twin-enabled adaptive optimization framework for balancing holistic comfort and energy efficiency in underground spaces
Effects of ventilation and thermal conditions on the formation and propagation of exhaled vortex rings
Optical–thermal synergistic enhancement of a bifacial photovoltaic louver air-cavity wall system: An outdoor experimental study
Geometrical levels of detail for indoor daylight simulation: An aperture-aware definition
abstract: This study proposes a formalised framework for defining indoor Geometrical Level of Detail (GLoD) for daylight applications, based on a solid angle descriptor called Area-Weighted Solid Angle (AWSA). Unlike previous approaches that rely on object size or semantics, the proposed method prioritises the inclusion of non-permanent indoor objects based on their obstruction to window surfaces. This allows for a more relevant abstraction and classification of indoor geometry for daylight simulations. Two use case rooms with single- and multi-sided window configurations were analysed under different sky conditions using Climate-Based Daylight Modelling (CBDM) and evaluated through Total Annual Illumination (TAI) on sensor grids placed either on a horizontal working plane or at multiple six cubic directions. Results show that annual illumination was over-predicted when using the simplest GLoD level (GLoD0), compared to the most complete (GLoD3), up to a 41 % at the working plane and up to 77 % at head positions. Sky conditions influenced absolute TAI values but did not markedly change the relative influence of GLoD on either directional (cubic) or non-directional (work-plane) evaluations.

title: How mountainous environmental settings reshape young adults' route perception: a multimodal on-site experiment in Chongqing, China
Associations of congruence and exposure sequence with indoor environmental quality perception and heart rate variability in an immersive residential experiment
abstract: Immersive experiments allow controlled manipulation of indoor environmental features while preserving a realistic sense of space; however, responses obtained across repeated exposures may also vary with participant context and progression through the experimental sequence. This study examined whether subjective environmental perceptions and heart rate variability (HRV) were associated with residential-context similarity, presentation position across repeated exposures, and directional changes in living-room and window size between consecutive scenes. Thirty-three adults completed four immersive residential sessions and were classified as Match (n = 25) or Mismatch (n = 8) based on whether the overall configuration of their home living room broadly matched the common simulated layout. Generalized estimating equations addressed residential context, presentation position, and directional transitions; additional analyses examined pre-exposure baselines, baseline-referenced changes, and exploratory principal component analysis. The residential-context group was not associated with scene-related subjective or physiological responses, although the Mismatch group showed higher resting lnRMSSD and lnSDNN before scene exposure. Primary analysis linked presentation position to lnRMSSD after correction, but not subjective perceptions; sensitivity analyses identified variation in pre-exposure lnLF/HF and baseline-referenced ΔlnRMSSD and ΔlnLF/HF. An HRV-dominant principal component also varied across presentation positions, whereas subjective environmental perceptions and the perception-dominant component did not. Directional changes in living-room and window size showed no associations that remained significant after multiplicity correction. These findings indicate that physiological responses may vary systematically across repeated immersive exposures even when concurrent subjective environmental perceptions do not. Presentation position should therefore be considered explicitly in the design and analysis of repeated immersive building-environment experiments.

title: Influence of hill-like topography on wind flow characteristics in downstream urban building arrays
UAV-Assisted quantitative infrared thermography procedure for thermal measurements in building inspections
abstract: The increasing adoption of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) equipped with infrared thermography (IRT) sensors offers new opportunities for rapid and non-invasive assessment of building envelopes. However, the transition from qualitative thermal anomaly detection to reliable quantitative measurements remains limited by the lack of standardized procedures for controlling acquisition conditions, radiometric corrections, and validation strategies. This study addresses this gap by developing and experimentally validating a UAV-assisted quantitative IRT procedure for acquiring external apparent surface temperature data on existing buildings under controlled field conditions. The proposed method combines preliminary terrestrial IRT surveys, environmental monitoring, contact surface-temperature measurements, repeated UAV-based thermal acquisitions for estimating reflected apparent temperature, and controlled post-processing based on documented spectral emissivity, target distance, relative humidity, and region of interest (ROI) definition. The methodology was experimentally evaluated through six case studies in Milan (Italy), using terrestrial IRT measurements as reference data and comparative measurements acquired with two different thermal imaging cameras mounted on UAVs, together with contact temperature sensors. The results show that UAV-derived apparent surface temperature values can be considered reliable only when a tightly controlled measurement workflow is adopted. Target distance, gain mode, reflected apparent temperature estimation, ROI geometry, and software averaging method significantly affect the resulting temperature values. The High Gain mode produced acceptable or borderline deviations in several short-distance acquisitions, whereas the Low Gain mode generated unacceptable deviations for the tested range of surface temperatures of the building envelope. The study transferability the acquisition, correction, and validation steps required to improve the reproducibility and transferability of UAV-based IRT in apparent surface temperature measurements for quantitative building-diagnostics applications.

title: AURA: Automated universal floor plan replication for airflow and thermal analysis
The link between aerosol dispersion, infection risk and air filtration
abstract: Portable HEPA filters are widely used to reduce airborne disease transmission in indoor environments. However, their performance is commonly evaluated using aerosol decay rates rather than infection risk. This study applies a radius-resolved infection risk framework that combines measured aerosol concentrations with CFD simulations to quantify infection risk and maximum occupancy time in classrooms with one or three portable HEPA filters, using a stale-air classroom as the baseline. An Aerosol Removal Model (ARM) is also developed to evaluate filtration performance. For the specific HEPA design and intake–discharge arrangements tested, the single-HEPA arrangement performed worse than the stale-air case under unfavourable airflow conditions because filter-induced circulation promoted infectious-aerosol dispersion. In contrast, the three-HEPA configuration substantially reduced exposure, although its effectiveness remained sensitive to filter placement and airflow alignment. The ARM predicted a removal time of approximately 50 min for the three-HEPA configuration, compared with about 5 hours for the single-HEPA configuration. The three-HEPA system approximately doubled the maximum occupancy relative to the stale-air case, whereas activating the tested single-HEPA arrangement after occupancy resulted in all occupants exceeding the infection threshold within approximately 2 min. These findings support operating HEPA filtration before classroom occupancy. The results further reveal a non-linear relationship between clean air delivery rate (CADR), airflow-induced mixing, and infection risk, demonstrating that filtration effectiveness depends not only on CADR but also on the airflow patterns induced by filter placement and orientation. The proposed framework provides a practical tool for optimising the design and operation of portable HEPA filtration systems.

title: Seamless daily 10 m urban land surface temperature via a cascading multi-scale satellite fusion framework: Development and multi-city validation
Indoor and outdoor thermal comfort impacts of dual-band electrochromic glazing: A multi-climate radiative evaluation
abstract: Electrochromic (EC) glazing enables adaptive solar control, yet no study has jointly evaluated the indoor and outdoor thermal comfort performance of spectrally selective dual-band EC (DB-EC) devices. This work addresses that gap through coupled simulations of a perimeter office across five European climates and two façade orientations, informed by experimentally characterised, state-dependent optical properties of a DB-EC prototype. Indoor comfort is characterised at multiple distances from the window via operative temperature Discomfort Degree Hours, radiant asymmetry exceedances, and a Predicted Mean Vote-based discomfort score; outdoor pedestrian comfort is quantified through longwave mean radiant temperature and Universal Thermal Climate Index profiles along a near-façade transect. DB-EC and single-band EC, both under rule-based control, are benchmarked against three static reference glazings. Both EC technologies substantially reduce perimeter overheating and radiant asymmetry relative to high-transmittance and moderately selective static references, while avoiding the cold-discomfort penalty that strongly selective static glazing incurs in heating-dominated climates. Under the same control logic the two electrochromic options achieve very similar thermal comfort, despite the higher spectral selectivity and the demonstrated energy and daylight advantages of the dual-band device. The associated rise in external surface temperature produces only a negligible outdoor thermal penalty, confirming that absorptive spectral control markedly improves indoor comfort without compromising pedestrian conditions.

title: Size-resolved aerosol transport and exposure risk in university dormitories driven by Stokes number topology and source-flow coupling
Children’s thermal sensation and comfort in a severe cold region primary school: Seasonal characteristics, body weight effects, and local sensitivity
A unified framework for global indoor air quality: transitioning from guidelines to actionable open regulatory standards
Air purifier performance in an occupied office: Field CADR and effectiveness from a reconstructed device-off condition
abstract: Air-purifier performance in an occupied building is hard to assess because the indoor concentration without the device cannot be observed under the same conditions. This study reconstructs that device-off condition from long-term field measurements in an occupied office. Two sequentially coupled physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), constrained by the CO 2 and PM 2.5 mass balances, estimate the time-varying air change rate, penetration factor and removal rate, and the removal rate is re-evaluated at each instant with the air-purifier input switched off. The difference between the two removal rates gives field CADR, and the modelled concentrations with the device on and off give steady-state and dynamic effectiveness. Field CADR is an equivalent removal rate specific to this room and device, not a chamber CADR. With the window and door closed, the median field CADR was 175 m 3 /h and the steady-state effectiveness was 0.79. With the window, the door or both open they fell to 50–66 m 3 /h and 0.09–0.31; the open-condition values are less precise, whereas the closed-open difference was reproduced in synthetic-data tests within the same model class. A conventional before/after comparison on the same record agreed with the reconstruction in the aggregate under the closed condition but not event by event, returned negative values under full opening, and yielded 59 estimates against 3613 from the proposed field CADR estimation. Its generality beyond one office remains to be established.

Sensitivity Analysis of CO₂ Mass Balance Equations: Implications for Ventilation and Space Conditioning
abstract: Steady-state CO 2 mass balance methods are widely used, both a posteriori (to derive classroom ventilation rates from timeseries CO 2 measurements) and a priori (to maintain design airflow rates, based on target indoor CO 2 concentrations). However, these methods rely on uncertain input parameters, including: occupancy, occupant CO 2 emission rates, indoor and outdoor CO 2 concentrations, and ventilation effectiveness. These uncertainties affect both the interpretation of monitored CO 2 data and the ventilation rates required to achieve indoor CO 2 targets. In addition, they have practical implications for airborne infection risk control, and space conditioning energy demand. This study analyses these effects for a classroom by combining a local sensitivity analysis, a Monte Carlo-based global sensitivity analysis, and a surrogate-model analysis of the heating demand implications of ventilation design uncertainties. The results show that steady-state ventilation rate estimates are most sensitive to ventilation effectiveness, followed by occupant CO 2 emission assumptions and room occupancy. Under identical indoor CO 2 concentration conditions, plausible variations in occupant CO 2 emission rates resulted in ventilation rate differences of up to 100 %, highlighting the limitations of using standardised fixed-rate emission assumptions for educational buildings with predominantly non-adult occupants. Reduced ventilation effectiveness could further increase the required ventilation rate by up to 200 % and, consequently, the specific heating demand by approximately 180 %. The findings show that CO 2 targets should not be interpreted as having fixed energy consequences. Rather, their implications depend strongly on the required ventilation rate, the ventilation system effectiveness and the classroom occupancy and use.

title: Multi-Year Placebo-Controlled Evaluation of an Integrative Lighting Design on Sleep, Behaviour, and Mental Health in Nursing Home Residents with Dementia
Supporting Building Thermal Resilience in Early Design Stages: A Framework Integrating Machine Learning and Large Language Models
Residential satisfaction in living spaces: An analysis of design and physical indoor environmental qualities based on the Kano model
abstract: The satisfaction with one’s residential spaces is affected by a multitude of factors related to Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ). When designing human centric residential buildings with reduced space sizes, it is important to understand the shape of the relationship between individual factors and the satisfaction. The objective of this study was such evaluation based on the Kano model of user satisfaction, which is suitable for such analysis. Data from a living lab study with N=32 participants and 508 data points was analyzed to examine the shape of the relationship between the satisfaction with eight IEQs and overall satisfaction with different residential spaces. The IEQs comprise flexibility, room size, thermal, air quality, acoustic, and visual perception, greenery, and openness to the outdoors. Exploratory, the Kano analysis enabled to examine which IEQs function as basic factors, performance factors, bonus factors, or indifferent factors. Flexibility, room size, and visual perception were classified as performance factors. Thermal and air quality perception as well as greenery and openness to the outdoors constituted the basic factors. Acoustic perception was classified as an indifferent factor. The results highlight the relevance of satisfaction with the different aspects of IEQ in relation to overall space satisfaction. Furthermore, the analysis provides practical guidance regarding individuals IEQs contribution to individuals satisfaction within smaller living spaces. Such guidance can indirectly foster the acceptance of more resource-efficient housing typologies.

title: Global Multiscale Analysis of Urban Morphology’s Influence on Surface Urban Heat Islands: A New Integrated Approach
A dynamic source term method for modeling traffic flow and pollutant dispersion in a street canyon: Comparison of URANS, SAS and LES
abstract: Traffic flows play a significant role in influencing airflow and pollutant dispersion in street canyons. The quasi-steady (QS) method is commonly used in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to model the traffic flows in street canyons. However, the QS method treats traffic flows as a whole and cannot account for the effects of individual vehicles. Therefore, this study proposes a dynamic source term (DST) method, which represents each vehicle as an individual moving source term. First, the DST method is coupled with unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (URANS), scale-adaptive simulation (SAS) and large eddy simulation (LES), and the velocity and concentration results are validated against wind tunnel (WT) data, showing satisfactory agreement. Next, the detailed mean and instantaneous velocity and concentration fields obtained from URANS, SAS, and LES are systematically compared, and the DST results from LES are compared with those of the QS method. The results show that the SAS performs comparably to LES, while URANS cannot adequately resolve turbulent instantaneous flow and concentration fields. Across all selected planes, the overall relative differences in surface-averaged normalized mean concentration for SAS vs. LES and URANS vs. LES are 9.6% and 17.1%, respectively. Compared with QS, DST better reproduces the mean streamwise velocity measured in the WT at z/H = 0.25 and 0.50, captures individual vehicle effects, and allows vehicle-specific source strengths. However, at the measurement positions away from the vehicles, the two methods give similar results for the mean lateral velocity, the turbulence quantities and the mean concentration, so DST shows no clear benefit in these locations. The present study provides new insights into the traffic flow modeling in street canyons and the accuracy of using URANS, SAS, and LES coupled with the DST method.

title: A Study of the Effects of Artificial Skylight on Occupant Mood and Visual Task Performance in Windowless Environments
Typology-preserving low-carbon optimization of campus functional zones using heterogeneous surrogate models
Infrared Thermography-based Personalized Thermal Comfort Evaluation in Radiation Environments
Real-Building Implementation of Human-in-the-Loop Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Personalized HVAC Control in a Multi-FCU Open Office
Morphology-based classification and error-controlled reduction of urban weather files with Torino as a case study
abstract: Urban morphology creates intra-urban thermal variability that a single airport EnergyPlus Weather (EPW) file cannot represent. This study develops a reproducible GIS-to-Urban Weather Generator (UWG) framework for Torino, Italy, separating morphological classification from weather-product reduction. A preliminary building-seeded cell method was audited before adopting 100 m assignment cells characterised through overlapping 500 × 500 m neighbourhood supports. Support-size (250–1000 m) and 50 m grid-shift sensitivities were tested. Building fraction, area-weighted height, facade-to-site ratio, tree cover, and grass cover were extracted for 12,997 locations; 10,593 quality-screened supports were classified using robust scaling and CLARA-style k-medoids. Seven morphology classes balanced interpretability and spatial coherence, although four ranked best statistically, and classification robustness was moderate. Under a common UWG template, four representative EPWs were retained by curve inspection and minimax selection, with a 0.10°C maximum-error screen and a diminishing-return criterion. Maximum medoid hourly dry-bulb RMSE was 0.06°C with the delivered one-decimal EPWs and 0.04°C at diagnostic three-decimal serialisation. Across 105 stratified non-medoid supports, weighted mean and 95th-percentile RMSE were 0.05 and 0.10°C, but a 1.33°C industrial-tail error required a conservative post hoc restriction, not a validated applicability boundary. Synchronised processed 2022 station comparisons improved annual RMSE relative to Caselle only at Consolata. Humidity limitations preclude interpreting temperature fidelity as complete EPW validation. The atlas links coordinates to morphology classes, UWG configurations, and candidate EPWs. The restricted library distinguishes simulator-conditional reduction fidelity from observational accuracy.

title: Applicability of Facial Expression Portrait for Soundscape Assessment Across Multiple Contexts in Urban Open Spaces
Legionella Risk Management in Building Water Systems: Current Perspectives from Industry Practitioners
abstract: Building water systems are internationally recognised reservoirs for opportunistic premise plumbing pathogens, including Legionella, the causative agent of Legionnaires’ disease. Inadequate design, operation and maintenance can promote Legionella proliferation and expose building occupants to potentially fatal infection. Effective management is therefore critical; however, there is limited international evidence regarding how guidelines for controlling Legionella risk are implemented in practice. Despite extensive Australian guidance, little is known about the practical management of Legionella risk in building water systems. This study explored current practices among hydraulic engineers, facility managers, plumbers, and water retreatment consultants. An online survey with follow-up interviews was conducted and the responses were then compared with existing guidelines and historical case studies published in the literature. Key findings indicated that current practice is predominantly risk-focused, with monitoring, system disinfection, routine maintenance, and targeted engineering modifications forming the core control measures. Case studies demonstrated substantial variability in how practitioners select and apply interventions, reflecting the complexity and diversity of building water systems. Insufficient maintenance and poor system design emerged as the leading contributors to Legionella proliferation, while control measures failed primarily due to incorrect or inappropriate selection. Budget constraints and lack of knowledge were identified as the major barriers to implementing effective and sustained control strategies. These findings are of international relevance, highlighting the need for control measures underpinned by risk assessment and comprehensive system monitoring and providing an evidence base to strengthen guidelines for effective Legionella management in building water systems globally.

title: Performance evaluation of a positive-pressure ventilation system in a radiation protection shelter: Field experiment and computational fluid dynamics analysis
abstract: Positive-pressure ventilation systems are installed in radiation-protection facilities in Japan to reduce internal exposure during nuclear emergencies. This study evaluated pressure maintenance and modelled air renewal at the Omaezaki City Hall West Building, located 1.9 km from Hamaoka Nuclear Power Station. Indoor–outdoor differential pressure was recorded at ten channels under nine operating conditions comprising sealed, airlock, and controlled opening configurations. Steady-state computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations employed approximately 1.9 × 10 8 cells and measured airflow boundary conditions for the C1, C7, and C8 conditions. Under the sealed condition, the differential pressure exceeded 20 Pa at all measurement locations. Airlock operations retained pressure above this criterion. Equal-area window openings on different floors produced distinct spatial responses: the three continuously monitored third-floor locations lost pressure under C7, whereas all nine monitored locations outside the pressurization-unit room fell below 20 Pa under C8. The CFD simulations suggested redistribution of air renewal, with improvement near some openings and reductions in remote spaces. Additional C1 simulations showed that heat loads and mesh resolution exerted greater influence on local ventilation-related outputs than on pressure. The pressure comparison was calibration-dependent, and age-derived per-person indices remained conditional on assumed room volumes and occupancies and did not constitute measurements of outdoor-air delivery. These findings support assessing pressure maintenance and room ventilation separately under the measured operating conditions.

title: Prediction-Enhanced Composite Control for Pressure-Gradient Stability in Multi-Zone Pharmaceutical Cleanrooms: Engineering Validation
Green Design Studio: A Modular Integration Layer for Cross-Domain Building Performance Simulation
abstract: Building performance simulation (BPS) remains underutilized in architectural practice due to three structural barriers: an ontological gap between architectural design representations and simulation engine inputs, redundant model specification across domains, and rigid platform architectures that resist modular extension. This paper presents Green Design Studio (GDS), a cross-domain BPS platform that mitigates these barriers through a two-dimensional modular architecture. Vertically, the platform separates the architect-facing interface, domain-specific translation pipelines, and simulation engine execution into independent layers. The interface layer comprises the Hub, which organizes simulation inputs into six task modules (Space, Enclosure, Service, HVAC, Site, and Advanced) corresponding to progressive design information, and the Refiner, which enables element-level property modification without whole-model authoring. Horizontally, the workflow progresses from a geometric skeleton through staged enrichment to simulation-ready model generation. A Custom Property Database separates architectural design decisions from detailed engineering specifications, exposing modular selections through the user-interface while preserving database-level customizability. The translation pipelines generate EnergyPlus-IDF files for energy simulation and CONTAM-PRJ files for multizone contaminant transport, ensuring geometric and spatial consistency across domains. Additional engines can be incorporated by adding new translation pipelines. The platform is validated against a whole-year end-use energy consumption data for a two-story dormitory with eight apartment units in Syracuse, yielding a monthly Coefficient of Variation of the Root Mean Square Error (CV-RMSE) of 9.2% and a Normalized Mean Bias Error (NMBE) of 3.5%, well within ASHRAE Guideline 14 calibration thresholds. GDS contributes a replicable architecture for extensible, multi-domain, designer-facing building performance simulation.

title: Subjective mental fatigue during prolonged cognitive work under different indoor air temperatures: A whole-day chamber study
Predicting Pedestrian Movement with Computer Vision and Machine Learning: Integrating Urban Visual Environment and Thermal Comfort in a Tropical City
Students’ responses to lighting CCT and wall color: A cross-cultural immersive virtual reality study
Multisensory effects of office soundscape and lighting environments on cognitive workload and attentional performance: A virtual reality-based multimodal study
WBGT Assessment in Transitional Urban Spaces Using a Radiation-Resolved Framework Extended from Indoor to Outdoor Conditions
abstract: Outdoor heat stress assessment in transitional urban spaces depends on spatially varying shortwave and longwave radiation, particularly under partial shading. This study extends a framework linking radiation inputs to WBGT, previously developed for indoor solar exposure, to an outdoor transitional corridor between two buildings in Milan. Hourly shortwave irradiance incident on a discretized human manikin was calculated using a geometry-resolved model accounting for direct, diffuse, transmitted, and reflected components. Time-varying exterior surface temperatures from a building energy simulation determined longwave mean radiant temperature. The shortwave and longwave components were combined through a shortwave adjustment and propagated through a tailored WBGT calculation against activity-dependent reference limits. Sensitivity was evaluated across six canopy configurations, six air speeds, three ground surfaces, and dry-bulb temperature increments of +2, +4, and +6°C. At the central position and 0.5 m/s, the share of working-hour records with no limit exceeded rose from 69.9% (no canopy) to 92.0% (opaque canopy), while the share with all limits exceeded fell from 8.4% to zero. Increasing air speed reduced WBGT exceedance most under the no-canopy condition, with a smaller effect beneath the opaque canopy. Ground-surface differences were concentrated under exposed conditions. A 90%-transmittance canopy changed exceedance little because longwave emission offset reduced shortwave exposure. Prescribed warming shifted WBGT distributions upward, while the 50%-transmittance canopy lowered exceedance at every warming level. The framework provides a common radiation-resolved screening basis linking this outdoor assessment to the previous indoor framework, without implying equivalent subjective comfort in both environments pending field validation.
